instruction: Tell me a myth about "Sif".
output: Sif's mythology is short in line-count and enormous in consequence: one act of malice against her sets the forges of the dwarfs to work, and the gods' six greatest treasures come out of the fire. Snorri tells the hair-myth whole; the Poetic Edda gives her two smaller scenes — a cup of mead poured for Loki, and a taunt flung at Þórr across the water — and Gylfaginning names her son. Beyond that the corpus is silent, and the silence is data: the tradition kept her at the centre of Þórr's household and gave her no wars of her own. [Skáldskaparmál] The Shearing of the Golden Hair: Loki Laufeyjarson, Snorri begins, did this for mischief: he cut off all Sif's hair. When Þórr came home and learned it, he seized Loki and would have broken every bone in him, had Loki not sworn to go to the svartálfar and have them make for Sif a head of hair from gold — hair that would grow like other hair. So Loki went to the dwarfs called the sons of Ívaldi, and they made the hair, and it grew to her head the moment it was set there, as if it were her own. The episode is told in a handful of sentences, but its logic is exact: the injury is domestic, the redress is craft, and the restitution exceeds the loss. Sif does not speak in her own myth — the shearing, the oath, and the making all happen around her — and the tradition leaves her golden hair standing where nature left the first. [Skáldskaparmál] The Wager That Forged Mjölnir: The sons of Ívaldi did not stop at the hair: in the same commission they made Gungnir, the spear that never misses, for [[odinn|Óðinn]], and Skíðblaðnir, the best of ships, for [[freyr|Freyr]]. Then Loki wagered his own head with the dwarf Brokkr that Brokkr's brother Sindri could not make three treasures as good. In the forge Sindri laid gold, a boar's hide, and iron in the fire in turn, while Loki, in fly-shape, stung the bellows-worker — and out came Draupnir the dripping ring, Gullinbursti the golden-bristled boar, and Mjölnir, the hammer whose handle came short only because the fly stung Brokkr's eyelid at the last draw. The Æsir judged Mjölnir the best of all the treasures, because with it the gods have their surest defence against the rime-giants. Loki saved his head on a quibble — his neck was not in the wager — and had his lips sewn up for the pleasure of it. Count the consequence of one shorn head of hair: the spear of Óðinn, the ship of Freyr, the ring, the boar, and the hammer of [[thor|Þórr]] all exist because Sif lost her hair. [Lokasenna 53–54] The Crystal Cup: In Ægir's hall, as Loki works down the company with slander and no one escapes — not the serving-woman Fimafengr, not the gods' wives — Sif alone rises and pours him mead in a crystal cup, and speaks the flyting's one courteous stanza: 'Hail to thee, Loki, and take the crystal cup, full of ancient mead; so may you say that I alone, among the Æsir's kin, am without blame.' It is a bid for exemption, gracefully made, by the one person in the hall who tries hospitality instead of abuse. Loki's answer is the flyting's coldest stroke: he grants she would be blameless indeed, wary and shy of men, were it not that he knows one who lay with her and drew the mighty Þórr's wife from home — 'and that was I, wretched one.' Whether the charge is truth or the poem's purest malice the text does not say; the Poetic Edda offers the accusation and no verdict, and Sif speaks no second stanza. [Hárbarðsljóð 48] The Taunt on the Shore: In Hárbarðsljóð, Óðinn in ferryman's disguise keeps Þórr waiting on the wrong side of the sound, and among the gibes he flings across the water is one aimed at the home Þórr cannot get back to: 'Sif has a lover at home; him you will want to meet.' The poem gives the charge no support and no sequel — it is one dart in a long volley, meant to sting a husband detained abroad, and it leans on the same rumour Lokasenna spent a stanza on. Between the two poems the scholarly tradition has made what little can honestly be made: the eddic poets twice insinuate and never narrate, and no surviving myth shows Sif unfaithful. The taunts are evidence about the poets' taste for needling Þórr, not about the goddess. [Gylfaginning 32] Ullr, Sif's Son: In Snorri's catalogue of the Æsir comes the genealogy that opens the one door in Sif's story: '[[ullr|Ullr]] is the name of a son of Sif and a stepson of Þórr. He is such a good archer and so fast on skis that no one can compete with him; he is also fair of face and has a warrior's skill.' Stepson — the word is the whole of it. Sif had a child before the thunder-god, by a father no source names, and the speculation that has filled the gap since (a frost-god, an older husband of the earth) is speculation, not attestation. Snorri's kennings keep the household straight thereafter: Þórr is 'husband of Sif, stepfather of Ullr, father of [[modi|Móði]] and [[magni|Magni]] and Þrúðr' — Magni by the giantess Járnsaxa, Þrúðr counted as Sif's daughter in the reference tradition. The goddess whose name means kinship-by-marriage presides, appropriately, over the Edda's most blended household.

instruction: Tell me a myth about "Fulla".
output: Fulla has no saga of her own: her dossier is four precise notices, and every one of them places her at Frigg's side. What the tradition lost in narrative it kept in definition — no goddess in the Edda is more exactly described in a single sentence. [Gylfaginning 35] The Keeper of the Casket: Snorri's catalogue of the ásynjur gives Fulla her entire portrait in one sentence, and the tradition never varies it: 'Fulla is a virgin and goes with her hair loose and a golden band about her head; she carries Frigg's eski, looks after her footwear, and shares her secret counsels with her.' The three duties descend in rank and rise in intimacy — the box is treasure, the shoes are service, the counsels are trust itself. She is named immediately after Gná, Frigg's errand-rider, and the pairing has stuck: where Gná carries the queen's words out through the worlds, Fulla keeps the queen's words that never leave the hall. Scholars since Grimm have read both as hypostases of Frigg — aspects of the queen walking about as attendants — but the Edda keeps them as persons, and Fulla's golden band and loose hair make her the most visually fixed of all the minor ásynjur. [Grímnismál (prose)] The Warning to Geirröðr: Fulla's one errand in the Poetic Edda is given in prose, at the head of Grímnismál. Óðinn and Frigg had quarrelled over their foster-sons: Frigg accused King Geirröðr, Óðinn's favourite, of being so stingy he tortured his guests for lack of food, and Óðinn laid a wager on his man and set off disguised to test him. Frigg, knowing the road, sent her handmaid Fulla to Geirröðr ahead of him, to warn the king to beware of a certain sorcerer coming to his land to bewitch him — and gave her the token by which he could be known: no dog, however fierce, would leap at him. The warning is the trap: Geirröðr seized the blue-cloaked stranger, named Grímnir, and tortured him between two fires — and out of that fire the god spoke the whole catalogue of the worlds. Fulla appears only to deliver the message and vanish, but the wager, the torture, and the poem's entire revelation turn on her errand. [Gylfaginning 49] The Ring from Hel: When Hermóðr rode nine nights to ransom Baldr and came home with the tidings, he brought tokens from the dead: Baldr sent back the ring Draupnir to Óðinn, and Nanna — Baldr's wife, who had died of grief on his pyre — sent gifts out of Hel to the two women of Frigg's hall: a linen headdress for Frigg, and a finger-ring for Fulla. It is the smallest bequest in the whole Baldr cycle, and the most telling: when a dead goddess thinks of Ásgarðr's household, she thinks of the queen and of the queen's handmaid by name, and Frigg's hall is remembered as having a second woman in it who mattered. Fulla stands in that sentence exactly where her office puts her — the second woman of the hall, remembered with jewellery from beyond the world. [Second Merseburg Charm] Volla, Friia's Sister: The one continental witness comes from a tenth-century Fulda manuscript, the Second Merseburg Charm — the only pagan theogonic text in Old High German. Phol and Wodan rode to the wood, and Balder's foal wrenched its foot; then the goddesses chant over it in sequence: Sinthgunt, Sunna her sister; Friia, Volla her sister; and at last Wodan, who knows how, and the limb is knit bone to bone and blood to blood. Since Jacob Grimm, Volla — Friia's sister — has widely been read as Fulla, Frigg's attendant: the name is the exact Old High German form of the same word, and the charm puts her, precisely as the Edda does, at Friia's right hand. The identification is argued, not proven, and the handbooks counsel the usual caution — but if it holds, Fulla is one of the very few Norse goddesses with a continental footprint older than the Icelandic books.

instruction: Tell me a myth about "Syn".
output: Syn's dossier is the shortest in the Edda: one sentence in Gylfaginning, one name in the ásynja þulur, one rule in Skáldskaparmál's grammar of kennings. No poem stages her; no saga gives her a second life; no adventure attaches. And yet the tradition never forgot her, because what she guards is not a story but a word — the small, indispensable word 'no' — and Snorri preserves the proverb that proves the North kept both the word and its goddess in daily use. [Gylfaginning 35] The Eleventh Ásynja: Snorri's catalogue of the goddesses moves from [[frigg|Frigg]] through [[saga|Sága]], [[eir|Eir]], [[gefjon|Gefjon]], [[fulla|Fulla]], [[freyja|Freyja]] and the rest, and arrives at the eleventh: Syn. 'She guards the door of the hall and shuts it against those who should not enter, and she is appointed to defend, at assemblies, the suits she wishes to refute.' Then the sentence that fixes her identity forever: 'hence the proverb that a denial is set up when a man says no.' The catalogue closes with Snotra and Gná, and Snorri adds that these ásynjur are of no lesser rank than the rest. The whole of her mythology is in that one entry. Two functions are given, and they are one function twice: the doorkeeper who excludes, and the defender who refutes. At the threshold and at the law-court, Syn is the power that keeps the wrong thing out. [Gylfaginning 35] The Word Made Goddess: Syn's name is not a theonym with a hidden etymology; it is the ordinary noun itself. Old Norse syn means 'denial, refusal'; the verb synja means 'to deny, to refuse', and it saturates the legal prose of the sagas wherever a claim is answered with a no. The lexica connect the word with the family of sannr, 'true' — the denial began as a law term, the truth-speaking by which a false accusation is refused. The goddess of saying no is, at root, the goddess of the truthful answer. Snorri knows exactly what he is doing when he appends the proverb: he is recording a figure the language itself had already made. Whether Syn was an old goddess whose function shrank to a saying, or an abstraction Snorri's tradition personified on the model of Vör, Hlín and Snotra, the handbooks will not decide; Simek and Lindow class her among the personified functions, and the evidence is too thin to overrule them. [Skáldskaparmál] The Kenning for a Woman: Skáldskaparmál's rules for the poets keep Syn in the craft of verse: a woman may be periphrased by the name of any ásynja, and Syn stands in the list of goddesses available to the kenning-maker — refusal lending her name to praise, as Baldr's name stands for a warrior and Freyja's for a lady of rank. The ásynja þulur, the versified name-lists preserved with the same section of the Edda, hold her in the catalogue by name. It is a humble survival, but it is survival: every skald who named a woman after an ásynja worked from a list that included her, and the scribes who copied the þulur kept the doorkeeper's name in the register of the gods long after any cult there may have been was gone. [The corpus as a whole] The Silence of the Poems: No eddic poem names Syn. Völuspá's seeress does not number her among the returning gods; Grímnismál's survey of heaven's halls gives her no dwelling; the lays of gods and heroes pass her by entirely. Her whole being rests on Snorri's prose, the þulur, and the noun the whole language spoke. Where [[nanna|Nanna]] at least has her household's halls in verse, Syn has only the sentence — and the saying. The silence is itself the evidence the handbooks weigh. A figure attested once, in a catalogue, beside a living proverb, is either a genuine minor cult figure the poems happened to miss or a personification the cataloguing mind of the thirteenth century promoted from grammar. The honest record keeps both doors open — which is, perhaps, the one indignity a doorkeeper must bear.

instruction: Tell me a myth about "Brynhildr".
output: Brynhildr's story is the tragic core of the Vǫlsung cycle — told across Sigrdrífumál, the Guðrún poems, Sigurðarkviða hin skamma, Helreið Brynhildar, and Vǫlsunga saga with a consistency the corpus rarely achieves: the sentence, the waking, the oath, the deceit, the quarrel, the pyre. [Sigrdrífumál (prose)] The Valkyrie's Sentence: The prose frame of Sigrdrífumál gives her the name Sigrdrífa, 'victory-urger', and tells how she fell: two kings fought, Hjálmgunnarr the old and Agnar the young, and Óðinn had promised the victory to Hjálmgunnarr. The valkyrie judged otherwise and gave the day to Agnar. Óðinn pricked her with the sleep-thorn in revenge and declared she should never again fight in victory and should be given in marriage — and she answered that she had bound herself with an oath to wed no man who knew fear. The whole tragedy is already here: a woman whose only crime was an independent verdict, sentenced to sleep until a fearless man should come. [Vǫlsunga saga · Sigrdrífumál] The Waking on Hindarfjall: Sigurðr, fresh from Fáfnir's hoard, saw a light on Hindarfjall as though a fire burned to the sky, and rode Grani through the vafrlogi — the horse would take no other rider through that flame. Within the wall stood a hall, and in the hall a figure in full armor. He cut the byrnie from her with Gramr, from the neck down, for it had grown fast to her flesh, and she woke and asked what had strength to break her sleep. 'Sigmundr's son,' he answered, 'with the sword that has lately slain Fáfnir.' She taught him then the runes of victory and the counsels of Sigrdrífumál — how to carve, how to trust, how to beware — and they plighted their troth, the valkyrie and the dragonslayer, before fate had its word. [Vǫlsunga saga (ch. 28)] The Ale of Forgetfulness: At the court of Gjúki, Queen Grímhildr gave Sigurðr a draught of forgetfulness, and the memory of Brynhildr went out of him like a light; he married Guðrún and swore brotherhood with Gunnarr and Hǫgni. Then Gunnarr desired Brynhildr — but his horse would not take the flame. By Grímhildr's craft the two men exchanged shapes: Sigurðr rode the vafrlogi in Gunnarr's form, won the bride for his sworn brother, and lay three nights beside her with the drawn sword Gramr between them. Before they parted he took from her hand the ring Andvaranautr and gave her another ring from Fáfnir's hoard. Every element of the catastrophe is a theft so small it could hide in a draught, a shape, a ring. [Guðrúnarkviða II · Nibelungenlied] The Quarrel of the Queens: It broke at the river. Brynhildr and Guðrún went to the water to wash their hair, and Brynhildr waded the farther out, for her husband had ridden the flame, and Gunnarr's was the greater deed. Guðrún answered with the truth: it was Sigurðr who rode through in Gunnarr's shape — and she held up Andvaranautr, the ring taken from Brynhildr's own hand that night, as proof. Brynhildr knew the ring and turned white as a dead woman, and went home and spoke no word that evening. The German Nibelungenlied keeps the same wound in a different key: the queens' quarrel at the minster door, and Brünhilt learning that it was Siegfried who mastered her for Gunther. In both traditions the betrayal is revealed by a woman to a woman, and the world comes down after. [Sigurðarkviða hin skamma · Helreið Brynhildar] The Pyre and the Road to Hel: Brynhildr could not live inside the deceit, and she would not let it stand: she turned Gunnarr to vengeance, and Sigurðr was slain in his bed by young Guthormr, the one brother bound by no oath — the dying hero cast Gramr after his killer and cut him in two. When Guðrún's wail rose over the body, Brynhildr laughed once, from the bottom of her heart; then she took a sword and stabbed herself, and with her death upon her gave her last commands: to be burned on the pyre beside Sigurðr, with a drawn sword between them as it had been before, 'when we both entered one bed and were called by the name of man and wife.' Helreið Brynhildar follows her past the fire: on the road to Hel a giantess by her mound chides her for the blood on her hands, and Brynhildr answers with her whole life — the sleep, the waking, the oath kept, the deceit endured. 'Let us ride together,' the poem has her say, toward the place where Sigurðr waits.

instruction: Tell me a myth about "Gunnr".
output: Gunnr has no adventure of her own; her mythology is her office, told in lists that are anything but dry. Four witnesses fix her in the corpus: the Völuspá seeress sees her ride, Snorri states her function in a single sentence, the þulur keep her name in the valkyrie roll, and the skaldic poems describe the choosing she personifies — the tradition's way of saying that battle, in the North, had a chooser, and the chooser had a name. [Völuspá 30] The Riders the Seeress Saw: Deep in the völva's prophecy, between the world's making and its burning, the seeress turns her eyes to a road in the sky: 'She saw valkyries come from far and wide, ready to ride to the gods' people; Skuld held a shield, and Skögul was with her; Gunnr, Hildr, Göndul and Geirskögul — now are counted Herjan's ladies, the valkyries ready to ride over the earth' (Völuspá 30, trans. Larrington). Herjan, 'lord of hosts', is Óðinn, and the company is his household cavalry, mustered with shield and spear like a war-band rather than a flock of omens. The detail that fixes Gunnr here is sequence: she is named fourth in the most famous roll-call of the Poetic Edda, riding behind a norn carrying a shield, among spear-women ranked and armed. The seeress tells no story about her because the tradition needs none — battle with a chooser is as fixed a feature of the Norse cosmos as the norms and the doom they enforce. In this poem her whole biography is one line of a list, and the list is the point: war has personnel. [Gylfaginning 36] The Choosers of the Slain: Snorri, explaining Óðinn's household to his skeptical king, gives the valkyries their job-description and Gunnr her one great sentence: Óðinn sends the valkyries to every battle, 'to allot death to men and to award victory'. Then the roll-call: 'Gunnr and Rota and the youngest norn, who is called Skuld, always ride to choose the slain and to decide the fighting' (Gylfaginning 36, trans. Faulkes). The grouping is precise and chilling — two choosers of the slain and one weaver of fate riding together, because in Norse thought the choice of the fallen and the doom of the fallen are one act seen from two sides. The same chapter fills Valhǫll with valkyries waiting, drinking-horns in hand, and Grímnismál's catalogue (st. 36) arms the mead-bearers with names like Hrist and Mist — 'shaker' and 'mist'. Snorri's Gunnr needs no adventure, because her function is the adventure of everyone else: she is what war looks like when a warrior culture refuses to call its harvest random. [Skáldskaparmál þulur] Kept in the Roll: The þulur — the metrical name-lists a skald learned as working vocabulary — file Gunnr among the heiti of the valkyries, and the same tradition hands her name back to the battlefield as a common noun: gunnr, 'war, battle', a word a poet could set inside a kenning. Cleasby–Vigfusson's dictionary gives both entries side by side, the woman and the war, without apology, because Old Norse poetry refuses to separate them. When a skald sang that 'Gunnr's snow' drifted on the field, his hearers were meant to catch the double exposure — snowfall and battle, the white thing that covers the slain. De Vries registers the same double filing in his etymological dictionary, and the þulur's matter-of-factness is itself the evidence: no gloss was needed, because everyone knew. The lists are usually called dry; here they are a theology in shorthand. To put battle in the feminine, give it a horse, and enter it in the god's roster of women is to personify without allegory — the word itself walks, armed, and the name it walks under is Gunnr. [The Office] What the Choosing Looked Like: No Eddic poem gives Gunnr a scene of her own, so the corpus describes her office instead — and the office is among the best-attested in Norse verse, though the honest record must say that none of these poems names her. Hákonarmál (Eyvindr skáldaspillir) sends Göndul and Skögul to weigh two kings in the balance and choose which falls; Geirskögul 'shook her spear' over Hákon's host, and the chosen king is greeted on the field by valkyries with wine. The anonymous Eiríksmál wakes the dead heroes Sigmundr and Sinfjötli because a king is coming whom the valkyries must receive in Valhǫll. Grímnismál's mead-bearers and the dying warrior's welcome — a horn from a woman's hand — are the consolation carved and cast across the Viking world, from the gilt-silver valkyrie of Hårby on Funen to the picture stones of Gotland. All of it is the meaning of gunnr when the word rides: war's harvest gathered by named women, and the fallen comforted at the moment of election. The tradition's reticence about Gunnr herself is the meaning — battle's chooser needs no biography, only a name.

instruction: Tell me a myth about "Skuld".
output: Skuld's dossier is short and of the highest rank: she appears where the world's frame is described, never in anecdote. The Poetic Edda names her twice — once beneath the tree, once in the air above the battlefield — and Snorri stitches the two sightings into one figure: the youngest norn who rides with the valkyries. What follows is the whole of the primary record. [Völuspá 19–20] The Three Beneath the Tree: The seeress surveys the world's frame: the ash Yggdrasill, tall, drenched with white loam, whence come the dews that fall in the valleys, ever green, standing over Urðarbrunnr. Thence come maidens, deep in wisdom, three from the lake that stands beneath the tree: one was called Urðr, the second Verðandi — they carved on slips of wood — Skuld the third. They laid laws, they chose lives for the children of men, the fates of men. The stanza is the foundation text of northern fate-doctrine, and it fixes Skuld's place in the triad without explaining it: the poem gives her no act, no speech, no attribute but her position — the third, the last named, the one whose name is a debt. [Völuspá 30] The Shield in the Tally: Late in the same poem the seeress looks up from the roots to the sky: she saw valkyries come from far away, ready to ride to the gods' host — Skuld bore a shield, and Skögul followed her, Gunnr, Hildr, Göndul and Geirskögul; now the tally of Herjan's maidens is told, valkyries ready to ride over the earth. The list is a roll-call, and Skuld heads it, shield in hand. No other norn appears in a valkyrie list. The double office is the interpretive crux of the whole figure: the maiden who allots life at the root is the same maiden who collects death in the field — the two ends of one ledger. [Gylfaginning 15–16] The Maidens Who Shape Men's Lives: Snorri's survey of the world-tree pauses at its heavenward root: beneath that root is the very holy well called Urðarbrunnr, and there the gods hold their court each day. By that well stand three maidens named Urðr, Verðandi and Skuld — these maidens shape men's lives, Snorri says, and we call them norns. He adds that there are other norns besides, who come to each child at birth to shape its life, of the races of gods, elves and dwarves — but the three at the well are the triad the tradition never enlarged. Snorri also preserves the tree's upkeep: the norns take water from the well and the mud around it and pour it over the ash so that its limbs do not wither or rot, and that water is so holy that all that comes within the well turns white as the membrane within an eggshell. Fate, in this picture, is not only decree but daily maintenance of the world's fabric. [Gylfaginning 36] The Youngest Norn Rides: In the chapter on the valkyries Snorri closes the roster with a sentence that completes Skuld's dossier: Odin's shield-maidens ride to every battle, choose who shall fall, and decide the victory — and with them, Snorri writes, always ride Gunnr and Rota and the youngest norn, who is called Skuld, to choose the slain and govern the engagements. The designation is precise: of the three at the well, she is the youngest — and she rides. The tradition thus hands the future its own grim office: what is owed is collected on the battlefield, where every life's account comes due.

instruction: Tell me a myth about "Hymir".
output: Hymir lives in one great poem and its prose retelling: Hymiskviða, the comic and terrible lay of the cauldron-quest, and Gylfaginning 48, where Snorri tells the fishing-trip for the Miðgarðsormr with all its sea-cold detail. It is Þórr's most famous adventure, and the giant is its immovable setting. [Hymiskviða 1–13] The Demand for the Cauldron: The Æsir had hunted and taken auguries from the blood, and saw that Ægir — called also Gymir — had brew-stuff in plenty. Þórr ordered the sea-giant to brew ale for the gods, and Ægir, to be rid of the demand, set an impossible price: first let them bring a cauldron a mile wide. Týr knew where one stood: east of the Élivágar lives the shrewd Hymir at heaven's end, and "my fierce father owns the roomy kettle, a mile deep." So Þórr and Týr drove to the giant's hall. There they met Týr's grandmother, loathsome, with nine hundred heads — and another woman, golden-browed, Týr's mother, who hid the guests under the great cauldron, for her husband was often cruel to visitors. [Hymiskviða 13–16 · Gylfaginning 48] The Host Comes Home: Hymir came in from the hunting with the ice rattling in his beard. The pillar he looked toward burst apart; eight cauldrons crashed from the broken beam, and one hard-forged kettle came down whole. The guests came out, and the hall fed them: three oxen were slaughtered, and Þórr alone ate two before he slept. In the morning the giant eyed his thinned herd and told his guest they must fish for the next day's meal — Þórr might row out with him, if the little fellow dared the cold and the long pull to his fishing-ground. [Hymiskviða 17–27 · Gylfaginning 48] The Fishing for the Miðgarðsormr: Asked for bait, Þórr went to the herd and wrenched the head from the black bull Himinbrjótr — Snorri calls him Himinhrjóðr. Hymir rowed hard, then harder, and still Þórr matched him, past the giant's own grounds into water he said was unsafe, where the serpent lies. Hymir pulled up two whales at once on his hooks; Þórr cast the ox-head overboard. The Miðgarðsormr gaped on the bait, the hook caught, and Þórr braced his feet through the bottom of the boat and hauled the serpent's head to the gunwale — the two glaring, the sea foaming, the boat nearly swamped — until the hammer struck and the serpent sank back into the sea. Hymir rowed home in gloomy silence. [Hymiskviða 28–39 · Gylfaginning 48] The Cup, the Skull, and the Carrying-Off: Back on land Hymir demanded proof of strength, and set his crystal cup: break that, and be counted mighty. Twice Þórr hurled it through the stone pillars, and twice it came back to the giant's hand unbroken — until the fair counsellor whispered to strike it on Hymir's own skull, harder than any cup. The cup shattered. Hymir mourned it with the formula of loss: he could no longer say over it "ale is brewed." Then, sullen, he yielded the wager — take the cauldron, if you can carry it out. Týr heaved twice and could not shift it; Þórr hoisted it over his head and strode off with the rim ringing at his heels. They had not gone far before he looked back and saw Hymir coming east from the caves with a troop of many-headed giants; he set down the cauldron, raised Mjöllnir, and slew the whole host. One of Þórr's goats went lame on the road — Loki's doing, the poem says — but the cauldron came to Ægir, who brews ale in it for the Æsir ever after.

instruction: Tell me a myth about "Baugi".
output: Baugi's entire mythology is one episode, and it is the most consequential single episode in the mythology of poetry: the mead heist of Skáldskaparmál. He appears only there and in the þulur of giant-names — a figure the tradition needed once, at the one door, and never again. But that once is the door through which all skaldic poetry claims to have come. [Skáldskaparmál] The Mead Comes to Hnitbjǫrg: The story begins before Baugi enters it. From the peace-making of Æsir and Vanir is made Kvasir, wisest of beings; the dwarfs Fjalar and Galar kill him and brew his blood with honey into a mead that makes a poet or a scholar of whoever drinks it, keeping it in three vessels — Óðrœrir, Boðn, and Són. The dwarfs then drown the giant Gilling at sea and kill his wife with a millstone, and Gilling's son Suttungr takes revenge: he sets the dwarfs on a tide-washed skerry, and they buy their lives with the mead. Suttungr carries it home, shuts it inside the mountain Hnitbjǫrg, and sets his daughter Gunnlǫð to guard it. Only now does Snorri bring Baugi on stage, in a single sentence of genealogy: Suttungr had a brother, and his name was Baugi. The hoard is sealed, the guard is set, and the god who wants the mead does not go to its owner — he goes to the owner's brother. [Skáldskaparmál] The Whetstone and the Nine Thralls: Óðinn comes walking to Baugi's land calling himself Bǫlverkr, 'Evil-doer' — a name that is not a disguise so much as an announcement. Nine of Baugi's thralls are mowing hay. Bǫlverkr offers to sharpen their scythes, and the whetstone he pulls from his cloak hones so well that all nine want to buy it. He says it will be sold dearly, and throws it up among them; in the scramble to catch it, each thrall swings his scythe at another's neck, and all nine lie dead in the field. That evening Bǫlverkr lodges with Baugi, and Baugi pours out his troubles: his nine thralls are dead and the hay harvest stands uncut. The god has engineered the vacancy he is about to fill — the labour shortage is the lock, and he made it himself. [Skáldskaparmál] Nine Men's Work for One Draught: Bǫlverkr makes the offer: he will do the work of nine men through the summer, and his wage is one drink of Suttungr's mead. Baugi is careful here, and Snorri gives him the one honest line in the story: he answers that the mead is not his to give — Suttungr alone has control of it — but he will go with Bǫlverkr and they will try together whether they can get it. The bargain is struck: a summer's labour against a hope, with Baugi as broker. Bǫlverkr does the work of nine all summer. When winter comes they go to Suttungr and Baugi puts the case — and Suttungr refuses flatly: not one drop of the mead. Baugi's brokerage has failed on its stated terms; what remains is the attempt he half-promised, the trying of stratagems. [Skáldskaparmál] Rati and the Two Blowings: Bǫlverkr now asks Baugi for other ways in, and produces the auger called Rati. Baugi bores into the mountain, and says the hole is through. Bǫlverkr leans down and blows into the bore — and the stone-chips fly back into his face. He knows then, Snorri says, that Baugi meant to betray him: the hole is blind. Baugi bores again, and this time when Bǫlverkr blows, the chips fly inward and away. The tunnel is through. Bǫlverkr turns himself into a snake and crawls into the hole — and Baugi strikes after him with the auger, and misses. It is the story's tightest instant: the accomplice becomes the assassin at the threshold, and the mead of all poetry hangs on one failed stroke. Inside waits Gunnlǫð; Óðinn lies with her three nights, wins leave for three draughts, and empties Óðrœrir, Boðn, and Són entire. Then he rises as an eagle with all the mead in him, Suttungr in eagle-shape hard behind, and the Æsir set out their vats in Ásgarðr's court — Baugi's door standing open in the mountain behind them all. [Hávamál 104–110] Óðinn's Own Version: Hávamál lets Óðinn boast of the same theft in his own voice, and the differences are instructive. The god names Rati — 'Rati's mouth I made room for me, and it gnawed the rock' — names Gunnlǫð and the golden seat, names Óðrœrir come up among the Æsir. He names Suttungr defrauded of his mead and Gunnlǫð left weeping, and he names the instrument of it: the baugeiðr, the ring-oath Óðinn swore and broke — 'who can trust him?' But Hávamál never names Baugi. In the god's own telling, the brother at the door has already vanished — the contract, the auger, the missed stroke, all absorbed into Óðinn's solitary cunning. Snorri's prose preserves what the god's boasting omits: that the door had a keeper, that the keeper had a price, and that the keeper tried, at the last moment, to close it on the snake.

instruction: Tell me a myth about "Brokkr".
output: Brokkr has one story, and it is the founding legend of the gods' three greatest treasures: the wager of the head, told in Skáldskaparmál with a smith's eye for process — what went into the fire, what came out, and what each casting cost. Every other dwarf in the corpus shares his craft; none of them shares his afternoon. [Skáldskaparmál 35] The Hair of Gold and the Sons of Ívaldi: It begins with Loki's mischief: for a prank, he cut off all the hair of [[sif|Sif]], [[thor|Þórr]]'s wife. Þórr caught him and was set to break every bone in his body when Loki swore to go to the svartálfar, the black-elves, and have them make for Sif a head of hair from gold that would grow like other hair. Loki went to the dwarfs called the sons of Ívaldi, and they made the hair, and with it two more wonders: the ship Skíðblaðnir, which has a fair wind wherever it is bound and folds up like a cloth into a pouch, and the spear Gungnir, which never stops in its thrust. Three treasures stood finished — and Loki, rich in gifts he had not paid for, looked for one more bargain. Grímnismál in the Poetic Edda keeps the first half of the record in verse: 'Ívaldi's sons went in days of old to make Skíðblaðnir, best of ships, for bright Freyr' (st. 43). The poem names the ship and its makers; Snorri supplies the rest of the morning's work — and the arrogance of a trickster carrying three unpaid masterpieces through the mountains, already hunting a fourth thing to steal. [Skáldskaparmál 35] The Wager of the Head: On his way home Loki stopped at the forge of the dwarf Brokkr and laid the strangest bet in the corpus: he wagered his own head that Brokkr's brother could not make three treasures as good as the three the sons of Ívaldi had just finished. Snorri names the brother at the forge Eitri; some manuscripts of the Prose Edda read Sindri, 'the sparkler', and the handbooks register both names for the same smith. Brokkr took the wager. The terms placed him at the bellows — Eitri would lay the work in the fire, and Brokkr was to blow without pause until it came out again, for the treasure would be exactly what the unbroken breath made it. It is worth pausing on the stake: no god in the corpus wagers more. Loki bet his head because he counted the errand already won — the sons of Ívaldi had set the mark impossibly high. Brokkr bet his craft against it, which is to say he bet on the one thing a dwarf owns outright: that afternoon, in that forge, the breath would not fail. [Skáldskaparmál 35] Three Castings, Three Stings: Eitri laid a pig's skin in the forge and Brokkr blew, and a fly settled on his hand and stung — but he blew on, and out of the fire came a boar with bristles of gold. Then gold was laid in the fire, and the fly settled on Brokkr's neck and stung twice as hard — but he blew on, and out came the ring Draupnir. Last, iron was laid in the fire, and Eitri said that everything would be spoiled if the blast faltered now; and the fly settled between Brokkr's eyes and stung the eyelid until blood ran down into his eye, and Brokkr swept the fly away and stopped the bellows for one instant — and when the work came out of the fire, the hammer's handle was short. The story never names the fly, and never needs to: the corpus has exactly one character who travels in small shapes and profits by other people's work. What the stings could not do is the point of the tale — twice they failed entirely, and at the last they bought only a shortened handle on a hammer that would still be judged the best treasure in the world. Sabotage, the myth says, can scar a masterpiece and still lose. [Skáldskaparmál 35] The Judgment of the Æsir: Brokkr carried the three treasures to Ásgarðr, and the Æsir sat in judgment, Óðinn, Þórr, and Freyr standing first as the receivers of the gifts. Loki set out what the sons of Ívaldi had made: the spear Gungnir he gave to Óðinn, the hair of gold to Þórr for Sif, and the ship Skíðblaðnir to Freyr, and he boasted that no dwarf could match the set. Brokkr gave his gifts against them: to Freyr the boar Gullinbursti, which can run through air and water, day and night, better than any horse, and whose golden bristles give light wherever it goes; to Óðinn the ring Draupnir, from which eight rings of equal weight drop every ninth night; and to Þórr the hammer Mjǫllnir — never missing what it is thrown at, never failing to return to the hand, small enough when wished to be carried inside the shirt, and flawed in one thing only, that the handle is rather short. The judgment was that the hammer was the best of all the treasures, and the greatest defense against the rime-giants. The wager was lost: Loki owed Brokkr his head. And the Æsir had, by a single vote on a single afternoon, acquired the only weapon that would matter at the end of the world. [Skáldskaparmál 35] The Head and the Neck: Loki offered to ransom himself, and Brokkr refused every offer — there was no gold that would buy the stake back. Loki tried to run, on the shoes that carry him over sea and land, and Brokkr asked Þórr to catch him, and Þórr did. Then Loki reached for the letter of the bargain: the head was Brokkr's, he conceded, but the wager had said nothing of the neck — and no part of the neck might be cut. It was a trickster's reading and the court allowed it; the head could not be taken. Brokkr took the price another way: he declared he would sew Loki's lips together, and pierced them with an awl and stitched the mouth shut with the thread called Vartari — the smile that had sold Sif's hair closed over the teeth for a while. Snorri ends the episode there, and it is one of the corpus's quietest verdicts: the wager was won, the loophole was honored, and the smith still left the hall with something. The gods keep the treasures; Loki keeps his head; and Brokkr keeps the only thing the story ever really put at stake — the record of having made Mjǫllnir.

instruction: How is "Fáfnir" pronounced?
output: Fáfnir is pronounced /ˈfɑːv.nir/ — approximately "'FAHV-neer' — hold the first vowel long like 'ah', let the f soften to a 'v' before the n, and trill the final r.". instruction: Tell me a myth about "Fáfnir".
output: Fáfnir is the dragon at the hinge of the Vǫlsung cycle — born the son of Hreiðmarr, remade by greed into the serpent of Gnitaheiðr, and slain by Sigurðr in the scene on which the whole heroic tragedy turns, when the cursed gold of Andvari changed hands and the curse changed hands with it. [Skáldskaparmál] The Weregild of Ótr: Óðinn, Hœnir, and Loki came traveling to a waterfall where an otter sat eating a salmon, half-asleep. Loki killed the otter with a stone, and the gods flayed it and carried the skin as a trophy — but the otter was Ótr , son of Hreiðmarr, who had the craft to take that shape. That night Hreiðmarr seized the gods and named the ransom: the otter-skin was to be filled with gold and covered with gold, inside and out. Loki borrowed Rán's net and caught the dwarf Andvari , who lived in the falls in the likeness of a pike, and stripped him of his hoard down to the last ring — Andvaranautr . Andvari cursed it as he went into the rock: the gold would be the death of two brothers and the strife of eight princes. When one whisker still showed, Óðinn had to give up the ring itself. The ransom settled a killing — and carried a spoken curse into the house that received it. [Reginsmál] The Patricide of Gnitaheiðr: Fáfnir and Reginn demanded the blood-gold from their father as their share after Ótr. Hreiðmarr refused — and Fáfnir put his sword through his father sofanda , sleeping, while the old man called on his daughters to witness that his life was spent. Fáfnir took all the gold, and when Reginn asked for his inheritance, Fáfnir gave him a plain no. Then Fáfnir went out to Gnitaheiðr , the Gnita heath, and there his greed finished what the curse had begun: he took on the likeness of a serpent — var í orms líki , as Reginsmál puts it — and lay brooding on the gold, wearing the ægishjálmr , the helm of terror that all living things feared, and blowing poison across the land so that none dared come near. Reginn, the cunning smith, went to the court of King Hjálprekr and became foster-father to the young Sigurðr, son of Sigmundr — and began, patiently, to point the boy at his brother. [Fáfnismál] The Strike from Beneath: Reginn forged for Sigurðr the sword Gramr , so keen it sheared a lock of wool drifting down the Rhine and split Reginn's anvil in two. On the heath Sigurðr dug a deep trench in the dragon's track to the water and lay down in it; when Fáfnir crawled overhead, blowing venom, Sigurðr thrust Gramr upward into the heart. The dying dragon did not scream but questioned his killer — Fáfnismál grants him a long, sardonic deathbed dialogue, testing the boy with riddles of the gods and the future — and warned him twice: þér verða þeir baugar at bana , these rings will be your death. The warning is the tale's cruel pivot: the victim knows exactly what the gold does, tells his killer plainly, and the killer takes it anyway. [Fáfnismál] The Blood and the Birds: Reginn cut out the dragon's heart and set Sigurðr to roast it. Testing whether it was done, Sigurðr burned his thumb and thrust it into his mouth — and the moment the dragon's heart-blood touched his tongue, he understood the speech of birds. The nuthatches in the thicket told him plainly that Reginn meant to betray him and claim the gold alone, and that he should strike first; Sigurðr struck off Reginn's head, ate the heart, and loaded the hoard onto his horse Grani. He had won the treasure — and inherited the curse. The gold rode with him to the hall of the Gjúkungs, where the ring Andvaranautr passed from queen to queen and brother to brother until it brought down the whole Vǫlsung line in fire and slaughter. Fáfnir's last gift, the blood of wisdom, bought its drinker exactly one honest moment — long enough to hear what the gold would do, and not long enough to refuse it.

instruction: Tell me a myth about "Reginn".
output: Reginn's dossier runs through the whole Völsung cycle: the otter's ransom in Skáldskaparmál, the fosterage in Reginsmál and Völsunga saga, the reforging of Gram, and the death on Fáfnir's heath when the birds spoke. He is the cycle's great ambiguous figure — the finest smith in the tradition and its coldest traitor, teacher and would-be murderer of the same boy. [Skáldskaparmál] The Otter's Ransom: It begins with a skinned otter. Óðinn, Hœnir and Loki came to Andvari's falls, where Reginn's brother Ótr fished in otter shape; Loki killed him with a stone, and that evening the gods carried the skin into Hreiðmarr's house and boasted of the catch. Hreiðmarr and his sons Fáfnir and Reginn seized the gods and demanded weregild: the otter's skin filled with gold, and covered with gold besides. Loki forced the dwarf Andvari to yield his hoard, and when Andvari tried to keep back one ring, Loki took that too — Andvaranautr. Andvari laid the curse: that gold would be the death of two brothers and the strife of eight princes, and no man should enjoy his wealth. The curse kept its accounts. Hreiðmarr refused his sons any share of the ransom; Fáfnir killed his father in his sleep and took all the gold, and Reginn got nothing. Fáfnir went out to Gnitaheiðr, brooded on the hoard in the shape of a dragon, and Reginn — wronged, patient, and very clever — went to find an instrument. [Reginsmál; Völsunga saga] The Foster-Father: The eddic prose introduces him with exact economy: Reginn was Hreiðmarr's son, 'the most skilled of all men, and a dwarf in stature; he was wise, grim, and skilled in magic'. He came to the court of King Hjálprek in Denmark, where the boy Sigurðr — son of the slain Sigmundr and Hjördís — was being raised, and Reginn became his foster-father. The Völsunga saga lets him teach the boy chess, runes and tongues, and all the while he worked on the boy's pride: Fáfnir lies on Gnitaheiðr in dragon shape, he said, and your father left you nothing. The foster-bond was the strongest tie the northern world knew short of blood — fosterage made family. Reginn made it in order to break it, and the tradition never forgives him for that inversion: every retelling keeps the same chill, that the hand which armed Sigurðr was already measuring him for the grave. [Völsunga saga; Fáfnismál] The Reforging of Gram: Sigurðr demanded a sword, and Reginn forged him one — the best his craft could make. Sigurðr took it to the anvil and struck, and the blade shattered. Reginn forged a second, better than the first; it broke too. Then Sigurðr went to his mother and asked for the fragments of his father's sword — the blade Óðinn himself had shattered in Sigmundr's last battle — and Hjördís gave him the shards. From them Reginn reforged Gram: it shone in the forge, says the saga, like fire, and when Sigurðr struck the anvil the blade bit down to the stock and did not break. They laid a pack of wool on the Rhine, and the current carried it against the edge, and the sword cut it in two as easily as it cut water. The scene is the tradition's purest statement about craft: Reginn's skill is real, peerless, and wholly in service of his revenge. He made the one weapon that could kill his brother — and put it into the hand of a boy he intended to outlive. [Fáfnismál; Völsunga saga] The Blood on the Tongue: On Gnitaheiðr Sigurðr dug a pit in the dragon's path and drove Gram up into Fáfnir's heart from below. Dying, the dragon spent his last breath on a warning: Reginn betrayed me, and he will betray you. Reginn crept out, praised the killing, and asked one service — cut out the heart, roast it, and let me eat it. Sigurðr set the heart over the fire, and when he touched it to test the roasting and put his finger to his mouth, the dragon's blood touched his tongue and he understood the speech of birds. The nuthatches in the branches said: there sits Sigurðr roasting Fáfnir's heart — he should eat it himself and become wise; and Reginn lies in the heather, planning to betray the boy who trusts him; let the ring be the brother's ransom, and cut off his head. Sigurðr took the counsel: he cut off Reginn's head, ate of the heart, and rode to the hoard. So the curse closed its second account — two brothers dead, Hreiðmarr and then Reginn, and the gold passed on with Andvaranautr, unspent and unenjoyed, exactly as the dwarf had sworn.

instruction: Tell me a myth about "Sindri".
output: Sindri's dossier is one long scene in Snorri and one stanza in Völuspá — a forge and a hall. The Prose Edda gives him the wager that produced the gods' three greatest treasures; the Poetic Edda gives him a golden house in the dwarf-fields and a kindred to fill it. Between the two stands the corpus's most consequential craftsman: everything the Æsir trust in the last battle came off his anvil in a single afternoon. [Skáldskaparmál 35] The Wager of the Head: It begins with a crime: Loki, for mischief, cuts off all the hair of Sif, Þórr's wife. Þórr seizes him and would break every bone, and Loki swears to get the svartálfar to make hair of gold for Sif that will grow like living hair. He goes first to the sons of Ívaldi, who make the golden hair and two more treasures — the ship Skíðblaðnir for Freyr and the spear Gungnir for Óðinn. Then, flushed with success, Loki goes to the dwarf Brokkr and wagers his own head that Brokkr's brother Sindri cannot make three treasures just as good. The bet is the whole engine of the chapter: a trickster's tongue staked against a smith's hands. Brokkr accepts, and the brothers go to the forge with the terms set — Sindri lays the metal, Brokkr works the bellows, and the bellows must not stop blowing until the work comes out of the fire. [Skáldskaparmál 35] Three Castings, Three Stings: Sindri lays a pigskin in the forge and tells Brokkr to blow and never cease. A fly settles on Brokkr's hand and stings, but the bellows do not stop: out comes a boar with bristles of gold, Gullinbursti. Next Sindri lays gold in the fire; the fly returns and stings Brokkr's neck, harder, but the bellows do not stop: out comes the gold ring Draupnir. Last Sindri lays iron in the fire — and now, Snorri says, the smith himself fears the work will fail if the blowing falters. The fly settles between Brokkr's eyes and stings the eyelids so the blood runs down and blinds him; Brokkr sweeps the fly away with his hand, and the bellows fall silent for one instant. When the iron comes out it is a hammer — and its handle is short by a finger's breadth. The fly, of course, is Loki, who cannot win the wager fairly and tries to spoil it instead. The chapter's precision is unforgettable: two perfect treasures and one marred, and the marred one — the hammer Mjǫllnir — is the greatest of the six. The sabotage succeeds exactly as far as the handle and no farther. [Skáldskaparmál 35] The Judgment and the Sewn Lips: The brothers bring their three treasures to Ásgarðr, and the Æsir sit in judgment with Óðinn, Þórr, and Freyr as assessors. To Freyr goes the boar, which runs through air and sea faster than any horse and lights the night with its golden bristles; to Óðinn the ring, which drips eight rings of equal weight every ninth night; to Þórr the hammer — it never misses what he throws at, it never breaks, it always returns to his hand, and it shrinks small enough to carry inside his shirt. Its one fault is the short handle. The judgment is unanimous: the hammer is the best of all the treasures, the surest defense against the frost-giants, and the brothers have won the wager. Loki offers to ransom his head, but Brokkr refuses every price. When Loki tries to flee on his sky-shoes, Þórr catches him. Then comes the trickster's last legalism: the head was staked, but not one inch of the neck. Brokkr cannot take the head without touching the neck — so he takes an awl instead and sews Loki's lips together, and the thread, Snorri says, is called Vartari. The smith does not get his stake; he gets something better, the silencing of the tongue that staked it. [Völuspá 37] The Golden Hall at Niðavellir: The verse tradition knows a grander Sindri than Snorri's forge-hand. Völuspá, in its survey of the world's dwellings, counts a hall that stands north on Niðavellir, made of gold, belonging to the kindred of Sindri — beside the giant Brimir's beer-hall at Ókólnir. Here Sindri is no lone craftsman but a dwarf chieftain, the head of a family rich enough to roof its house in the metal his name throws off as sparks. The dwarf þulur preserved with Skáldskaparmál keep the name in the catalogues of dwarf heiti, and the manuscript tradition splits on the forge-scene itself: where part of the tradition names Brokkr's brother Sindri, another part calls him Eitri, and the handbooks read the two as one smith under two forge-names. The name itself is the trade: sindra is 'to sparkle, throw off sparks', sindr is the slag and spark of the forge — kin to Old English sinder and the modern English cinder, the cooled spark of the smith's fire.

instruction: Tell me a myth about "Niflheimr".
output: Niflheimr's mythology is the mythology of before: it stars in no adventure and houses no hero, because its story is over before the gods' stories begin — and yet every river, every frost giant, and every corpse that sinks past Hel is still paying its tribute to the mist-world. [Gylfaginning 4] The World That Came First: Snorri's chronology begins not with a god but with a climate. 'It was many ages before the earth was made,' he says, 'that Niflheimr was made' — and in its middle stands the well Hvergelmir, 'the roaring kettle,' from which flow the rivers named one by one in Gylfaginning 4 and already in the verse lists of Grímnismál 27–29: Svöl the cool, Gunnþrá the battle-defiant, Fjörm the swift, Fimbulþul the loud-babbling, Slíðr the fearsome and Hríð the storming, Sylgr and Ylgr, Víð the broad, and Leiptr the flashing — and Gjöll, the resounding, which runs nearest the gate of Hel. Snorri is careful to say the mist-realm was not found but made: the first work of whatever order preceded the gods. Before there was a world to water, the mist-world already had its watershed — the Norse cosmos keeps, at its bottom, a memory that geography came first and inhabitants came after. [Gylfaginning 5–7 · Vafþrúðnismál 21] The Yeasty Venom and the Quickening: The Élivágar ran so far from their source that the yeasty venom in them hardened, like dross running out of a fire, and turned to ice; rime and fog rose layer upon layer across Ginnungagap's northern half, while sparks and molten flecks flew out of Muspellsheimr in the south. Where the warm breath met the rime, the ice thawed and dripped — and the dripping drops quickened into the likeness of a man, named Ymir by the gods and Aurgelmir, the mud-yeller, by the rime-giants who descend from him. The Poetic Edda keeps the same recipe in three lines: out of Élivágar spurted venom-drops, Vafþrúðnismál says, and grew until a giant was made. The first life in the North was brewed from poisoned ice thawed by a fire it could not see. [Gylfaginning 15–16 · Grímnismál 26] The Root Over the Well: When the world was finally built, Niflheimr kept the oldest seat in it. Yggdrasill's third root, Snorri says, extends over Niflheimr, and beneath that root is Hvergelmir, and the serpent Níðhöggr gnaws the root from below — the ash is always being eaten at its oldest corner. Grímnismál completes the water-cycle: the hart Eikþyrnir stands on Valhöll's roof cropping the leaves, and from his horns it drips into Hvergelmir, whence all waters have their course. The rivers of gods and giants alike — the Fjörm and the Slíðr, the Gjöll and the Leiptr — are one well's outflow, and the well sits in the mist. [Vafþrúðnismál 43 · Baldrs draumar 2 · Gylfaginning 3] Niflhel, Down in the Ninth World: In the poems the mist-world darkens into something lower. Óðinn, proving his wisdom to the giant Vafþrúðnir, says he journeyed through nine worlds below Niflhel; in Baldrs draumar he saddles Sleipnir and rides down to Niflhel to wake a dead seeress and wring the prophecy of Baldr's death from her. Snorri states the grim geography plainly: evil men go to Hel, and thence down to Niflhel — that is down in the ninth world. The world that was first becomes the world that is lowest: creation's old north pole, demoted to the cellar of the dead.

instruction: Tell me a myth about "Muspellheimr".
output: Muspellheimr is the world of fire, the southern realm that burned before the cosmos was shaped and will burn it again at Ragnarǫk. Home of Surtr and his sons, it is both the furnace whose sparks quickened Ymir's rime and the terminal conflagration that ends the ordered world. [Völuspá 47–52] Surtr Comes from the South: The seeress of Völuspá ends her prophecy with Muspell's arrival: Surtr comes from the south, and the sun of the battle-gods shines from his sword. Behind him ride the sons of Muspell, and the rainbow bridge Bifröst breaks beneath their company as they cross. The wolf Fenrir has swallowed the sun; the ship Naglfar, built from the nails of the dead, sails with Loki at the helm; and in the tumult Surtr finds Freyr and kills him — the fertility god defenseless because he gave his own sword to his messenger Skírnir for love of Gerðr. Then Surtr casts fire over the earth: the sun grows dark, the land sinks in the sea, the bright stars vanish, and a life-nourishing flame licks against heaven itself until the sky splits. Fire here is not punishment but atmosphere — the world's element returning to claim it. The stanzas make Muspellheimr the last thing the seeress sees before the earth rises green from the sea: its fire ends the world and, by clearing it, permits the renewal. [Gylfaginning 5] The First Melting: Snorri's Gylfaginning sets the physics of creation as a collision: from the north, the rivers of Niflheimr poured into Ginnungagap and froze into rime and hoarfrost; from the south, sparks and molten fragments blew out of Muspellheimr into the same void. Just as cold and all harsh things came from Niflheim, Snorri writes, so that which lay nearest Muspell was hot and glowing — and where the heat met the rime, the ice began to melt and drip. From the quickened drops came the sweat of Ymir, the primordial giant from whose body the worlds would later be built. Muspellheimr is thus written into the world's first paragraph as one of its two parents. Without its fire the rime of Niflheimr would have lain on the void forever, unmelting and lifeless; creation begins exactly at the frontier where the two realms touch. The realm that will destroy the world is, in the beginning, the reason the world can exist at all — the furnace and the funeral pyre are the same fire, seen from opposite ends of time. [Gylfaginning 4, 8] Surt at the Border: Of Muspellheimr's interior Snorri says almost nothing, because nothing in it needs describing: it is brightness, heat, and flame, impassable to anyone not born to it. What matters is its border, where he who sits at the world's end to defend it is called Surt; he has a flaming sword, and at the end of the world he will go and wage war and defeat all the gods and burn the whole world with fire. The southern realm also gave the heavens their lamps: when the sons of Borr built the world, they caught the sparks and glowing embers that flew about loosely and had been cast out of Muspellheim, and set them in the sky — fixed in their places as sun, moon, and stars. The image is exact and beautiful: every star is a spark of Muspell caught and pinned. The realm's fire is therefore both guard and clock — the wall of flame at the world's edge and the burning points by which giants and men tell the hours until Surtr leaves his post. Muspellheimr never does anything; it simply is, at both ends of everything. [Muspilli] The Word Travels South: The name escaped the north. Around 870 an anonymous monk in the south of the German-speaking world composed a poem on the Last Judgment in which muspilli means the destruction of the world by fire: Elias will fight the Antichrist, but bitter will be the muspilli for the souls unprepared — a word reused, evidently, from the old Germanic vocabulary of the world-ending blaze. The poem survives incomplete in a Munich manuscript (Clm 14098), and a generation earlier the Old Saxon Heliand had already used mūdspelli, 'day of doom,' in its gospel harmony. Whether the word itself is pre-Christian Germanic or a Christian coinage is a question scholars have argued for a century without settlement; what is certain is that the southern fire-realm of the Norse cosmos left its name in monasteries that had never heard of Surtr. Muspell crossed the frontier the way the myth says its sparks do — thrown outward from the burning world to lodge, still glowing, in foreign darkness.

instruction: Tell me a myth about "Vanaheimr".
output: Vanaheimr has no myth of its own: no surviving story is set inside it, no traveller describes it, no poem is located there. Its whole mythology is told from outside, by and about the gods who left it — the hostages and immigrants through whom the Vanir entered the Æsir's world, and the war whose peace made the two kindreds one household. [Vafþrúðnismál 39–40] In Vanaheimr the Wise Powers Created Him: In the wisdom-contest with the giant Vafþrúðnir, Óðinn asks whence Njörðr came among the sons of the Æsir, he who rules so many temples and sanctuaries though he was not raised among the Æsir. The giant's answer is the realm's one great attestation: in Vanaheimr the wise powers created him and gave him to the gods as a hostage — and at the doom of the age he will come back home among the wise Vanir. The stanza does everything at once: it names the realm, names its people the wise ones, explains Njörðr's double citizenship, and promises him a homecoming that the surviving corpus never narrates. Vanaheimr is the only divine home defined not by what happens there but by who came from there — and by who is owed a return. [Völuspá 21–24] The First War in the World: The seeress remembers the world's first war, and it begins inside the Æsir's own hall: Gullveig — the thrice-burned, thrice-born witch whom the Vanir sent or the Æsir harboured — is speared and burned in Hárr's hall, yet lives. Then the gods took counsel on whether the Æsir should pay tribute, and when battle was joined it was the Vanir who broke the wall of Ásgarðr and trod the field in victory — the seeress says the Vanir themselves “trod the field with war-spells” — knáttu Vanir vígspá vǿllu sporna. No poem says who won in the end, and the silence is the point: the war could not be won. What follows in every account is not conquest but exchange — the peace that can only be made by giving hostages. Vanaheimr enters the mythology as the country strong enough to stalemate heaven and wise enough to settle it. [Gylfaginning 23; Ynglinga saga 4] The Hostage Exchange: Snorri and the Ynglinga tradition tell the peace from both sides. The Vanir gave their foremost: Njörðr, raised in Vanaheimr, and with him his son Freyr. The Æsir gave Hœnir, tall and comely and thought fit to be a chieftain, and with him Mímir, wisest of men. When Hœnir proved helpless in council without Mímir at his shoulder, the Vanir reckoned themselves cheated — and they cut off Mímir's head and sent it to Óðinn, who preserved it with herbs and spells and consults it to this day for the hidden lore it tells him. From the peace itself came the third wise being: both kindreds spat into a single vat, and from the spittle the gods shaped Kvasir, wisest of all — reconciliation given a body. So the exchange that sealed the peace also seeded its bitterness. Njörðr and Freyr thrived among the Æsir and became so naturalized that Lokasenna's Loki must remind Njörðr he was only ever a hostage sent from the east. Mímir's head became Óðinn's oracle. The Vanir kept their country; the Æsir kept the immigrants; and the corpus keeps the asymmetry forever unreconciled. [Ynglinga saga 1] Vanaland by the Tanais: Snorri's Heimskringla opens its euhemerized geography with the river the medieval world called the Tanais — the Don — flowing between the peoples, and names the country on its eastern side Vanaland or Vanaheimr, and the river itself Vanakvísl. Here the mythic homeland becomes a border province of legendary history, the starting point of the migration that will carry Óðinn's people north to Sweden and set the Yngling kings at Uppsala. The move is characteristic of the Icelandic historians: every otherworld is also a country, every god also a king — and every border a river someone will cross with a dynasty in tow. Yet even euhemerized, the pattern holds — Vanaheimr remains the place one leaves to found dynasties elsewhere, the eastern home whose children rule in the west and never quite stop being foreigners.

instruction: Tell me a myth about "Yggdrasill".
output: Yggdrasill has no adventures — it is the stage on which all adventures happen. The sources do not tell stories about the tree so much as they take attendance at it: the seeress sees it first, Óðinn hangs on it, the gods ride to it daily, the creatures live in it, and at the end of things it shudders and stands. The mythology of Yggdrasill is a set of sightings, each one from a different height of the cosmos. [Völuspá 19–20] The Seeress's First Vision: The seeress of Völuspá, reciting the world's history to [[odinn|Óðinn]], comes to the tree before almost anything else: 'An ash I know standing, called Yggdrasill, a high tree, sprinkled with white clay; from it come the dews that fall in the dales; it stands ever green over Urðr's well.' Earlier still she remembered nine worlds and the mjötviðr, the measuring tree, beneath the earth — the frame was there before the filling. Beneath the tree she sees the three maidens who come from the lake under it — Urðr, Verðandi, and Skuld, the norns who carve on slips of wood and lay down laws, allotting life to the children of men. The poem's first cosmology is not a geography but a picture: one tree, one well, three women, and everything else arranged around them. [Hávamál 138–141] Nine Nights on the Windy Tree: Hávamál never names Yggdrasill, but the tradition has always read its most terrible stanzas onto it: 'I know that I hung on the windy tree nine whole nights, wounded by the spear, given to Óðinn, myself to myself, on that tree of which no man knows from what roots it rises.' No bread fed him, no horn refreshed him; he peered downward, took up the runes screaming, and fell back. The name itself is the commentary. Yggr, 'the Terrible', is an attested heiti of Óðinn, and drasill is the poets' word for a horse: the tree is 'Yggr's steed' — the gallows the hanged god rides, in the old kenning-logic by which the gallows is the hanged man's horse. The axis of the universe is named for a death, and specifically for the death a god inflicted on himself to buy knowledge. [Grímnismál 29–35] The Burden of the Ash: Grímnismál's [[odinn|Óðinn]], bound between the fires, recites the tree's census. Three roots run in three directions: one among the Æsir, one among the frost-giants where Ginnungagap once yawned, the third over Niflheimr, where Hvergelmir boils and Níðhöggr gnaws the root from below. In the branches sits an eagle, wise in much, with the hawk Veðrfölnir between its eyes; Ratatoskr the squirrel runs up and down bearing the eagle's words of spite to the serpent; four stags — Dáinn, Dvalinn, Duneyrr, Duraþrór — bite the highest shoots. Then the poem delivers its verdict, the darkest thing said about any tree: 'The ash of Yggdrasill suffers more agony than men know — a stag bites it from above, its sides are rotting, Níðhöggr gnaws it from below.' The world-order is not a monument but a wound that keeps standing. Snorri, who knows these stanzas well, builds his own account on them. [Gylfaginning 15–16] Snorri's Map of the Worlds: Snorri systematizes what the poems scatter. The chief sanctuary of the gods is the ash Yggdrasill, greatest and best of all trees: its branches spread over the whole world and reach above the sky. Of its three roots, one is among the Æsir at Urðr's well, where the gods hold their court daily, riding over [[bifrost|Bifröst]]; the second is among the frost-giants at [[mimir|Mímir]]'s well, where wisdom and understanding are hidden and Óðinn pledged his eye for a drink; the third stands over Niflheimr and the spring Hvergelmir. At Urðr's well stand the norns who shape men's fates; they take water and the clay that lies by the well and pour it over the tree so its limbs shall not wither, and the dew that falls from it men call honey-dew, the food of bees. Snorri keeps the eagle, the hawk, the squirrel, the serpents, and the stags from Grímnismál, and adds the detail that turns cosmology into hygiene: the tree must be watered, or the world dries out. [Völuspá 47; Vafþrúðnismál 44–45] The Tree at Ragnarök: When the end comes, the seeress gives the tree one line of pure dread: 'Yggdrasill's ash shudders as it stands, the old tree groans, and the giant slips free.' The cosmos announces its collapse through its axis — not by falling, but by trembling. Snorri's account of [[ragnarok|Ragnarök]] keeps the same note: heaven cloven, the sons of Muspell riding, and the ash shaking. Vafþrúðnismál looks past the fire. Óðinn asks the giant what comes after, and learns that Líf and Lífþrasir will hide in Hodd-Mímir's wood through Fimbulvetr, living on the morning dews, and from them the new mankind will spring. The scholarly tradition has long connected that sheltering wood with the world tree itself — the tree that is named for a gallows ends as the refuge of the living.

instruction: Tell me a myth about "Ginnungagap".
output: Ginnungagap has no adventures, because it is not a character but a place — or rather the condition of there being places at all. Its mythology is the first chapter of everything: the Norse creation, told in Völuspá's three terse lines and unpacked by Snorri into the finest cosmogony the Germanic world preserved. [Völuspá 3] The Gap of Ginnungs: The seeress of the Völuspá reaches back before memory, and her third stanza is the northern world’s first sentence: ‘It was at the beginning of time, when Ymir had settled — there was no sand nor sea nor cool waves; earth existed nowhere, nor sky above; a gap of ginnungs was there, but grass nowhere.’ That is the entire notice the oldest poem gives — two words, gap ginnunga , in the reversed order the later prose preferred — and everything Snorri builds hangs on them. Nothing acts in the verse; no god speaks. The poem simply registers an emptiness where the world will later be, with the first giant already housed at its edge and no grass yet anywhere. The compound itself is a puzzle the stanza declines to solve: whether ginnunga means ‘magic-charged powers’ or is kin to ginna , ‘to deceive, bewitch’, the lexica still argue. The void enters literature already wearing its oldest trick: a name no one could agree on, and a silence no one could fill. [Gylfaginning 4–5] Fog in the North, Fire in the South: Asked what was before the earth, Hár tells Gylfi that Niflheimr was made many ages before the world: a dark world of mist with the spring Hvergelmir at its heart, from which run the rivers called the Élivágar — Svǫl, Gunnþrá, Fjǫrm, Fimbulþul, Slíðr and Hríð, Sylgr and Ylgr, Víð, Leiptr, and Gjǫll, which flows nearest the gate of Hel. Far from that spring the rivers hardened like the slag that runs from a forge, turned to ice, and spread rime and freezing fog northward. But the southern part of Ginnungagap faced Muspellsheimr, the bright, burning world no foreigner can enter, where Surtr stands guard at the border with a flaming sword — and the sparks and glowing embers that flew out of Muspellsheimr lightened the gap from below. [Gylfaginning 5–6] The Mild Void and the Quickening: Between the two, Snorri says, Ginnungagap was as mild as a windless sky. Where the warm air from the south met the rime from the north, the ice thawed and dripped — and by the power of the one who sent the heat, the running drops quickened and took the likeness of a man. He is named Ymir, though the rime-giants call him Aurgelmir, and from him their whole race descends; asked whether Ymir was a god, Hár answers flatly that he and all his kin were evil. From the same rime-drops came the cow Auðhumla, whose four rivers of milk fed the giant, and who licked the salty rime-stones until, over three days, a man emerged whole from the ice: Búri, the grandfather of the gods. [Gylfaginning 7–8] The Flood and the Fashioning: Búri's son Borr married Bestla, daughter of the giant Bǫlþorn, and their sons were Óðinn, Vili, and Vé — and the first act of the new gods in the old void was a killing. They slew Ymir, and so much blood ran from his wounds that the whole race of rime-giants drowned, save one: Bergelmir, who climbed with his wife onto his lúðr — a word that may mean a boat or a chest — and from whom the giants of the frost descend anew. The brothers dragged Ymir's body into the middle of Ginnungagap and made the world of it: the earth from his flesh, the sea and lakes from his blood, the mountains from his bones and teeth, the sky from his skull, held up at the four corners by the dwarfs Norðri, Suðri, Austri, and Vestri, and the clouds from his brains. The sparks that flew out of Muspellsheimr they set in the sky as stars. Thus the gap was not filled so much as furnished: everything that exists is a giant's body arranged inside the old emptiness. [Vafþrúðnismál 21 · Grímnismál 40–41] The Poets' Version: The Poetic Edda confirms Snorri’s outline from its own witnesses. Vafþrúðnir the giant, questioned by Óðinn about the first origin of giant-kind, answers that out of the Élivágar sprang venom-drops, eitr , which grew and hardened until a giant quickened from them (Vafþrúðnismál 21). And Grímnismál gives the fashioning in verse: ‘From Ymir’s flesh the earth was shaped, the mountains from his bones, the sky from the skull of the frost-cold giant, and from his blood the sea’ — adding that the gracious powers made Miðgarðr for the sons of men from his eyebrows, and the hard-mooded clouds from his brains (Grímnismál 40–41). The poems do not name the gap as often as Snorri does, but they supply its inventory: ice-rivers, venom, melt, and a world assembled from a corpse. Between verse and prose the account is told twice from independent witnesses — a redundancy rare enough in Norse myth to count as corroboration, and the reason this cosmogony is among the best-attested in the medieval North.

instruction: Tell me a myth about "Wyrd".
output: Wyrd has no mythology in the usual sense — no birth, no hall, no marriage — because Wyrd is not a figure but the Old English word for fate itself. What it has instead is a dossier of sentences: the moments where the poets reach for the word and the whole Anglo-Saxon theory of destiny shows through. Four witnesses matter most — the Wanderer, Beowulf, the proverb poems, and Alfred's Boethius — and one northern mirror, the norn Urðr. [The Wanderer 5] Fate Is Wholly Fixed: The Exeter Book's exile opens his elegy with the coldest sentence in Old English: 'Wyrd bið ful ārǣd' — fate is wholly fixed, fully resolved, past all appeal. He has buried his lord, crossed the winter seas, and found no hall that will take him in; the word wyrd is the name he gives the weight of all of it. Near the poem's end the word returns in its grandest frame: 'eall is earfoðlīc eorþan rīce, onwendeð wyrda gesceaft weoruld under heofonum' — all is full of hardship in the earthly kingdom; the decree of fates turns the world under heaven. Note what the poem does not do: it gives Wyrd no face, no spindle, no shrine. The word stays a noun of process — the way things go — and the poem's consolation is not that Wyrd can be moved but that God alone is the fastness that stands when her turning is done. [Beowulf 455, 572] Fate Goes as She Must: Beowulf speaks the word at every threshold. Before Grendel he commits the night to it: 'Gǣð ā wyrd swā hīo sceal' — fate goes always as she must. Surfacing from the mere's edge of disaster he states the exception that governs his whole career: 'Wyrd oft nereð unfǣgne eorl, þonne his ellen dēah' — fate often spares the undoomed man, when his courage avails. The two sentences together are the poem's whole theology: doom is real for the doomed (fǣge), but for the undoomed, courage and fate divide the work. When the dragon comes, the old king feels the balance tip: he knows himself fǣge, and wyrd no longer negotiates. The poet's grammar is exact — fate is spoken of as 'she' (hīo), grammatically feminine, half-personified by the pronoun alone, yet never once given a name, a household, or a cult. [Maxims II; Solomon and Saturn] Fate Is Strongest: The proverb tradition keeps the word's power in its bluntest form. Maxims II, the catalogue of how things are, ranks her first among forces: 'Wyrd byð swīðost' — fate is strongest — ahead of winter's cold and spring's frost. The dialogue of Solomon and Saturn gives Saturn the matching proverb: fate is hard to turn, and neither wealth nor kinship can turn her. These are the word's working senses — what the farmers and homilists meant when the poets were not listening: the unalterable course of what happens, stronger than every other thing the maxims catalogue. The homilies sharpen the point: in the Vercelli and Corpus tradition wyrd names the world's turning that must not be trusted, set against the God who stands unmoved above it — the same noun, but already half-tamed toward Alfred's settlement. [Alfred's Boethius] The Christian Taming of Wyrd: When King Alfred's circle translated Boethius's Consolation of Philosophy into Old English, they had to decide what to do with Fortuna and her wheel. They kept the native word: wyrd translates Fortuna throughout — but the translation is a conquest, not a courtesy. Alfred's text subordinates her absolutely: wyrd is God's work and God's instrument, the name for his providence as it is felt from below, turning the world the way a wheelwright turns a wheel — while the nave, God himself, stands still. The Alfredian additions are explicit: Lady Philosophy rebukes the translator's own people for blaming wyrd, and the prose preface promises that Boethius's book will teach them what power she truly has — none, save what God lends her. It is the great re-founding of the word: the pagan noun of unalterable event is retained, baptized, and set to work inside a Christian providence. Every later English use of wyrd and weird lives downstream of this translation. [Völuspá 19–20; Gylfaginning 15–16] The Northern Sister: The Old Norse cognate is not a common noun but a name: Urðr, 'what has become', eldest of the three Norns. Völuspá sets the scene beneath Yggdrasill, where the well stands under the tree: thence come three maidens, deep in wisdom — Urðr one is called, Verðandi the second, Skuld the third. They laid down laws, they allotted life to the children of men, fates to be told. Snorri adds the daily rite: the Norns draw water from Urðr's well and pour it with the clay over the tree's roots, so its branches do not wither. England kept the word a noun; Iceland made it a person. The two traditions preserve one inheritance in two grammars — and the PuniCodex lexicon files Wyrd under the Norse pantheon precisely for this kinship, the English word recorded in Beowulf answering its sister at the well.
