instruction: Tell me a myth about "Macha".
output: Macha's dossier is one great tale and a family of namesakes: the Debility of the Ulstermen gives her the race, the twins, and the curse; the Táin harvests the consequences; the Lebor Gabála remembers her as Nemed's wife and as the red-maned queen; and the genealogies fold her into the three of war beside [[badb|Badb]] and [[morrigan|the Morrígan]]. [Noínden Ulad] The Woman at Cruinniuc's Door: Cruinniuc mac Agnomain was a rich farmer of the Ulaid, a widower with sons, and one day a woman he had never seen walked into his house, set about the work of it without a word, and lay with him that night. She stayed, and under her hand everything prospered — the house, the cattle, the table — and she told him the one condition of their life together: he must never speak of her, never boast of her. It is the old compact of the otherworld wife, and it held as long as he kept his mouth shut. The tale that tells this — Noínden Ulad, 'The Debility of the Ulaid', one of the fore-tales of the Táin — is a sovereignty story before it is anything else: the land's own woman comes to the man of the land, and her condition is silence about the source of the plenty. Cruinniuc kept it until the day of the great assembly of the Ulaid, when the talk turned to the king's horses and there was nothing in the world faster. [Noínden Ulad] The Race, the Twins, and the Curse: At the assembly Cruinniuc forgot the condition and boasted: his wife could outrun the king's chariot-horses. Conchobar had him seized, and sent for the woman — who was nine months gone with twins. She begged the gathering for delay until she had given birth, 'for a mother bore each of you'; the Ulaid refused. She was set against the horses and raced them, and she beat them at the line — and at the line the pangs took her, and she was delivered of a boy and a girl on the field. Then she cursed them: as she had been given no mercy in her labor, so the men of Ulster, in their hour of greatest straits, would suffer the pangs of a woman in childbirth — five days and four nights, for nine generations, every man save the boys and the women. And in most recensions she died there. The twins gave the royal seat of Ulster its name: Emain Macha, 'Macha's twins'. It is the most economical curse in Irish literature — one wrong, answered in exact kind, for nine generations. [Táin Bó Cúailnge] The Debility in the Táin: The curse is the engine of the greatest Irish epic. When [[medb|Medb]] of Connacht marches into Ulster for the Donn Cúailnge, the men of the province are down in the ces noínden, gripped by the pangs Macha laid on them — the curse spared the boys and the women, and it spared [[cuchulainn|Cú Chulainn]], who stands alone against the host of Ireland while the warriors of Emain writhe. The whole boyhood-deeds section of the Táin is narrated against the debility: one boy holding a province because a goddess was made to race in labor. The Táin keeps her name in the language of battle as well. Its phrase for the harvest of heads is mesrad Machae, 'Macha's mast' — the crop the war-goddess gathers from the field. And the Lebor Gabála had already counted her among the three daughters of Ernmas: [[badb|Badb]] and Macha and Anand, 'of whom are the Paps of Anu' — the triple face of Irish war, the sisters the sources also gather under the one name [[morrigan|Morrígan]]. [Lebor Gabála Érenn] The Queens and the Naming of Emain: The book of invasions remembers two earlier Machas. The first is Macha wife of Nemed, who came with the Nemedians in the days before the Túatha Dé Danann; she died in Ireland, and Ard Macha — Armagh, 'Macha's height' — and Mag Macha, 'Macha's plain', the country around it, are named from her grave. The second is Macha Mongrúad, the red-maned daughter of Áed Rúad. When her father and his brothers Díthorba and Cimbáeth had held the kingship of Ireland in rotation, seven years each, and Áed died, the brothers refused the daughter her turn. She took it by war: she married Cimbáeth, defeated Díthorba's five sons — after going to them, the tale says, in the guise of a leprous hag — and held the kingship herself. It was she who marked out the rampart of Emain Macha with the brooch of her neck, her eo-muin, and made the captives dig it. The dindsenchas keeps both etymologies side by side — Macha's twins and Macha's brooch — and the tradition never chose between the goddess of the race and the queen of the fort.

instruction: Tell me a myth about "Fionn".
output: Fionn's cycle is the fullest hero-corpus Ireland kept: the Boyhood Deeds that make him wise, the Fenian lays and ballads that make him captain, and the two late romances — the pursuit of Diarmaid and the lay of Oisín — that make him tragic. [Macgnímartha Finn] The Boy in the Wild: Fionn's father was Cumhall mac Trénmhóir, captain of the Fianna, who abducted Muirne, daughter of the druid Tadg, when her father refused her. Tadg's appeal brought the king's army, and Cumhall fell at the battle of Cnucha to Goll mac Morna, head of the rival Clann Morna. Muirne bore the child in danger and gave him to two women to rear in secret: Bodbmall the druidess and Liath Luachra the warrior-woman, who raised him in the wild places away from his father's enemies. When the boy grew strong he went openly to his grandfather Tadg and exacted the blood-price for Cumhall — the hill of Allen, Almhain, which would become the Fianna's seat. The women they hid him from gave the world the name by which the manuscripts remember him: the boy they raised was named Demne; the name the world would keep was still swimming in the Boyne. [Macgnímartha Finn] The Salmon of Knowledge: Demne came to learn poetry from Finn Éces, Finn the poet, who had waited seven years on the Boyne for the salmon of knowledge — the fish that had fed on the nuts of the nine hazels dropping into the well of Segais, so that all the knowledge of the world was in its flesh. When at last the salmon was caught, the poet set the boy to cook it and forbade him to taste any part of it. A blister rose on the fish's skin; Demne pressed it down with his thumb, burned himself, and thrust the thumb into his mouth — and the knowledge was his. Finn Éces asked the boy his name, heard 'Demne', and told him: Finn is your name now, for it was Finn who was prophesied to eat this salmon. The boy ate what remained, and ever after needed only to chew his thumb to know what was hidden. [Macgnímartha Finn] Aillén and the Burning of Tara: Every Samain night for twenty-three years, Aillén of the three tongues came out of síd Finnachaidh and burned Tara: he played his timpán so sweetly that every man in the fortress fell asleep, and then he breathed fire over the hall. Fionn came to Tara on Samain, and Fíacha mac Conga, who had served his father, gave him a magic spear and the instruction: hold its naked point to your forehead, and you will not sleep. So Fionn sat wakeful while the court slept around him, and when Aillén turned back for the síd, Fionn cast the spear through him. For that deed Conn Cétchathach restored to him his father's treasure and made him head of the Fianna — and Goll mac Morna, his father's killer, accepted the peace and became the most loyal of his captains. [Tóruigheacht Dhiarmada agus Ghráinne] The Pursuit of Diarmaid and Gráinne: In his age Fionn was betrothed to Gráinne, daughter of Cormac mac Airt, but at the feast she gave a sleeping-draught to the company and laid a geis — the bond no Fenian could refuse — on Diarmaid Ó Duibhne to take her away. Diarmaid bore a ball seirce, a love-spot on his forehead that no woman could see without loving him, and Gráinne had seen it. For sixteen years the Fianna hunted the pair the length of Ireland, with Óengus of the Brug shielding Diarmaid where he could, until the tale came to the boar-hunt on Ben Bulben: the beast was Diarmaid's own foster-brother, transformed, and it was fated to be his death. Diarmaid killed the boar and took its venom in the doing. Fionn could heal any wound with water carried in his two cupped hands — he had the gift since the salmon — and twice he brought the water from the well and let it slip through his fingers, remembering Gráinne; when Óscar's reproach sent him back the third time, Diarmaid was dead. [Acallam na Senórach / Laoi Oisín] Oisín in Tír na nÓg and the Long Memory: Fionn's son Oisín was taken across the sea by Niamh of the Golden Hair, daughter of the king of Tír na nÓg, the Land of Youth, riding behind her on a white horse that never touched water. What he counted as three years in that country were three hundred years in Ireland. Homesick, he was lent the horse to visit and warned on no account to set foot on Irish soil; he found the Fianna gone and their names become legend, and as he stooped from the saddle to help men shift a stone, the girth broke. Oisín touched the ground, and three hundred years fell on him at once. The medieval Acallam na Senórach frames the whole Fenian memory on this survival: the old, blind Oisín and Caílte mac Rónáin traveling Christian Ireland with Saint Patrick, naming every hill and ford and telling how they were won — the Fianna kept alive as long as one man could still remember them.

instruction: Tell me a myth about "Ogma".
output: Ogma's dossier is compact and exact: the Lebor Gabála gives his lineage, Cath Maige Tuired gives his deeds — the serf-labor under Bres, the flagstone test at Lugh's coming, the killing of the Fomorian king's son, and the talking sword — and the learned tradition gives him his strangest honor, the invention of the ogham. [Lebor Gabála Érenn] The Son of Elatha: The Lebor Gabála Érenn, Ireland's medieval book of invasions, writes Ogma into the divine genealogy: Ogma son of Elatha, of the line of Delbaeth, and so the brother of the Dagda himself. The surname carries a sting the saga does not hide — the same Elatha, the beautiful Fomorian prince who came as an arbiter to the Túatha Dé, is father of Bres by a Fomorian woman, which makes the champion of the gods the half-brother of the usurper who will set him hauling firewood. When the Túatha Dé Danann came to Ireland out of the four northern cities, Ogma came with them as the champion of the race — in trenfer, the strong man, the standing title the texts give him. His place in the pantheon is therefore double from the first mention: the arm of the Túatha Dé Danann, and the brother of their all-father, with the enemy's blood already in his own house. [Cath Maige Tuired] The Firewood of the Serf-Years: When the half-Fomorian Bres was made king and laid the Túatha Dé Danann under tribute, the greatest of them were put to work like serfs — deliberately, for the tribute was calculated to break the mighty. The Dagda was set to building raths, and Ogma — the champion of the whole divine race — was set to hauling firewood for the fortress. The tale does not spare him: so weakened was he by hunger that the sea washed over him as he carried the fuel. The servitude did not blunt him; when the war came he killed the Fomorian king's son with his bare champion's art, and the firewood years became the measure of what was repaid. But the image stands as the tradition's sharpest statement of what Bres' kingship cost: the strong man of the gods, bent double under a usurper's faggots, with the tide at his knees. [Cath Maige Tuired] The Flagstone Test: When Lugh came to Tara before the battle, asking admission by his arts, it fell to Ogma to test the stranger's strength — the doorkeeper's office, and the champion's. Ogma hurled the great flagstone of the rath, a stone beyond the lifting of ordinary men, and Lugh answered by hurling it back through the rath to its own place. Ogma then challenged the newcomer to single combat, and Lugh declined: his arts, he said, would be tested soon enough against the Fomorians. The episode is the tradition's own changing of the guard, and it is conducted with a courtesy the Túatha Dé rarely manage elsewhere — a test, a verdict, and no feud. The old champion made way, stone by stone, for the many-skilled king who would lead the war, and the championship of Ireland passed hands without a blow struck in anger. [Cath Maige Tuired] Indech Slain, and the Sword That Spoke: At the second battle of Mag Tuired the champion earned his title back. In the press of the fighting Ogma killed Indech, son of Dé Domnann, a king of the Fomorians — the same Indech whose blood the Mórrígan had promised the Dagda at the ford. And after the battle came the strangest prize in the Irish corpus: among the spoils Ogma found Orna, the sword of Tethra, king of the Fomorians. He unsheathed it and cleaned it, and the sword recounted all the deeds that had been done with it — for it was the custom of swords in those days, when drawn, to tell what they had done. The champion of the gods carried the only weapon in the world that could bear witness to itself: in Ogma's hand even the enemy's steel testified, because testimony is what this champion is for. [Cath Maige Tuired] The Recovery of the Harp: After the rout, the Fomorians had carried off the Dagda's harper, Uaithne, and the harp itself hung on the wall of the hall where Bres feasted. Three of the Túatha Dé Danann went in pursuit: Lugh, the Dagda, and Ogma — the king, the all-father, and the champion. The Dagda called the harp by its names, Daur Da Bláo and Coir Cethar Chuir, and it sprang from the wall to his hand, killing nine men in its path, and played the three strains of weeping, laughter, and sleep until the whole enemy host slept. Ogma walked out of that hall beside his brother and his king, through sleeping foes — the serf of the firewood years restored to the company of the gods' great deeds. [Auraicept na n-Éces] The Father of the Ogham: The Scholars' Primer — the Auraicept na n-Éces, the medieval Irish grammar of the poets — closes Ogma's dossier with the honor no other Irish god receives. Ogma, a man well skilled in speech and in poetry, invented the ogham for the speaking of Gaelic; and the tract fixes the paternity in a formula: the father of the ogham is Ogma, and the mother of the ogham is the hand or the knife of Ogma. Cormac's Glossary, compiled a generation before the Primer, already glosses the god's name from ogum, the ogham itself — in the Irish learned tradition, the alphabet and its father were one word. The glossarial tradition adds the epithet Grianainech, the Sun-faced. The champion who hauled firewood under a usurper is the same figure the learned tradition made the author of the alphabet itself — strength and letters, in Ireland, kept in one hand.

instruction: Tell me a myth about "Arawn".
output: Arawn's whole dossier is one story, and it is the opening movement of the Mabinogi: the hunting-debt at Glyn Cuch and the year-long exchange that turns an insult into the strongest friendship in Welsh prose. Every word of it is preserved in the First Branch, Pwyll Pendefig Dyfed. [First Branch · Pwyll Pendefig Dyfed] The Wrong at Glyn Cuch: Pwyll, lord of Dyfed, goes hunting at Glyn Cuch, and there he sees a sight he has never seen: a pack of hounds shining white with red ears bringing down a stag. He drives them off and sets his own hounds on the kill — and the stranger who rides up is Arawn, king of Annwn, and it was his hunt. Arawn names the discourtesy plainly: he will not take revenge, but a man who feeds his hounds on another's kill has wronged him, and Pwyll offers to buy back his friendship at whatever price. Arawn names it. He has a rival, Hafgan, king of the other realm of Annwn, who wars on him without end; let Pwyll take Arawn's shape and his place for a year and a day, and meet Hafgan at the ford at the year's turning. The insult that opens the Mabinogi is small; the answer to it is a year's borrowed life, and the tale means to show what a king is made of when the test is set by his enemy and graded by his wife. [First Branch · Pwyll Pendefig Dyfed] The Exchange of Shapes: Each king takes the other's form and goes to the other's court, and neither realm suspects. Arawn rules Dyfed so well that there had never been so good a year in it. Pwyll enters Annwn in Arawn's likeness, and that first night he is led to the bed of Arawn's wife — the fairest and most comely woman he had ever seen. He turns his back to her, and he does so every night of the year: he speaks to her with courtesy by day, and in the bed he never once turns his face toward her. The queen never knows. The whole test of the tale is here, in the dark, where no one could have seen the difference — and that is exactly the point. The First Branch argues that honor is what a man does when the only witness is himself, and it stakes the argument on a bed no court could inspect. [First Branch · Pwyll Pendefig Dyfed] The Single Blow at the Ford: Arawn's instructions were exact: Hafgan — the name suggests 'summer-white' — can be slain by one blow, and only one; strike him a second time and he will rise as strong as before and fight again the next day. At the appointed time the two kings meet at the ford, and at the first clash Pwyll strikes Hafgan one blow that shears through his shield and his armour to the ground, and Hafgan knows that he is dead. 'For God's sake,' he begs, 'finish me' — and Pwyll refuses: the stroke he gave is all Hafgan will have from him. Hafgan's nobles declare their king lost, and Pwyll takes the submission and hostages of Hafgan's realm, so that the two kingdoms of Annwn are made one under Arawn's crown. Restraint, the tale says, is the last weapon of the strong: the blow withheld did what no blow could, and won a war with half a sword-stroke. [First Branch · Pwyll Pendefig Dyfed] The Restoration and the Title: The two kings meet again at the ford where they had arranged it, each in his own shape, and embrace and go home. Arawn's queen, rejoicing at his return, remarks that he has not spoken to her so sweetly for a whole year — and Arawn praises God for a friend so true. In Dyfed, Pwyll's court hears the story and tells him he did well to make such a friend. From that time the two realms send each other gifts every year: horses and greyhounds and hawks, and every kind of treasure they think will please. And because Pwyll had ruled Annwn and joined its two kingdoms in one, he was called from then on Pwyll Pen Annwn — Pwyll Head of Annwn — in place of Pwyll lord of Dyfed. The exchange ends where the best contracts end: both parties richer, neither diminished, and the friendship audited annually in horses, hawks, and hounds. [Later Welsh tradition] The Hounds and the Spoils of Annwn: The Mabinogi never brings Arawn back on stage, but his world keeps growing. The poem Preiddeu Annwfn, 'The Spoils of Annwn', preserved in the Book of Taliesin, sends Arthur's men in three ships to raid the Otherworld for the cauldron of the Head of Annwfn — Pen Annwfn, the very title the First Branch gives Pwyll as an honor — and only seven come home. The poem never names Annwn's king, and honest scholarship leaves him unnamed. Later Welsh folklore knows the Cŵn Annwn, the Hounds of Annwn — white with red ears, exactly Arawn's pack — whose baying across the night sky was heard as a death-omen, and folk tradition gave their mastery to Gwyn ap Nudd rather than to Arawn. The hounds outgrew their first master; the year of the exchange did not. Arawn's afterlife is that of a perfect guest: he appears once, conducts the greatest test in Welsh prose, and is thereafter remembered in the hounds, the title, and the ford.

instruction: Tell me a myth about "Gwydion".
output: Gwydion fab Dôn is the enchanter of the Fourth Branch of the Mabinogi, 'Math fab Mathonwy': nephew of Math the king of Gwynedd, brother of Gilfaethwy, and the foremost magician of medieval Welsh literature. He is poet, trickster, foster-father, and avenger in one figure — the man who makes illusions that pass for wealth, who pays for his crimes in animal skins, and who ends the tale as the careful hand that puts a broken world back into shape. [Math fab Mathonwy] The War for the Swine: King Math of Gwynedd could live only with his feet in the lap of a virgin, except in time of war, and the maiden Goewin held that office. When Gilfaethwy desired her, Gwydion devised the remedy: war. He went to Pryderi of Dyfed in the guise of a poet and asked for the swine — the hobeu, the first pigs ever brought to Wales, a gift from Arawn of Annwfn. Refused, he conjured twelve stallions with golden harness, twelve greyhounds with golden collars, and twelve golden shields, and traded the apparitions for the herd. By the time Pryderi's glamour faded, Gwydion was gone, and Pryderi came north with an army. While Math marched to meet him, Gwydion and Gilfaethwy forced Goewin. At the peace-talks Pryderi demanded single combat, 'for it was because of me that the hosts came'; at Maenor Penard, the tale says, Gwydion slew him 'by strength and valour and by magic and enchantment', and Dyfed went home under tribute. The victory is real and so is its cost: Gwydion's finest trick is also his crime, and the Fourth Branch never lets the two be separated. [Math fab Mathonwy] The Punishment of the Brothers: Math's justice is the strangest in the Mabinogi. He struck Gwydion and Gilfaethwy with his magic wand and turned them into a stag and a hind, and sent them into the wild for a year; when they returned with a fawn, he made them a boar and a sow for the second year, and a wolf and a she-wolf for the third. Each year their offspring — Hyddwn, Hychddwn Hir, and Bleiddwn — were sent to the court, baptized, and raised. After the third year Math struck them back into their own shapes: 'You have had punishment enough, and you have been greatly shamed.' The punishment is exact and even-handed — the brothers suffer in the flesh what they did, and when the debt is paid the king takes them back into honour. It is the Fourth Branch's doctrine of justice in miniature: transformation as sentence, restoration as mercy. And it matters that the wand passes finally into Gwydion's own hand: the man punished by shape-shaping becomes the master of it, and the tale watches to see what he does with the power that once unmade him. [Math fab Mathonwy] The Naming and Arming of Lleu: When Gwydion proposed his sister Arianrhod as Math's new footholder, she stepped over the wand for the virginity test and dropped a yellow-haired boy — Dylan, who made for the sea — and 'something small' that Gwydion hid in a chest at the foot of his bed. From the chest came the boy who would be Lleu. Gwydion fostered him, and Arianrhod, shamed, laid three tynghedau upon him: he should have no name until she named him, no arms until she armed him, and no wife of any race then on earth. Gwydion undid the destinies by craft. Disguised as a shoemaker with the boy at his side, he came beneath Caer Arianrhod, and when Lleu flung a stone and struck a wren's leg askew, Arianrhod cried that the fair one had struck it with a skilful hand — and so named him Lleu Llaw Gyffes. For the arms, Gwydion conjured a phantom fleet against the castle until Arianrhod herself armed the defenders. The magician wins not by force but by arranging the world so that his opponent speaks the words he needs: the tynged is a lock, and Gwydion's trade is keys. [Math fab Mathonwy] The Flower-Maiden and the Eagle: For the third tynged there was no earthly answer, so Gwydion and Math made one: from the flowers of the oak, the broom, and the meadowsweet they fashioned the fairest woman anyone had seen, and named her Blodeuwedd, 'Flower-face'. She married Lleu — and betrayed him with Gronw Pebr of Penllyn, drawing from her husband the secret of how he could be killed, so that Gronw's spear struck him at the impossible meeting of conditions and Lleu flew off in the shape of an eagle, screaming. Gwydion searched Gwynedd and Powys until he followed a sow to an oak where rotten flesh fell to her snout, and in the top of the tree sat the eagle. He sang three englynion down the perches of the years until Lleu came to his knee, then struck him with the wand back into human shape — skin and bone, to be nursed with doctors and good care. The vengeance was as crafted as the rescue: Blodeuwedd he would not kill, but turned into an owl, 'the shape hated by all the birds'; and Gronw, standing where Lleu had stood, took Lleu's spear-cast through the slab at Llech Gronw and died. Maker of the woman, finder of the man, instrument of the sentence: Gwydion's whole domain is in this last movement. [Kat Godeu] The Battle of the Trees: Outside the Mabinogi, the Book of Taliesin preserves Gwydion's other great fame: Kat Godeu, 'The Battle of the Trees', in which he enchants the trees of the forest to march as an army — the alder in the van, the oak amid the hosts. The poem's speaker, Taliesin, boasts that he was there when Gwydion 'made the sally of the trees'. In the tale-material gathered around the poem, the sons of Dôn fight the forces of Annwfn over a white roebuck, a whelp, and a lapwing, and the battle turns when the hidden name of the enemy's champion is guessed from the alder twigs in his hand — the same magic of the name that the Fourth Branch shows in the wren scene. Whether the poem preserves older myth or later learned fancy is honestly debated, but its Gwydion is unmistakably the Mabinogi's: the magician whose weapons are other things' natures, who wins by knowing what a thing is called and what it can be made to do.

instruction: Tell me a myth about "Eachuisge".
output: The each-uisge has no medieval manuscript behind him: his mythology is oral, and its primary witnesses are the great nineteenth-century field collections of the Highlands — Campbell of Islay's Popular Tales of the West Highlands and John Gregorson Campbell's Superstitions of the Highlands and Islands of Scotland. The tales agree on the essentials with the consistency of a warning passed from shore to shore. [Highland oral tradition] The Rider Taken: The core of every telling is the same. A traveler on the shore of a loch finds a beautiful horse standing idle — fine beyond any horse in the parish, saddled by luck, or so it seems. He mounts; the horse is smooth and willing; and then the rider finds his hands fast to the hide, stuck as if with bird-lime, and the horse's head already turned toward the water. The loch takes them both. In the grimmest tellings the loch gives the rider back in pieces — the tradition is exact about this: the each-uisge devours the whole body, and what floats ashore is the liver alone. That detail is the Highland folklore's way of drawing the line between its own water horse and the Lowland kelpie, which drowns but does not eat. [Highland oral tradition] The Boy Who Cut Off His Finger: The best-known of the warning-tales gives the creature a longer game. A fine horse appears to children playing by a loch, and one by one they climb its back — and the back lengthens to take them, seat after seat, until all are mounted save one wary boy, who will only touch the hide with a finger. The horse springs for the water with its load of children, and the boy, stuck by that single finger, does the one thing left: he cuts the finger off and escapes. The loch gives back the others the next day, piecemeal. The collectors recorded the tale across the Highlands, and Briggs notes it among the each-uisge's defining episodes: the compound's lesson compressed into a single image — touch with everything and you lose everything; touch with a finger and a finger pays for the lesson. [Highland oral tradition] The Handsome Stranger: The horse is only the working shape. The each-uisge also walks ashore as a fine young man, and the tales of the loch-side courting are as consistent as the tales of the ride. A girl meets a handsome stranger by the water; he lays his head in her lap and sleeps; and as she combs his hair with her fingers she finds in it the sand and weed of the loch bottom. She understands what is sleeping on her knee, eases her skirt free, and runs — and behind her the shape comes apart into horse and water. The weed in the hair is the tradition's signature: the shape-shifter can borrow any face but cannot shed the mark of the element he came from. The weed is the tale's thesis: no disguise cancels origin, and the element always signs its work. [Highland oral tradition] The Red-Hot Iron: The record also remembers that the each-uisge can be killed, and how. Ordinary iron and ordinary courage fail against a thing that lives in the water; the answer the tales keep is fire carried into iron. In the well-known Highland account preserved by John Gregorson Campbell, a smith destroys a water horse with a red-hot iron — a spear or bar heated in the forge and driven home while the creature is held fast. The pattern is the old one the collectors noted across Gaelic tradition: the supernatural yields to the smith, whose craft joins the two elements the water horse cannot master — fire, and the metal that remembers it. The tale matters to the record because it is nearly unique: almost everything else the Highlands says about the each-uisge is a way to avoid him.

instruction: Tell me a myth about "Izanami".
output: Izanami's mythology is central to Japanese understandings of creation, death, and the boundary between the living and the dead — and it never forgives her for speaking first at the pillar. [The Stirring] She Who Stirred the Brine: The heavenly kami gave the command to the pair, but it was Izanami who set her hand on the spear. Standing upon the Floating Bridge of Heaven, she and Izanagi lowered the jeweled Ame-no-Nuboko into the formless ocean and stirred; the brine dripping from its tip congealed into Onogoroshima, and upon that first island the couple founded their union and their hall (Kojiki 1). The chronicles, even while making her the mother of everything, mark her as the one who stepped outside the ritual order — she spoke the first greeting at the pillar — and who suffered for it. Everything that follows, islands, gods, death, night, proceeds from her equal hand on the spear. The creation is a marriage as much as a manufacture: the world begins in a couple's shared labor, and its first law is how they address each other. [The Wrong Word] Hiruko, the Leech-Child: When the couple circled the heavenly pillar to greet each other and beget, Izanami spoke first; their firstborn, Hiruko, was a boneless child who could not stand even at the age of three, and they set him adrift in a reed boat (Kojiki 1). Consulting the heavenly kami, they learned the error — the man's voice must come first — and repeated the rite in the proper order; Izanami then bore the eight great islands and the gods of wind, river, sea, and mountain. Modern readers have reclaimed Hiruko as a poignant emblem, the 'sun-child' as the name can be parsed, the disabled firstborn of the gods; some traditions even drifted to connect the drifting child with Ebisu. But the chronicle records him only as the price of a word out of place. For Izanami the myth is a double wound: blamed for the error, she is then consumed bearing the children that redeem it. [The Burning] Death by the Fire Child: Her last birth was Kagutsuchi , the fire god. The child burned her as he was born, and Izanami lay dying, her lower body seared. Even in death the creation did not stop: from her vomit came the mountain-smith Kanayamahiko , from her excrement the clay-god Haniyasu, from her urine the water-goddess Mitsuhanome — and from her head, breast, belly, loins, left and right hands and feet came the eight thunder deities, Yakusanoikazuchi, who would one day guard her in Yomi (Kojiki 1). She named the mountain of her burial before she died: Mount Hiba, in the land of Kibi. The passage is the Kojiki at its most elemental: the mother of everything dies of her most brilliant child, and her dying body, catalogued organ by organ, becomes the map of the underworld she is about to rule. [The Curse] One Thousand, One Thousand Five Hundred: In Yomi, when Izanagi broke his promise and lit the comb, Izanami — maggot-crowned, thunder-fleshed — cried that he had shamed her, and sent the hags and the eight thunders after him. He escaped to the slope of Yomotsu-hirasaka and rolled the great boulder into the pass between them. Then the dead queen pronounced the verdict that still governs the world: each day, she said, I will strangle a thousand of the people of your land. From the other side of the stone Izanagi answered: then each day I will cause fifteen hundred to be born (Kojiki 1). Her curse is not repealed but outpaced — death legislated in daily arithmetic, answered by a larger birthrate. The exchange is Japan's theodicy in a single statistic: the grave wins every skirmish and loses the census.

instruction: Tell me a myth about "Ninigi".
output: Ninigi's mythology is the bridge between the heavenly realm of Amaterasu and the earthly rule of the emperors: four scenes — the descent, the negotiated surrender of the land, the ordeal by fire that proved his wife's fidelity, and the genealogy that produced Jimmu — suffice to carry three regalia and a nation from the Floating Bridge of Heaven to Kashihara. [Kojiki I] The Descent from Heaven: When Amaterasu resolved that the land of reed plains should be governed from heaven, she chose not her son but her grandson. She gave Ninigi the Three Sacred Regalia — the mirror Yata, the sword Kusanagi that Susanoo had won from the eight-forked serpent, and the curved jewel Yasakani — and sent him down, escorted by the deities Ame-no-koyane and Futodama, from the Floating Bridge of Heaven to Takachiho in Kyūshū. The Kojiki (Book I) frames the descent as a transfer of title: heaven holds sovereignty, and the earth must receive it. One detail sharpens the stakes. As Ninigi left, Amaterasu told him the mirror was to be worshipped as her own spirit — the warrant of his rule was simultaneously her presence. A thousand generations of imperial ideology condensed into a single instruction: the emperor rules because he carries what Ninigi carried. The myth means that legitimacy, in the Japanese telling, is a thing handed down, not taken. [Kojiki I] Ōkuninushi's Withdrawal: The earth, however, was occupied. Its master, the great kami Ōkuninushi, had built and governed the land — some say he had won it by ordeal and war — and heaven's envoy could not simply take it. The Kojiki (Book I) tells how Ninigi pressed the matter through negotiation rather than battle, with pressure from the celestial host. Ōkuninushi consulted his sons; his wise son Kotoshironushi, recognising heaven's claim, withdrew of his own accord and is still honored at Mount Miwa. His father then set his price: a great sanctuary built for him at Kizuki in Izumo — the origin of the shrine now called Izumo Ōyashiro — and the keeping of the land's hidden, numinous affairs. In one stroke the myth explains two of Japan's greatest shrines and establishes a template of Japanese statecraft: conquest by diplomacy, and the defeated party honored, not erased. The Nihon Shoki gives variant versions, but the pattern holds. The myth's deepest meaning may be that sovereignty is best taken by leaving the former holder something greater than his loss. [Kojiki I] The Ordeal of Fire: Standing one day at Cape Kasasa, Ninigi saw a woman more beautiful than any other and asked her name. She was Konohanasakuya-hime, daughter of the mountain-god Ōyamatsumi; she consented, and that same night conceived. Ninigi doubted her when the pregnancy showed at once — whose child could be born in a day? The princess answered with fire. She entered a parturition hut, sealed it, and set it alight, vowing that if the children were truly Ninigi's they would be unharmed. In the midst of the flames she delivered three sons: Hoderi, the luck of the sea; Hoori, the luck of the mountains; and Hosuseri. Mother and infants survived, and Ninigi's suspicion was answered with living proof. The episode is one of the most vivid ordeal-births in world mythology, and it quietly elevates the bride: it is her fidelity, tested by fire, that founds the dynasty. The myth means that legitimacy flows not from the doubting husband but through the mother whose truth outlasts the flames. [Nihon Shoki] From Ninigi to Jimmu: The Nihon Shoki (Books I–III) completes the genealogy. Hoori, the mountain-lucky son, married Toyotama-hime, daughter of the sea-god, and their son Ugayafukiaezu wed his aunt Tamayori-hime; of that union was born Kamuyamato-Iwarebiko, who marched east from Hyūga, fought through the Kumaso, and acceded at Kashihara — Emperor Jimmu, the legendary first emperor. Ninigi is thus Jimmu's great-grandfather, and every imperial genealogy in Japanese history has run through him. The same chapters preserve the succession stories the official line passed over: in one Nihon Shoki variant, Ninigi's elder brother Ame-no-hohi was sent to the earth first and never returned, and Ninigi's descent was the second attempt. The sources are candid that more than one heir was considered. The myth's function is transparent and, for over a millennium, was effectively constitutional: it makes the emperor a descendant of Amaterasu in the fourth generation. It means that the state located its origin not in a conquest but in a birth — a genealogy, not a battlefield.

instruction: Tell me a myth about "Raijin".
output: Raijin's mythology is a palimpsest: the thunder kami of the Kojiki , the Buddhist guardian of esoteric temple art, the storm god of the Mongol-invasion legend, and the bogey of nursery warnings — four layers of one drumbeat. The sources are layered and partly at odds, and each layer tells us what thunder meant to a different Japan. [Kojiki] Thunder Born of the Dead Goddess: In the Kojiki , Izanami dies from the burns of the fire god Kagutsuchi, and her grieving husband Izanagi pursues her into Yomi, the land of the dead. When he breaks his promise not to look, he sees her body corrupted; in her fury Izanami sends the yakusa no ikazuchi — the eight thunder spirits — in pursuit, together with the hags of Yomi. The text explains that these thunderers were born from the filth of Izanami's dying body. Izanagi escapes at the Even Pass of Yomotsu Hirasaka and seals the way with a boulder. Thunder, then, is older than the cleanly born gods: it issues from death itself, from the corruption of the beloved. Fūjin, by contrast, is born later, from Izanagi's breath during his river purification — wind as the breath of the purified, thunder as the voice of the dead. The later Buddhist painters gave this archaic terror his demon drums and his cloud-island, but the Kojiki keeps the older truth: the storm speaks with the voice of the world we have lost. [Buddhist adoption] Guardian of the Dharma: With the arrival of esoteric Buddhism, the thunder power was enrolled in the defenses of the Dharma. From the Heian period, Raijin appears among the Jūni-ten , the Twelve Devas who guard the four directions and the zenith and nadir of the mandala, and with Fūjin he comes to stand at temple gatehouses — the pair most famously at the great Nioh-mon gates of Zen temples, where their sculpted forms confront visitors with the storm itself. His drumbeats scatter demons; his lightning burns away obstacles; his ugliness is itself a weapon, since in Buddhist iconography the fierce faces (the same grammar as the Nioh guardians) are shields that frighten evil before it can enter. Native kami and Buddhist guardian are not rivals here but one figure read twice: the Kojiki 's thunderer and the mandala's defender are the same sound heard through two theologies. Japan's thunder god guards the gate because thunder has always guarded the boundary between worlds. [The Divine Wind] Raijin and the Mongol Storms: In 1274 and again in 1281, typhoons destroyed the invasion fleets Kublai Khan sent against Japan. The warrior Takezaki Suenaga, who fought in both campaigns, commissioned the picture-scroll Mōko Shūrai Ekotoba (c. 1293), whose final scenes show the fleet shattered and drowning in the tempest. Medieval chronicles credited the court's prayers to Hachiman and Amaterasu, but in the popular imagination the storms were the direct work of the storm gods — Raijin drumming the clouds open above the strait while Fūjin filled them with wind. Later tradition named the typhoons kamikaze , the 'divine wind'. The legend grew into one of Japan's foundational stories of being saved by the gods, invoked again in the twentieth century — for catastrophic ends — as proof that the islands enjoyed supernatural protection. Whatever the theology, the myth records a real memory: that the sea between Japan and the continent belongs to the storm gods , and that they have defended it before. [Folk belief] Thunder and the Navel: Japanese folk belief holds that Raijin eats the navels of children. During thunderstorms, parents ordered children to cover their bellies — heso o kakusu — and the custom persists idiomatically today, where covering the navel is also said to prevent catching cold. Behind the bogey lies an older logic: the navel is the body's center and its first scar, the mark of the cut that began independent life, and in folk anatomy it is the belly that illness and hunger strike first. Lightning, the sky's predator, seeks the exposed center of life just as thunder frightens the body's center of courage. The belief turns Raijin into the most domestic of terrors — not a god of cosmic battles but the reason a child clutches a blanket in a storm. The thunder god lives in the nursery because that is where fear is taught, and where protection is first learned.

output: Jizō's mythology blends Indian scripture, Chinese translation, and Japanese folk belief. He is one of the most actively worshipped Buddhist figures in Japan — a bodhisattva whose statues outnumber his temples . [Sutra] The Original Vow: The Kṣitigarbha Bodhisattva Sūtra recounts that in a previous life the bodhisattva was a Brahmin maiden whose mother had slandered the Dharma. After her mother's death, the daughter made vast offerings at a temple and was transported in vision to hell, where a guardian demon told her the offerings had not yet redeemed her mother. Moved by the suffering around her, she vowed before the Buddha to save all beings in the hell realms, life after life, until not a single one remained. The sūtra frames this as an intercessory chain — the Buddha entrusts the helpless, in the long night between one buddha's passing and the next's arrival, to Kṣitigarbha's keeping. The myth's engine is refusal: heaven has no vacancy so long as hell has a single prisoner, and the bodhisattva is content to wait. [Japanese lore] Sai no Kawara: On the banks of Sai no Kawara, the stony riverbed where dead children must labor, the little souls pile stones as penance for having caused their parents grief — and each night demons scatter their work. Jizō comes in the guise of a wandering monk, hides the children in the sleeves of his robe, and comforts them until their karma is spent. The red bibs and caps set on his statues are gifts intended to warm these child-spirits, since the dead feel the cold. The tale first flowers in the medieval picture scrolls and story collections, where the riverbed's naked little laborers are shown weeping over their scattered stones — and Jizō arrives with his staff ringing. It is the sentimental heart of Japanese Buddhism: hell is real, labor is endless, and yet someone keeps coming down to the riverbed, night after night, to hold the children until morning. [Folk tale] The Monk Who Was Jizō: Countless Japanese tales tell of a wandering monk who helps a traveller in distress — carrying the load, pointing the road, sharing the fire — only to vanish, leaving the traveller to realize that the monk was the roadside Jizō himself. In the most beloved version, a poor but kind farmer sweeps the snow from the statues each New Year and, having no offering, gives them his own straw hat; in the night the Jizō come in procession to thank him, and his house is blessed. The stories encode a popular theology: Jizō is not distant in a pure land but present on the road, in the rain, at the crossroads where ordinary people lose their way. In a religion of vast vows, the tales insist on small gifts — a hat, a bow, a swept stone. [Ritual] The Thirteen Gifts of the Memorial: Japanese esoteric Buddhism folded Kṣitigarbha into its map of the afterlife. In the rites of the Thirteen Buddhas, each of the memorial services after a death — the seventh day, the forty-ninth, the hundredth, the anniversaries — is entrusted to a different bodhisattva or buddha. Jizō's own watch falls on the thirty-fifth day, when the soul has crossed the first judgment and most needs a guide; the rites of his day kept his name in the villages, and the summer Jizō-bon observances with their lanterns still light the roads for the returning dead. The assignment is telling: the church gave the freshly dead, still close to the living, to the one bodhisattva who specializes in the helpless. Between the funeral and the first anniversary, salvation is less a doctrine than a relay, and Jizō runs the longest leg of it.

instruction: Tell me a myth about "Amida".
output: Amida's mythology runs from the Indian vows of Dharmākara through Chinese translation into Japan's nenbutsu movement: the radical teaching that calling the Buddha's name with faith is itself the path . His stories are devotional rather than epic — vows, recitations, and descents — and they reshaped how Japan faced death. [The Primal Vow] The Forty-Eight Vows of Dharmākara: In the Larger Sukhāvatīvyūha Sūtra the Buddha tells how, in an inconceivably remote past, the monk Dharmākara knelt before the Buddha Lokeśvararāja and set himself a task no being had dared: to survey every Buddha-field in the ten directions, gather the best of each, and build from them a single land where no one who trusted him would fail to reach enlightenment. After five aeons of contemplation he pronounced forty-eight vows. The eighteenth — the Primal Vow ( hongan ) — promises that anyone who, with sincere entrusting, desires rebirth in his land and calls his name even ten times will be born there. Dharmākara then practiced for countless kalpas until the vows stood fulfilled, and he became Amida, whose Sukhāvatī lies to the west like a shore beyond every storm. The sūtra's logic is startling: enlightenment is not climbed but received, because someone else finished the climbing first. [The Nembutsu] Hōnen Selects the Single Practice: By the twelfth century the Tendai establishment taught that every practice could lead to awakening — and therefore, argued the monk Hōnen, none was being done wholeheartedly by ordinary people mired in the latter days of the Dharma. In 1198 he set down his answer in the Senchakushū : select the one practice the Buddha himself had promised would suffice — the nenbutsu, the calling of Amida's name, Namu Amida Butsu — and let every other good act adorn it rather than compete with it. His disciples carried the teaching from the capital to the fishing villages, until peasants and soldiers who had never read a sūtra were reciting the Buddha's name in fields and on battlefields. The authorities proscribed the movement in 1207 and exiled Hōnen, but the nenbutsu had already escaped every gate: the single practice made the highest path the commonest road. [Other Power] Shinran and the Tannishō: Hōnen's disciple Shinran pushed the nenbutsu one step further — and into a new religion. If salvation depended on Amida's Primal Vow, then even the recitation must be the Buddha's own working through the believer; even faith was a gift, not an achievement. The saying attributed to him in the Tannishō became the movement's signature: even the good person attains birth in the Pure Land, how much more so the evil person — because the good still secretly trust their own goodness, while the evil have nothing left to trust but the vow. Driven from Kyoto and settled among the peasants of Kantō, Shinran married, raised a family, and wrote the Kyōgyōshinshō in huts and borrowed halls, founding what became Jōdo Shinshū, Japan's largest Buddhist school. The scandal of his teaching is its mercy: it works precisely for those the other paths screen out. [The Descent] Raigō and the Buddha Who Would Not Stay: The myth Amida's devotees painted most is the raigō — the Welcoming Descent: on clouds, flanked by Kannon and Seishi, Amida comes down to meet the dying, and deathbed practice aimed every sense toward that arrival. Temple legends gave the descent a mischievous edge. Zenkōji's own tradition ( Zenkōji engi ) tells that when a summons came from the retired emperor in Kamakura, the temple's Amida image rose at night and set off eastward; the abbot Eikan chased it through the dark and caught hold of it, but the Buddha slipped from his arms — and only the head remained, the body going on to Kamakura, leaving Zenkōji the Eikanbetsu Amida, a face without a body eternally gazing east. A Buddha who refuses to stay put is the legend's whole point: Amida is bound to no temple, because his vow already covers every deathbed.

instruction: Tell me a myth about "Fuji".
output: Fuji generates story because it cannot be ignored: a volcano that sleeps for centuries at a time, a goddess of fire hidden under snow, and an image so constant that a whole civilization has measured its seasons, its festivals, and its art against one unchanging silhouette. [Name lore] The Name and Its Power: Folk etymology explains the name as fushi , 'without equal,' or fuji , 'inexhaustible' — both appropriate to a mountain with no rival on the horizon. In the early chronicles the peak's deity was treated as female, a kami of fire, and in the medieval period she was identified with Sengen (Asama-no-kami) and with Konohanasakuya-hime , the blossom princess of the Kojiki, whose marriage to the heavenly grandson Ninigi bound heaven's line to the earth. When Fuji smoked or rumbled, the interpretation was immediate: the goddess of the volcano was stirring, and the province looked to its Sengen shrines. The shrine cult kept the mountain's divinity local and specific — not an abstraction like 'nature,' but a named power with festivals, priests, and a genealogy reaching back to the age of the gods. The mountain's own name became the nation's shorthand for what is highest, purest, and most alone. [Fuji-kō] Fuji as Lotus Mandala: In the medieval imagination Fuji was not climbed so much as entered. Buddhist exegetes mapped the mountain as a lotus mandala , its ridges the lotus petals, its crater the heart of the world; ascending it was circumambulation and pilgrimage at once. In the sixteenth century the ascetic Hasegawa Kakugyō is credited with founding the Fuji-kō confraternities, and by the Edo period tens of thousands of pilgrims climbed in white robes reciting sutras, carrying miniature shrines up the stations and building fujizuka — small replica Fujis — in the cities, so that those who could not travel could still 'climb' the mountain. Some confraternities worshipped the crater itself as the Pure Land. The practice reveals the mountain's genius as an image: Fuji is endlessly reproducible, and every reproduction is still Fuji — a mandala you can ascend with your feet, a paradise with a weather problem. [Hokusai / Hiroshige] The Floating World's Mountain: Between about 1830 and 1850 the ukiyo-e masters fixed Fuji's image for the world. Hokusai's Thirty-Six Views of Mount Fuji placed the same snow-cap behind the Great Wave, a lumberyard, a tea-house balcony, a thunderstorm — proving the mountain was a measuring stick for every human activity. Hiroshige answered with travel series in which Fuji appears at a roadside halt, over a river, beyond a station bell. The prints used the newly imported Prussian blue so lavishly that the pigment itself became a fashion, and when Japan opened, these images were among the first things the West saw and imitated. The lesson of the series is visual relativism: Fuji never changes, but every viewpoint is a different picture. The mountain became the constant against which a whole floating world arranges and rearranges itself — and the proof that a sacred image, printed a hundred thousand times, loses none of its sanctity. [Hōei 1707] The Last Eruption: On the twenty-third day of the eleventh month of 1707 — mid-December by the modern calendar — Fuji woke. The Hōei eruption blew ash downwind for weeks, darkening the sky over Edo itself, where official memoranda and ink paintings measured the fall in handspans and the city coughed through a winter of grey snow. The eruption opened vents on the southeastern flank and built the cinder cone still called Hōei-zan, but no lava flow reached the villages, and no death was recorded. Contemporaries read the smoke as the mountain kami's displeasure; modern seismologists read it as a warning clock — more than three centuries quiet, but the magma plumbing intact beneath a sacred cone. Either way the meaning is the same: Fuji is worshipped precisely because it is not safe — a goddess who sleeps with one eye open over forty million people, and whose last performance is remembered in ash that fell on the shogun's capital.

instruction: Tell me a myth about "Ise".
output: Ise's mythology is inseparable from the mythology of Amaterasu and the imperial house. The city exists because the sun goddess needed a dwelling worthy of her. [Imperial legend] Amaterasu Comes to Ise: According to tradition, the imperial princess Yamatohime-no-mikoto traveled for twenty years searching for a permanent dwelling for Amaterasu. She finally received an oracle at Ise, where the goddess declared her love for the place. The Inner Shrine was established there, and the imperial house has maintained it ever since. [Ritual] The Twenty-Year Rebuilding: The shikinen-zōtai tradition requires that the shrine buildings be reconstructed on adjacent plots every twenty years. The old structures are dismantled, and their timber is distributed to branch shrines. This cycle ensures that the architecture remains fresh and that the skills of sacred carpentry are passed down through generations. [Pilgrimage] Okage-mairi: In the Edo period, mass pilgrimages to Ise called okage-mairi swept the country. Villages would pool their resources and send representatives — sometimes whole communities — to walk the Ise-kaidō. These pilgrimages expressed popular devotion to Amaterasu and shaped the culture of travel in early modern Japan. [The Regalia] The Cave of Heaven and the Mirror: The mirror enshrined at Ise enters myth at the crisis of the Kojiki: when the storm god Susano-o's rampages drove Amaterasu to hide in the heavenly cave, Ama-no-Iwato, the world went dark, the eight hundred myriad gods assembled in council, and Ama-no-Uzume danced an outrageously comic dance on an upturned tub. The gods roared with laughter; Amaterasu, curious, peered out — and saw her own radiance reflected in the mirror Yata-no-Kagami hung on a sakaki tree. Drawn out by what was, in the end, her own light, the sun returned to the sky and Susano-o was punished with exile (Kojiki; Nihon Shoki). Tradition holds that this same mirror rests at the Ise Inner Shrine, where Amaterasu has dwelt since the imperial princess Yamatohime received her oracle there. The shrine's holiest object is thus a device for seeing the sun: Shinto's deepest sanctuary keeps, at its center, the story of how light was persuaded back into the world — by laughter, and by a reflection.

instruction: Tell me a myth about "Takachiho".
output: Takachiho's 'mythology' is a convergence of scripture, landscape, and performance. The Kojiki and Nihon Shoki agree that Ninigi, grandson of Amaterasu, descended at the peak of Takachiho in the land of Hyūga; the town that bears the name claims the story as its own and keeps it alive each winter in the all-night kagura dances that reenact the cave of heaven. [Kojiki / Nihon Shoki] The Descent at the Peak of Takachiho: The Kojiki and Nihon Shoki agree on the itinerary: when Amaterasu resolved that her grandson Ninigi should rule the visible world, she sent him down from the Plain of High Heaven at the head of a divine escort, bearing the mirror, sword, and curved jewel that became the Three Sacred Regalia. Both texts name the landing place Takachiho no mine — the peak of Takachiho — in the land of Himuka, present-day Miyazaki Prefecture (Kojiki; Nihon Shoki, Age of the Gods). Ninigi wed the blossom-princess Konohanasakuya-hime, and from the line of their son Hoori came the first emperor, Jimmu. The tradition is the charter of Japanese kingship, and it plants that charter on a real mountain in Kyūshū. What Takachiho means is therefore not merely 'where the gods came down' but where heaven first accepted a Japanese address — the point where the divine genealogy touches soil that can still be walked. [Kojiki / Local tradition] The Cave of Heaven: The classical texts do not say where the Rock Cave of Heaven stood. The Kojiki tells how Amaterasu, frightened by her brother Susanoo's rampage, sealed herself inside Ama-no-Iwato and plunged the world into darkness, until the goddess Uzume's bawdy dance on an overturned tub drew the gods' laughter and lured the sun back out (Kojiki, Age of the Gods). Local tradition in Takachiho locates the cave on the Iwato River gorge, where Ama-no-Iwato Shrine keeps the memory — the sacred rope, the crowing rooster, the mirror hung on the sakaki tree. Scholars note that the identification is devotional rather than textual: many places in Japan claim the cave, and the sources are silent. But the gorge gives the story a theatrical setting, a narrow chasm where sunlight and shadow trade places across the water. The myth's engine is social: order is restored not by force but by laughter, performance, and a community coaxing its sun back into view. [Folk tradition] The Dance That Reenacts the Dawn: Each year from mid-November to mid-February, the villages around Takachiho perform the yokagura — the night kagura — a cycle of some thirty-three episodes danced from dusk until dawn to make the fields fertile and the year safe. The climactic piece is always the cave: Uzume's dance, the gods' laughter, the sun's return, reenacted with masks and drums by the villages' own performers. The tradition was designated an Important Intangible Folk-Cultural Property of Japan in 1978, and the Takachiho Kagura has become one of the country's most watched winter rituals, with performances staged nightly for visitors at Takachiho Shrine. The myth survives here the way medieval mystery plays carried scripture: not as text recited but as action repeated, so that every winter the community itself plays the part of the gods who once, in its own gorge, brought the sun back out of the rock. [History] From Sacred Peak to Pilgrimage Town: For most of its history Takachiho was a remote mountain district whose chief asset was the descent narrative itself. Pilgrims came despite the distance, and the Meiji state's promotion of the imperial cult gave the town's shrines new standing as way-stations of the emperor's divine ancestry. The railway from Nobeoka reached the town only in 1972 — the same mountain line that closed in 2008 after typhoon damage — and motor tourism turned the gorge, the shrine, and the night kagura into the town's living. The gorge, geologically, is young: the Gokase River cut its columned walls down through the basalt laid down by Mount Aso's eruptions, and the Manai Falls drop seventeen metres at the chasm's head. Takachiho's mythology thus layers like its rocks: an imperial charter, a cave of the sun, a dancer's dance, and a modern community that keeps all three reenacted.

instruction: Tell me a myth about "Kumano".
output: Kumano's mythology blends imperial foundation legend, mountain asceticism, and the medieval fusion of kami and Buddha. Its sources are chronicle, mandala, and ritual text rather than epic, and its stories are walked as much as told: the crow who guided an emperor, the hermits who heard sermons in waterfalls, and the retired sovereigns who came on foot to meet them. [Imperial legend] Yatagarasu and Emperor Jimmu: When Emperor Jimmu, the first emperor of the chronicles, led his eastern expedition into the mountains of Kumano, his army lost its way among the peaks. The Kojiki and Nihon Shoki tell that the heavenly gods sent Yatagarasu , a great three-legged crow, to guide him: it flew before the host as a living arrow, and Jimmu emerged from the mountains to claim Yamato. The tale plants the imperial founding inside Kumano's forests and makes the crow — black, solar, three-footed — the sign of divine guidance through wilderness. A thousand years later the mountain shrines still claimed that protection: emperors did not command Kumano, they visited it, and the crow they had followed remained the region's emblem. Guidance through trackless country is Kumano's first gift, and Japan still uses it — the three-legged crow stands on the crest of the national football association. [Shugendō] Mountain Asceticism: Kumano became the greatest mountain center of Japan's ascetic tradition, Shugendō . Its legendary founder, En no Gyōja, was said to have wandered the Kii peaks in the seventh century working miracles; by the Heian period the yamabushi — 'those who lie down in the mountains' — walked the Kumano Kodō in straw sandals, performed cold-water ablutions beneath Nachi's falls, and sought visions in the cedar dark. They understood the mountains not as scenery but as a mandala: every peak a deity, every waterfall a sermon. The sources for this layer are late and hagiographic, but the practice they describe is real and documented for over a millennium: to enter Kumano was to enter a realm where the boundary between the human and the divine wore thin, and discipline was the price of crossing it. [Heian period] The Court Comes on Foot: From the tenth century the court itself came. Retired Emperor Uda opened the fashion with pilgrimages in the early 900s; by the late Heian age the journey to Kumano had become the highest form of aristocratic devotion, and the retired Emperor Go-Shirakawa is said to have made it some thirty times. These were not retreats but processions — hundreds of riders, boats up the coast, poetry composed at each shrine — yet they ended in mountain humility. Court diaries and shrine records preserve the pattern in detail, and the routes they used still run under the cedars. Pilgrimage was politics performed on foot: every journey bound the imperial house more tightly to the mountains' protection, and broadcast to anyone watching from the pilgrimage roads that the sovereign's power was rooted in the gods of the land. [Sacred union] Kami and Buddha in the Mountains: In the medieval theology of honji-suijaku , 'original ground and local manifestation,' Kumano's kami were declared the local appearances of Buddhas: Hongū's deity was Amitābha, Hayatama's Śākyamuni, Nachi's the waterfall-god Hiryū Gongen , read as an emanation of Kannon. Painted Kumano mandalas show the mountain shrines floating as a Buddhist paradise, the Nachi falls descending like a golden thread of the bodhisattva's compassion. Pilgrims too old or poor to walk could gaze on the mandala and receive the same merit — one famous print added the words, 'those who see this picture will be born in the Pure Land.' The synthesis was not a trick but a theology: the local gods had always been Buddhas in disguise, waiting for the teaching to say so. When the Meiji state forcibly separated the two religions in 1868, Kumano kept both memories — the kami's names and the Buddhas' faces — in a single landscape.

instruction: Tell me a myth about "Ebisu".
output: Ebisu has no single founding myth. He grew from several older figures — the castaway child Hiruko, the oracular Kotoshironushi, and deities of the foreign sea — into the cheerful merchant god of the Edo period. The sources disagree about which ancestor is truly his; the smile, the fishing rod, and the sea bream are the tradition's own answer. [Kojiki] Hiruko, the Leech Child: The Kojiki tells that when Izanagi and Izanami first coupled, their child Hiruko was born 'without bones', like a leech or a premature thing; at three he could not yet stand. The dismayed parents set him adrift in a boat of reeds and let the sea decide. He survived — and later tradition, above all at Nishinomiya Shrine near Kōbe, identified the foundling with Ebisu: the child the gods abandoned who became the god of those who make their own living from the water. The chronicles themselves never call Hiruko 'Ebisu'; the identification is medieval and early-modern tradition, and scholars treat it as a genealogy of meaning rather than a datum. Its content is exact: Ebisu is the outsider who prospers — the stranger, the latecomer, the one the palace forgot . [Kojiki] Kotoshironushi and the Yielding of the Land: Another line of descent runs through Kotoshironushi, son of Ōkuninushi, the great god of the land. When the heavenly grandchild's envoys demanded that the earth be yielded, Ōkuninushi deferred to his son's counsel: Kotoshironushi answered on his father's behalf and then withdrew to the sea, or hid his body, leaving the land to the new line (Kojiki; Nihon Shoki). He was a god of oracles, of fishing, and of the boundary between the human settlement and the deep water; he is still enshrined at Shirayama-hime in Kaga and at Miho in Izumo, shrines that keep exactly the oracle-and-fishing profile the Ebisu cult later borrowed. Several shrine genealogies — and much popular etymology — have since folded him into Ebisu, which is why the fortune god carries a fishing rod rather than a purse. The merger makes theological sense: the god who surrendered territory and kept the sea became the patron of everyone who draws wealth from outside the city's walls. [Edo period] Ebisu the Smiling Merchant: By the Edo period the composite figure had found his final form: the smiling god with a fishing rod in one hand and a great red sea bream ( tai ) under the other arm, guardian of shops, fish markets, and honest trade. His image stood by the cash box and the shop curtain; his festival, Tōka Ebisu at Osaka's Imamiya Ebisu Shrine (10–12 January), became one of Japan's greatest commercial rites, with its lucky-straw charms ( kichi-zuna ) and the red-and-white 'lucky maidens' ( fuku-musume ) who crowd the lanes. The sea bream is itself a pun: tai echoes medetai , 'auspicious.' In Ebisu, Japan canonized a god of small prosperity honestly won — the daily takings, not the treasure vault. Merchants wrote his name on their ledgers and brewers on their casks; the god of the millionaire's district, Naniwa's own, had made the corner shop his shrine. [Folk religion] The Deaf God and the Treasure Ship: Folk tradition supplies the mythic punchline to his outsider status: when all the kami of Japan assemble at Izumo in the tenth month, Ebisu — who is deaf, the stories say — never hears the summons and stays home . That is why the tenth month is kannazuki , 'the month without gods', almost everywhere, but kamiarizuki , 'the month with gods', in the east, where Ebisu keeps watch alone. At New Year the picture reverses: the Seven Gods of Fortune sail into port on the takarabune , the treasure ship, Ebisu's rod and bream prominent among the cargo of rice bales and coral, and children sleep on a takarabune print in the hope of a lucky first dream ( hatsuyume ). The god who missed the meeting becomes, once a year, the first guest of fortune to arrive .

instruction: Tell me a myth about "Ōkuninushi".
output: Ōkuninushi's cycle, preserved in the Kojiki (712) and the Nihon Shoki (720), is the longest and most novelistic narrative in Japanese myth — a story of escape, ordeal, sovereignty and renunciation at the meeting-point of earth and heaven. Every stage of it, from the healed hare to the final treaty, teaches one art of rule. [The First Prescription] The White Hare of Inaba: In the Kojiki (Book I), a hare from the isle of Oki tricks the wani sea-beasts into forming a bridge, is flayed for the deception, and meets the eighty cruel brothers of Ōnamuji, who mockingly prescribe a bath in salt sea-water — agony for its wounds. The youngest brother, Ōnamuji (later Ōkuninushi), advises instead a rinse in fresh river water and a roll in the pollen of katami, the cattail rush; the hare is healed. Grateful, the hare prophesies that Ōnamuji — not his eighty brothers — will win the hand of the princess Yakami-hime of Inaba. It is the first medical prescription in Japanese myth, and the deed that marks the future land-master out from his rivals: where the brothers offer cruelty disguised as counsel, the youngest offers the right remedy and wins a prophet for his pains. [The Ordeals Below] The Trials of Ne-no-Kuni: Fleeing his brothers' repeated attempts to kill him, Ōnamuji descends to Ne-no-Kuni, the root-land of Susanoo, as the Kojiki (Book I) relates. There he loves Susanoo's daughter Suseribime, and the storm-god tests him: a night in a hall of snakes, a night in a hall of centipedes and wasps — each survived through Suseribime's protective scarves — and a burning meadow where a mouse leads him to safety underground and retrieves the arrow Susanoo had fired. When Ōnamuji at last washes the great god's hair and steals away with Suseribime, Susanoo's sword, bow and heavenly lute, the pursuing god yields and proclaims him Ōkuninushi-no-kami, Great Land-Master, bidding him drive out his brothers and rule the land. The trials invert the heroic pattern: the hero wins not by strength but by endurance, courtesy, and a mouse's friendship — the virtues of a healer, not a berserker. [Nation-Builders] The Dwarf from Across the Sea: While Ōkuninushi labours to order the land, the Kojiki (Book I) tells, a tiny god arrives across the waves in a skiff of kagami pod-husks, wearing the skin of a moth: Sukunabikona, son of the great producer Kamimusubi (the Nihon Shoki variants name Takamimusubi). The two make and consolidate the land together, and devise the arts of medicine and protective magic for gods, men and beasts. When the work is done, Sukunabikona departs for Tokoyo no kuni, the far land beyond the sea, leaving Ōkuninushi to guard the realm they built. Nation-building, the myth insists, is a partnership across every scale: the land-master who stands tall and the dwarf whose boat is a seed-pod complete what neither could finish alone — and the smaller partner leaves first, as if greatness were only ever a loan. [The Great Abdication] Kuni-yuzuri — the Transfer of the Land: When Amaterasu resolves that her line shall rule the Central Land of Reed-Plains, the Kojiki (Book I; cf. the Nihon Shoki, Age of the Gods scrolls) records that the warrior-god Takemikazuchi is sent to Izumo, where he thrusts his sword into the shore and demands Ōkuninushi's answer. The land-master defers to his sons: Kotoshironushi consents at once, while Ajisuki-takahikone resists and is subdued in a divine wrestling-bout. Ōkuninushi then cedes the land — on terms: a grand palace is to be built for him with pillars raised high and crossbeams thick, and his worship is to be perpetuated by the heavenly line itself. That promised palace is Izumo no Ōyashiro, the Grand Shrine of Izumo, and the treaty-in-myth is remembered as kuni-yuzuri — the word Japan still uses for a peaceful transfer of sovereignty. He is the rarest thing in myth: a sovereign who negotiates his own surrender and wins eternity by it.

instruction: Tell me a myth about "Kagutsuchi".
output: Kagutsuchi's mythology is brief and absolute: a birth that kills, a death that multiplies life, and a legacy of fire that Japan's volcanoes still preach. The Kojiki spends little more than a page on him — yet that page is the hinge of the whole cosmogony, for it is at his birth that the creator goddess dies and the world divides into the living and the dead. [Kojiki I.8] The Burning Birth: After the islands were born, Izanami bore the last child of the creation — the fire kami Kagutsuchi — and his birth burned her. The Kojiki (I.8) tells it with terrible economy: the fire from the child's body scorched her, and from the agony of the wound the dying goddess brought forth still more kami — Kanayamabiko and Kanayamabime, the kami of metal, from her vomit; Haniyasubiko and Haniyasubime, the kami of clay and pottery, from her feces; and Midorikonomikami from her urine. Then, her body spent, Izanami died. She who had borne the islands and the thirty-odd kami of the land was destroyed by her final child: creation consuming its maker is the first law the new world teaches, and the fire god learned it in the only way a newborn can — by being it. [Kojiki I.9] The Blade of Grief: Izanagi's grief turned to rage — 'Why must I lose my beloved for this one child?' — and drawing the Totsuka-no-Tsurugi, the ten-handled sword of the brine, he cut the fire kami down. What fell from the blade was life. From the blood on its point came Iwasaku and Nesaku, the 'stone-cutting' kami; from the blood on its hilt came Mizuhanome, the goddess of water who quenches fire; and from the severed body came the mountain kami whose peaks still steam along the Japanese chain (Kojiki I.9). The Nihon Shoki preserves variant versions of the same burning-birth and gives the child the parallel names Homusubi and Hi-no-Kagutsuchi. Kagutsuchi thus dies the only death in the cosmogony struck by a god's own hand — and the dismemberment, like the birth, manufactures gods: fire destroys, and destruction is revealed as one of generation's ordinary forms. [Kojiki I.10–11] The Child Who Created Death: Because Izanami died, Izanagi followed her down to the land of Yomi; because he followed, he saw her body corrupted, guarded by the eight Thunder Kami; because he fled from the sight, Izanami cursed him, and the world split in two at the Even Pass of Yomi — Izanagi swearing to give life its thousand generations, Izanami to take a thousand a day. Then, purifying himself in the river of the plain, Izanagi washed from his left eye Amaterasu, from his right eye Tsukuyomi, from his nose Susano-o — the three sovereign children of the later pantheon (Kojiki I.10–11). None of it happens without the fire child's birth. Kagutsuchi is the pivot of the entire Japanese cosmogony: the instant at which the world of undying creators ends and the world of birth and death begins. One page of story carries every assumption the later shrines and epics must make — the sun included, for even Amaterasu exists because a fire once killed a mother. [Folk tradition] Homusubi, the Hearth: The Kojiki gives Kagutsuchi no cult and no further adventures — his worship was the ordinary reverence of fire itself. Under the names Hi-no-Kagutsuchi and Homusubi, 'fire-producer,' he was honored at the hearth and the forge, where fire cooked, warmed, and smelted; fittingly, the metal and clay kami born from Izanami's dying body minister to the same fireplace and furnace. Folk tradition kept a careful double feeling toward him: fire was the gift no household could live without and the force that could erase the household in an hour, and in parts of Japan a prayer was still spoken before the first fire of the new year. This is the myth reduced to its element — no temples, no epics, only the daily negotiation between human beings and the one power in the house that must never be insulted. The volcanoes are his body; the kitchen fire is his ghost; both demand the same attention.

instruction: Tell me a myth about "Hiiaka".
output: Hiiaka's mythology is the longest continuous narrative in Hawaiian tradition: the Pele cycle, preserved in chant and family memory, in which the youngest volcano-goddess crosses every island on her sister's errand and comes home to a betrayal that splits the heavens' first family in two. [Pele Cycle] The Egg at ʻĀinahou: Pele's migration legend carries the volcano family westward from Kahiki — the Hawaiian name for Tahiti — until the goddess finds her home in the pit of Kīlauea. Beckwith's digest of the tradition (Hawaiian Mythology, 'The Pele cycle') preserves the birth of her youngest sister: at ʻĀinahou on Kauaʻi, Pele discovers an egg and takes it into her bosom to keep it warm; from the egg hatches the goddess whose name, Hiʻiaka, is traditionally explained as 'carried in the bosom' (Hawaiian hiʻi, to hold a child close; Pukui & Elbert, Hawaiian Dictionary). The myth makes kinship the first fact of Hiʻiaka's being: she exists because Pele carried her, and her whole career will replay that carrying as loyalty, as errand, and finally as grievance. [Pele Cycle] The Quest for Lohiʻau: Sleeping in the crater at Kīlauea, Pele sees in a dream the young chief Lohiʻau of Kauaʻi and falls in love with his image. Because she cannot leave her volcanic work without peril, she binds her youngest sister by an oath: Hiʻiaka must cross the islands, find Lohiʻau, and bring him back within forty days — and Hiʻiaka in turn binds Pele to guard her sacred lehua groves and her beloved friend Hopoe until she returns (Beckwith, Hawaiian Mythology; Emerson's Pele and Hiiaka, 1915, is the classic literary retelling of the cycle). The journey becomes the longest road in Hawaiian myth: Hiʻiaka battles the moʻo monsters that bar the passes, wins kupua allies of her own, and at last finds Lohiʻau dead of longing — and slays the serpent who killed him, passing her pāʻū over his body until he breathes again. The quest myth turns the islands into a single moral geography: every valley crossed is a test of the oath, and love in this family is always love at the end of a long and dangerous errand. [Pele Cycle] The Death of Hopoe: Hiʻiaka's double charge was the lehua groves and Hopoe, the dancer-friend of her girlhood at Puna. When the fortieth day passed with no sister on the road home, Pele's jealousy did what her fire always does: the lava took the groves, and it took Hopoe. Beckwith records the scene as the Puna coast's own aetiology — the dancer caught by the advancing flow at the shore — and later tellers of the cycle say her dance was fixed in the stone where the wave of lava stopped. Hiʻiaka, racing home with Lohiʻau alive, found her friend dead and her groves burned by the very goddess she had sworn to serve. The myth builds its tragedy on crossed oaths: Pele broke the pledge her sister trusted most, and the volcano-goddess's oldest excuse — that fire cannot help itself — is asked to answer for a deliberate grief. [Pele Cycle] Sister Against Sister: When Hiʻiaka reached home and found Hopoe dead, she broke the last restraint: she embraced Lohiʻau before Pele's altar — the final insult in the sisters' escalating war — and Pele's answer was to burn Lohiʻau where he stood and open the earth under Hiʻiaka. The battle that followed, along the Hilo and Puna coasts, set the two sisters' powers against one another until their brothers, led by Kāmohoaliʻi the shark-god, forced a peace (Beckwith, Hawaiian Mythology). Hiʻiaka's last labor in the cycle is her descent to the spirit-realm of Lua-o-Milu, whence she brings Lohiʻau's soul back and restores him by her own power. The Pele cycle ends not with victory but with partition: each sister keeps her domain — the fire and the dance, the volcano and the healing chant — and Hawaiian tradition thereafter treats them as one household's two halves, destruction and restoration, both of them family.
