instruction: Tell me a myth about "Kamapuaa".
output: Kamapua'a's cycle, best preserved in the O'ahu traditions Beckwith summarized and Westervelt printed, is a trickster epic with a strange ending: the ravager marries the destroyer, and the islands get a farm treaty. [Birth] The Child of the Cliffs: Kamapua'a was born in Kaliuwa'a , the sheer valley of the Ko'olau range on O'ahu — the valley the Hawaiians call Sacred Falls — to the goddess Hina . From the first he was double: a child who was also a hog, fair-faced as a young chief, yet able to swell into an enormous boar whose bristles swept the ferns. He grew among the cliff country of the windward coast, and the cycle follows him as he raids the coastal plantations — pulling up taro and yam, devouring or carrying off the stored wealth of the district — while the farmers' traps and the chiefs' hunters fail against an animal that is also a man. (Beckwith, Hawaiian Mythology; Westervelt, Hawaiian Legends of Gods and Ghosts.) The myth's heart is in the name itself: kama, child; pua'a, pig — the beloved and the pest as one being, as any farmer who has watched a feral boar in the taro already knows. [The Hunt] The Chiefs Who Could Not Catch a God: The raids brought the hunt. The chiefs of the coast — in the longer versions led by 'Olopana , lord of the district — pursued the sacred hog into the mountains with spears, ropes, and traps, and Kamapua'a made fools of every formation: he vanished into fog, doubled back as a handsome stranger who ate at the pursuers' own fires by night, and was the boar again bursting their cordons by day. The versions collected in the nineteenth century delight in these escapes — the hog bleeding one moment into mist, the next a man laughing on the cliff — and they end the same way: the hunters quit, and the hog keeps the mountain. (Fornander, An Account of the Polynesian Race; Beckwith, Hawaiian Mythology.) What reads as a folk tale of an uncatchable pig is a charter: the uplands belong to the wild thing, and human order stops at the tree-line. [The Courtship] Rain on the Volcano: Then Kamapua'a came down the island chain to Pele . She mocked him as a hog, and he answered with his other nature: he wrapped Kīlauea in fog, drowned its fires in rain, and thundered at the crater until the volcano hissed and steamed in its own pit — the first power in the islands to beat Pele at her own game. At the height of the storm the cycle turns: Pele, outmatched, yields, and the hog and the volcano marry — fire taking water for its mate. (Beckwith, Hawaiian Mythology; Westervelt, Hawaiian Legends of Volcanoes.) The courtship is the cycle's masterpiece of imagery: the flood that courts the volcano — water proposing to fire, and fire, astonishingly, accepting. [The Treaty] What the Marriage Settled: The marriage was a constitution. By its terms, the cycle says, Pele's lava would keep to the forests and the uplands and leave the cultivated lowlands to live; and Kamapua'a's rains would water the farms and fatten the gardens he had once ravaged. The boar who destroyed plantations became the god who protects them — agriculture's own dangerous patron, the wild force inside cultivation that must be married, not killed. In the closing chapters he returns to O'ahu and to his mother Hina, honored as a god of plenty, his feral children the pigs of the mountain and his gentler children the crops of the field. (Beckwith, Hawaiian Mythology; Kamakau, Ka Moolelo Hawaii.) The myth understands something modern conservation is relearning: the destructive force is not the enemy of the garden but its spouse — and the only bad outcome is war without a treaty.

instruction: Tell me a myth about "Poliahu".
output: Poliahu's mythology is preserved chiefly in nineteenth- and early twentieth-century Hawaiian-language and Hawaiian-authored texts — above all Emma Nakuina's Hawaii, Its People, Their Legends (1904), synthesized in Beckwith's Hawaiian Mythology (1970). Its centerpiece is the great contest of snow and fire for the mountain, a duel that Hawaiians read in the island's very lava flows and snowfields to this day. [The Sled Race] The Stranger on the Mountain: On the slopes of Mauna Kea, Poliahu and her snow-sister friends were challenged to a hōlua sled race by a beautiful stranger. The stranger lost — and flung off her disguise: she was Pele , goddess of volcanoes, and she erupted in fire down the mountainside (Nakuina, Hawaii, Its People, Their Legends , 1904; retold in Beckwith, Hawaiian Mythology , 1970, and Westervelt, Hawaiian Legends of Volcanoes , 1916). Poliahu rose to her full height and answered with snow and hail, beating the flames back. The race ran on the great hōlua slide of the mountain's flank, whose stone track can still be traced — the legend pins its scene to a course its first audience knew. The battle of the two goddesses scarred the mountainThe battle of the two goddesses scarred the mountain — fire trenches, snowfields — and the legend still reads the landscape: every cinder and snowbank on Mauna Kea is a stroke of that duel . [The Snow Sisters] The Household of the Peak: Poliahu does not keep the summit alone. Her companions are her sisters — Lilinoe , who rules the mountain's mists, Waiau , who dwells in the sacred lake that bears her name, and Kahoupokane — together the cold maidens of the high mountain (Nakuina 1904; Beckwith 1970). Waiau's water lies nearly four thousand meters above the sea and never truly warms; tradition held it cold and pure as the goddess herself, and chiefs drank of it only after ceremony. Lake Waiau, among the highest lakes in Oceania,Lake Waiau, among the highest lakes in Oceania, was kapu — its water reserved for the highest chiefs and for the goddess's own uses. The mythology does the work of a natural history: it distributes the summit's phenomena — snow, mist, lake, wind — among a family, making the mountain a household rather than a heap of rock . [The Frozen Suitor] Poliahu and ʻAiwohikupua: The Kauaʻi chief ʻAiwohikupua came to the mountain and won the goddess's love — but he was betrothed to a woman of his own island, and Poliahu discovered the truth. Her anger fell on him like weather: he shivered at her touch, and when he fled homeward she sent the cold after him — snow fell on Kauaʻi's heights , a sign of her reach (the legend cycle as recorded in Beckwith 1970, from the Hawaiian-language newspapers; Westervelt 1916 gives a parallel). The courtship also explains the weather: the snow that touches Kaua'i's peaks on the rarest nights is Poliahu's answer still, and old Kaua'i families retold it as a standing warning to oath-breaking chiefs. The tale carries a chiefly moral in goddess form:The tale carries a chiefly moral in goddess form: love given to a sworn heart is a debt the weather itself will collect . [Fire Against Snow] The Great Battle for the Mountain: The full combat of Poliahu and Pele — the longest form of the legend — raged from Mauna Kea down toward the sea: Pele vomiting rivers of lava, Poliahu calling up snowstorms and hail, the land between them torn and remade, until the fire was driven to its own country in the south and the white mountain stood (Nakuina 1904; Beckwith 1970). Modern kūpuna retell the battle as an account of balance — that the island needs both fire and snow, and that it is the goddesses' long truce, not either one's victory, which keeps the land alive. Hawaiians watching real eruptions reach toward Mauna Kea's snowsHawaiians watching real eruptions reach toward Mauna Kea's snows had the myth for what they saw. Read geologically, the story is a memory of the islands' living duel of elements; read theologically, it grants the cold goddess and the hot one equal sovereignty — fire rules the rift, snow rules the summit, and the island is their treaty line .

instruction: Tell me a myth about "Haumiatiketike".
output: Haumia-tiketike's stories are chapters of the Māori creation cycle: the separation of sky and earth, the war among the children, and the settlement of the food quest. His single decisive act is a refusal — to leave the earth-mother's body — and from that refusal the wild food of Aotearoa takes its sanctity. [Creation] Child of the Sky and the Earth: In the Māori creation cycle recorded by George Grey in Polynesian Mythology (1855) and in the fuller recensions of John White's Ancient History of the Māori , the sky-father Rangi and the earth-mother Papa lay locked in an embrace that left no room for light or life. Their children — Tāne, Tangaroa, Tāwhirimātea, Tūmatauenga, Rongo-māui, Haumia-tiketike and the rest — grew cramped in the darkness between them. Among them Haumia was the quiet one, the god whose portion was to be everything the forest floor offered without planting. When at last the brothers voted on whether the parents should be separated, Haumia stood with Tāne: the world must be divided so that light, food, and people could come into it. The genealogy is short and absolute: every wild root dug in Aotearoa descends from this moment, when the children of the dark chose to break their parents' embrace and make room for a harvest. [The Separation] Hidden in the Earth-Mother: Tāne thrust his parents apart, raising the sky on his shoulders and pressing the earth down, and the world took its shape. But the separation left some children with nowhere to go. Tāwhirimātea, god of winds and storms, raged at what had been done and turned on his brothers; Tāne and Tangaroa fled to the forests and the sea. Rongo-māui took refuge inside the body of Papa, and Haumia-tiketike went with him — into the earth-mother's bosom, where the two brothers have remained ever since (Grey, Polynesian Mythology , 'The children of Heaven and Earth'). The story explains the Māori food world with an elegant symmetry: Rongo, who hid in the earth, is the god of the kūmara that must be planted; Haumia, who hid with him, is the god of the fernroot that is only gathered. What the mother shelters she does not surrender to the cultivator. [The War of the Brothers] The Food of the Conquered: When Tāwhirimātea's storms failed to unmake the world, Tūmatauenga — the fierce brother of humankind — took revenge on all who had sided against him. One by one he hunted his brothers down: Tāne's birds, Tangaroa's fish and seals, the very forests and waves were made food for Tū and his children, which is why people eat them to this day. But two brothers escaped him. Rongo and Haumia had hidden so deep within the body of Papa that no attack could reach them, and so Tū declared his sentence over them instead: because they dared not face him, they would be dug up — unearthed with the digging stick as the food of the conquered (Grey, 'The war of the children'; Orbell 1998). The myth gives uncultivated food its permanent rank in the Māori order: kūmara and fernroot are the flesh of gods who would not fight, and every meal of them replays the ancient war. [The Food Quest] Aruhe, the Fernroot: Haumia's living cult was the gathering of aruhe. From late winter into spring the people went out to the bracken clearings, dug the starchy rhizomes of the bracken fern with the foot-driven kō, and carried them home in baskets. The roots were beaten clean, washed in running water to leach the bitterness, and steamed for hours in the earth oven — hāngī, or umu tī, 'the fern oven'. When the kūmara crop failed, as it did in cold or wet years, aruhe carried whole communities through; Elsdon Best records that karakia were spoken over the digging, the cooking, and the first taste (Best, Māori Religion and Mythology ). In Haumia's domain there is no sowing and no fence: only the earth's own stores, opened by labor and gratitude. The god of wild food teaches that plenty does not always need a garden — it needs a country loved enough to be read.

instruction: Tell me a myth about "Whiro".
output: Whiro's mythology is an antagonist's dossier — he exists in the Māori corpus chiefly as the power Tāne and the tohunga must overcome. The sources are nineteenth-century records of oral tradition (Grey 1855; White 1887–90; Best 1925), and they agree on his office while differing on his genealogy and extent. [The Rival of Tāne] The War Over the Baskets of Knowledge: In the great myth preserved by George Grey ( Polynesian Mythology , 1855; Nga Mahi a nga Tupuna ), Tāne ascends through the layered heavens to obtain the three baskets of knowledge ( ngā kete o te wānanga ) for humankind. Whiro — Whiro-te-tipua — marshals the powers of darkness against the ascent, and the myth is explicitly a war: each heaven is contested, and Tāne prevails only with the aid of the winds and ancestor-gods above. Grey's text, dictated by Māori experts in the 1850s, is our fullest witness; the Tūhoe versions add that the battle-lines were drawn anew in each heaven as Tāne climbed. The variant accounts collected by Elsdon BestThe variant accounts collected by Elsdon Best ( Tūhoe , 1925) and John White ( Ancient History of the Maori ) fill in different battle-lines. Whatever the version, the structure is fixed: knowledge descends only through victory over darkness, and darkness is a person who resents the delivery . [The Eater of the Dead] Whiro and the Descent to Pō: Māori eschatology sends the dead ( ngā mate ) to the underworld of Rarohenga , in the keeping of the goddess Hine-nui-te-pō. Within that realm the sources assign Whiro a dreadful office: Best ( Tūhoe , 1925) records that Whiro consumes the dead — the final extinction that awaits those who pass fully into his night — while other authorities make the underworld a guarded, not devoured, existence. Best records how carefully the dying were guarded: kin kept vigil so the soul's journey began rightly, for a misstep on the path meant falling among the powers that answered to Whiro rather than to the ancestors. The disagreement is itself instructive:The disagreement is itself instructive: Māori tradition was not systematic about its dark gods. What holds across the accounts is the direction of dread: after death lies a jurisdiction Whiro administers, and his administration is nothing to hope for . [Father of the Lizards] The Ngarara His Children: Whiro's epithet 'the lizard of death' is not metaphor alone: Māori genealogical chant makes him ancestor of the ngarara — the lizards, tuatara, and reptiles — whose cold eye and sudden movement marked them as his embodied kin (Best, Tūhoe ; Orbell, A Concise Encyclopedia of Māori Myth and Legend , 1998). A lizard in the house could be an omen or an emissary; killing one carelessly was dangerous. The tuatara — a living fossil, stranger than any creature the Māori had names for — was the most charged of all his children, and some traditions set it as guardian at the very threshold of Hine-nui-te-pō. The genealogy does ecological work:The genealogy does ecological work: it assigns the island's most alien-seeming creatures to the one god who is himself alien to the world of light. The reptiles are Whiro's diaspora — small darknesses walking in the daylight world . [Sender of Sickness] Illness as His Assault: In Māori medical tradition, sickness ( mate ) was the work of hostile atua , and Whiro stood behind the host: Best's ethnography ( Tūhoe ; 'Maori Medical Lore') describes the tohunga diagnosing which atua had 'shot' the patient and performing rites to drive the invader out. The rite was theater as much as medicine: the tohunga named the invading atua aloud, drove it toward the sea with the village's shouting, and bound the patient with cords — law, drama, and therapy in one operation. The afflictions attributed to Whiro's sideThe afflictions attributed to Whiro's side of the spirit world were grave and creeping — the wasting illnesses, the illnesses that came at night. The practical corollary was a therapy of confrontation: healing was a battle with Whiro's agents, fought with chant, gesture, and the authority of ancestors who had beaten him before . Illness had an enemy, and therefore a remedy.

instruction: Tell me a myth about "Tagaloa".
output: Tagaloa's mythology is cosmogony in the strict sense — stories of how land, people, and rank came to be . It survives not in epic but in creation chants recorded by nineteenth-century missionaries and ethnographers, whose accounts disagree in detail but agree that the world began when the Lord of the Heavens acted upon the sea. [The Making of the Isles] The Vine Let Down into the Sea: In the beginning Tagaloa dwelt alone in Lani-uli , the highest heaven, and beneath him lay only the boundless sea. He let down into the waters a vine from the sky; where its parts touched the surface, the islands of Samoa rose. On the largest he set the first settlement, and from the sky he watched over it. The fullest form of this creation account was recorded by the missionary J. B. Stair in Old Samoa (1897) and compared with related versions by Augustin Krämer in The Samoa Islands (1902); George Turner had published a shorter form in Nineteen Years in Polynesia (1861). Manu'a, the island group of the myth's first landing, is still styled the 'beginning of Samoa' in formal oratory, and the creation chant remained the deep charter for its paramount titles. The story is the charter of Samoan identity:The story is the charter of Samoan identity: the homeland is not discovered but made — thrown down from heaven and rooted in the sea . [The Daughter of Heaven] Sina and the Eel: Tagaloa's daughter Sina came down to the pool of Mata o le Alelo to bathe, where a great eel, Tuna, confessed its love. When the eel was killed at Sina's command, she buried its head, and from it grew the first coconut palm — its two eyes, mouth, and body still showing on the nut. The tale was recorded across Polynesia (Gill, Myths and Songs from the South Pacific , 1876; Beckwith, Hawaiian Mythology , 1970, §§ on the coconut cycle) and became the most retold of all Samoan stories. In Samoa the cycle carries a chiefly resonance as well: Sina's name became a byword for beauty in proverb, and her bathing pool, Mata o le Alelo, was pointed out to visitors into the twentieth century. The myth answers a child's questionThe myth answers a child's question — why does the coconut look like a face? — and binds the staple tree of island life to the death of an impossible love . [The Heavens Above] The Storeys of the Sky: Samoan cosmology stacks the sky into storeys — Lani-uli, Lani-ʻula, and the heavens beneath them — and places Tagaloa at the summit, above the winds that carry rain. Krämer ( The Samoa Islands , 1902) recorded prayers addressing the ascending heavens by name, each storey ruled or traversed on the way to the Lord's seat. No text gives a complete, consistent map; the ethnographers themselves note that districts preserved different orders of the heavens. Below the storeys of the sky the same cosmology placed the underworld and the remote ends of the earth, and prayers were imagined to rise through the layers like visitors announced at the thresholds of a great chief's house. Yet the structure is constant:Yet the structure is constant: the sacred is vertical, and the higher the heaven, the nearer the Lord . Cosmology here is not speculation but orientation — the same layering a navigator reads in cloud and star. [The Polynesian Dispersal] Tangaroa Driven to the Sea: In the Māori version of the same divine name, Tangaroa is a child of Ranginui and Papatūānuku, the sky-father and earth-mother crushed in their parents' tight embrace. When Tāne thrust his parents apart to let in the light, Tangaroa fled to the ocean, and his enmity with Tāne — whose forests silt the sea — endures in myth (Grey, Polynesian Mythology , 1855; Orbell, A Concise Encyclopedia of Māori Myth and Legend , 1998). The Hawaiian Kanaloa and Tahitian Ta'aroa preserve further branches of the same god. Linguists reconstruct the shared ancestral form and read the god's names as a map of settlement itself — each island's dialect keeping its own office for the one Lord. Read across the ocean, the dispersalRead across the ocean, the dispersal of Tagaloa's name is itself the story: wherever Polynesians voyaged, the Lord went with them, changing office — creator in Samoa, sea-god in Aotearoa — but never name .

instruction: Tell me a myth about "Nafanua".
output: Nafanua's cycle, recorded from Sāmoan oral tradition in the nineteenth century, is Samoa's great story of concealed power: a goddess hidden in the earth, a people crushed by tribute, and a victory that made a woman the ruler and prophet of the islands. [The Twins] The Tattoo Voyage of Taema and Tilafaiga: Before Nafanua's story begins, the sources tell of her mother Tilafaiga and her twin Taema. Born joined at the back, the girls were cut apart at 'Aopo on Savai'i with the obsidian teeth of the Fijian king Tui Fiti. Sent to Fiji to fetch a gift for their father, the underworld king Saveasi'uleo, they returned with the tattoo instruments — and, laughing, reversed the words of the song that told which sex should bear the marks, so that in Samoa it was the women who were tattooed first. In the recorded genealogies (Turner, Samoa a Hundred Years Ago , 1884; Stair, Old Samoa , 1897) this voyage of the twins explains the origin of Sāmoan tattooing, and it frames everything that follows: Nafanua's drama of concealment and emergence belongs to a family that already moves between worlds — Samoa, Fiji, and Pulotu, the land of the dead. The myth reads Samoa's geography of kinship as a single story. [The Hidden Child] Nafanua, 'Hidden in the Earth': Nafanua was the child of Tilafaiga and her own father Saveasi'uleo — a union the tradition does not hide and does not excuse. Because of it, the infant was spirited away and hidden in the earth at Falealupo, at the western tip of Savai'i; her very name is her biography, glossed in the early records as 'hidden in the earth' (Stair 1897; cf. fanua , 'land, earth'). She grew beneath the ground, fed in secret, known to the village only as a rumor. The detail is theological as much as narrative: Samoa's savior is not born in a chiefly house but underground, the child of a shame that had to be buried. When the chiefs' tyranny later breaks over the district, it is precisely the person the earth was hiding who rises out of it. The myth of her concealment makes Nafanua the standing answer to disgrace — what a family buries, the land remembers. [The War] The Woman Who Gave Water: In the generations after Nafanua's kin divided the districts, the young men of the ruling chiefs turned custom into tribute: every household at Falealupo was ordered to furnish pigs and food for the chiefs' work-parties. A woman of the village, ordered to give up her only pig and her kava, instead befriended the stranger who lived in the earth — bringing her water, sharing her griefs. Nafanua told her: refuse. When the chiefs' messengers came and the woman answered that the hidden one had forbidden it, the chiefs sent armed men to crush the defiance. Nafanua rose out of the earth with her war club — named in the accounts Televave , 'blows in different directions' — and the village rose with her. In the battle at Falealupo the oppressors were struck down, and the rule they had abused passed away from them forever (Stair; Kramer, The Samoa Islands , 1902). The story makes salvation begin with a small act of mercy: a cup of water offered to someone no one else would see. [The Prophecy] The Government from the West: The records agree that Nafanua was more than a war leader: she was a prophet of Samoa's political future. After the victory, the chiefs ceded the malo — the rule — to her, and tradition remembered her proclamations: that the government would one day come from the west, and that 'only a remnant would remain for that single day' ( aupito mavae ma la aso e tasi ), words later read as foretelling both the missionaries and the colonial powers who arrived from the west in the nineteenth century (Stair 1897; Mead, Social Organization of Manu'a , 1930, for the later life of the cycle). The exact wording varies with the teller, as is normal for an oral tradition, but the structure is constant: Nafanua's rule is legitimate because she can see beyond it. The myth declares that Samoa's salvation is historical, not eternal — each age must recognize the new thing coming over the horizon.

instruction: Tell me a myth about "Makemake".
output: Makemake is the creator god of Rapa Nui (Easter Island): father of fertility, lord of the seabirds, and the hidden face behind the island's birdman cult. The sources are late — the tradition was recorded in the late nineteenth and early twentieth centuries, after the population's collapse — and they must be read as the memory of a wounded tradition. [Creation] The Creator in the Chants: When the first ethnographers asked the islanders who made the world, the answer was Makemake. Alfred Métraux, working on Rapa Nui in 1934–35, recorded chants in which Makemake appears at the beginning of things as the great god, the maker of humankind, attended by the aku aku, the guardian spirits of the caves; Katherine Routledge heard related accounts during the Mana expedition of 1914–15. The surviving material is fragmentary — Peruvian slave raids and smallpox had shattered the population in the 1860s, carrying off the initiated experts, and much of the theology survived in the mouths of a handful of elders. In the recorded lore Makemake stands at the head of the pantheon, paired with the sea-god Tangaroa. What can be said with confidence is this: on the most isolated inhabited island on earth, creation was not a distant cosmic event but a local one, governed by a god whose staring face was carved into the living stone of the island itself. [Tangata Manu] The Birdman Contest: Each spring the men of Rapa Nui gathered at Orongo, the stone village on the rim of the Rano Kau crater, to compete for the title of tangata manu — the birdman. Swimmers called hopu descended the sea cliffs and crossed shark-filled water to the islet of Motu Nui, there to await the sooty tern's first egg of the season. The sponsor whose hopu returned first with an unbroken egg won: he was shaved, painted red and black, given the egg to wear against his body, and seated for a year in sacred seclusion as Makemake's chosen — the year's lord of fertility, whose fortune was read in the fortunes of land and sea. Métraux reconstructed the full ritual cycle from informants' testimony, and Routledge saw the last performances in 1914. The contest means that on an island without kingship, legitimacy came not from conquest but from a god-given sign: the birdman's egg was the island's crown, and Makemake alone conferred it. [Iconography] The Eyes of Orongo: The village of Orongo is itself Makemake's great icon. Its flat lava slabs are covered with petroglyphs — birdmen with human faces and birds' bodies, frigatebirds, Komari fertility symbols, and above all the staring face of Makemake himself, the eyes hugely enlarged, peering from the rock beside the contest grounds. Georgia Lee's survey, The Rock Art of Easter Island (1992), catalogued some twelve hundred designs and showed the wide-eyed faces clustered at the very village where the tangata manu contest was held: the god carved as witness. Métraux had already recorded that the islanders named these faces as Makemake's. The image means that knowledge is sight — the lexicon's gloss of the name, 'to see, to know', is literally carved at Orongo, where the god's whole function is to watch, and where being seen by Makemake is the entire power of the ceremony. [Survival] The Silence and the Return: The cult did not survive contact intact. Peruvian slavers carried off around a thousand islanders in 1862–63, including the last initiated experts; smallpox followed; by 1868 the survivors stood for mass baptism. Métraux heard the birdman cycle from men who had never seen it performed, and Routledge found Orongo already standing empty, its sacred houses abandoned. Yet the name never died. In the later twentieth century the Tapati Rapa Nui festival began staging the birdman legend again — canoe races, body-painting, and the choosing of a festival queen — and the tangata manu story became the emblem of the islanders' revived identity. In 2008 the astronomers who found the bright dwarf planet beyond Pluto gave it Makemake's name. The history means that a god once reduced to a stone face watched over the slow return of the people who had made him: the watcher outlasted the silence.

instruction: Tell me a myth about "Svarog".
output: Svarog has no surviving epic and no surviving cult — his entire dossier is a few chronicle lines, a gloss, and a name. The mythology below is therefore an archaeology of attestations: each 'myth' is a document, read as closely as the evidence allows, with the tradition's silence stated plainly. [The Book God] Named in the Izbornik of 1073: The earliest notice of Svarog comes not from a pagan shrine but from a court book. The Svyatoslav Izbornik of 1073 — a miscellany compiled for Prince Svyatoslav of Kiev — pauses over the Slavic gods to say: 'There is a god named Svarog' , and in the surrounding passage draws the comparison with the smith-god Hephaestus, whose forge was read as an image of heaven's fire. The compiler's source was probably a South Slavic manual translated for Duke Svyatoslav's court, which would make the notice the fossil of a lost Slavic mythographic handbook. The sentence is three words in Old Russian,The sentence is three words in Old Russian, yet it proves that in eleventh-century Rus', a century and a half after official conversion, learned men still needed to name and explain the old sky-smith. The attestation tells us less what Svarog did than how stubbornly he survived — a god preserved in the margin of a Christian book . [The Sun's Father] Svarog and the Birth of Dažbog: The Primary Chronicle (Povest' vremennykh let), in its anti-pagan sermon, records the genealogy plainly: 'from him was born Dažbog' — the Giving God, the sun — a line preserved in the Laurentian and Hypatian codices (Cross & Sherbowitz-Wetzor, trans.). Dažbog in turn gave his name to the Rus' themselves in the chronicler's bitter pun — 'Dažbog's grandchildren,' a folk memory the sermon meant to shame into silence. With it comes the whole logicWith it comes the whole logic of the sky-smith: what a smith fathers is a made light, a produced radiance, and Dažbog's very name ('the giver') reads like the boast of a successful forge. Scholars caution that the chronicler's sermon is polemic, not ethnography. Even so, the fragment preserves a genuine Indo-European intuition in Slavic dress: the sun is not a body but a work — hammered out, handed down, and called a gift . [The Western Witness] Zuarasici among the Slavic Gods: Writing around 1172, the German priest Helmold of Bosau lists the gods the Slavs revere — and among them, Zuarasici , the form his Latin ear gave to Svarog (Helmold, Chronica Slavorum I.52). The notice is a single name in a hostile catalogue, yet it matters: it places the god west of Kiev, among the Obodrite Slavs of the Baltic coast, suggesting his name once ranged across the whole Slavic world. The same passage gives him neighbors — a storm-hurling chief god and a god of war — so one hostile paragraph sketches the entire Obodrite pantheon. Helmold's list is our only Western-witness checkHelmold's list is our only Western-witness check on the Russian sources. A name without a story, recorded by an enemy, is fragile evidence — but it is evidence, and for a Slavic god that is rare enough to be precious . [The Little Svarog] Svarožič, Fire of the Hearth: In a Novgorod copy of Hilarion's Sermon on Law and Grace , a copyist 'corrected' the text to write Svarožič — 'Little Svarog' — the name scholars take for a fire-god or the domesticated form of the sky-smith (Ivanits, Russian Folk Belief , 1989; Gieysztor, Mitologia Słowian ). Later South Slavic and folk materials preserve hearth rites — the fire doused, fed, and addressed with honor — which the scholarship has long connected to this doubled name. South Slavic folklore collected in the nineteenth century still addresses the hearth fire with honorific formulas, and Serbian scholarship has long read in them the memory of a flame that was once a god. The tradition is fragmentary and the reconstruction debated;The tradition is fragmentary and the reconstruction debated; what stands is the shape of the idea: the cosmic smith had a small form that fit inside every house , so that tending the stove was, in origin, tending a god.

instruction: Tell me a myth about "Simargl".
output: Simargl has no mythology in the ordinary sense — no tale was ever told about him. He exists as a single line in a chronicle, a name of Iranian ancestry, and a century of scholarly argument about what a winged guardian was doing in a Slavic pantheon. [Kyiv, 988] The Idols in the Dnieper: In 988 the Primary Chronicle's procession of drowned gods includes, between Stribog and Mokosh, a name no Slavic tongue built: Simargl. The chronicler lists him without curiosity, one idol among six, but modern scholarship has never been able to leave him alone — because his name betrays a long journey, from the Iranian Simurgh, through the speech of steppe peoples who traded and raided along the Black Sea, into the capital of Christianizing Rus'. A pantheon is a nation's self-portrait; Kyiv's included a god borrowed from Persia's. The chronicle line is the whole dossier: no oath, no gloss, no sorcerer, no saint. One drowning, recorded by the enemies who arranged it — and a foreign accent still audible in the name as it went under. No later source ever asked who had carried him there; only modern scholarship heard the accent at all. [Iranian Origin] A Name from Persia: The Simurgh of Iranian tradition is one of the oldest great birds of world mythology. In the Avesta she roosts in the branches of the sacred tree; across Sogdian and Sasanian art she spreads composite wings over the Tree of Life; and in Ferdowsi's Shahnameh she rears the hero Zal and guides his son Rostam through every impossible task — part dog, part lion, part bird, and wholly wise. How her name crossed into Slavic as Simargl is the ordinary work of steppe history: Alanic- and Sarmatian-speaking peoples of the north Pontic steppe served as carriers, and a worn-down Simurgh entered East Slavic speech generations before a chronicler wrote it down. The borrowing tells its own myth: a god can be an import, and a pantheon a port — Kyiv's sky had been in conversation with Persia's for centuries before either had a church. [The Rybakov Hypothesis] Guardian of Seeds?: Boris Rybakov, the most influential historian of Slavic religion, gave Simargl his modern job description: guardian of seeds and plant life. The argument runs on two legs — the Simurgh's Iranian role as protector of the Tree of Life and of vegetation, and the presence in Slavic folklore of the Sey Div , a chthonic being who guards sown fields and must be placated at sowing and harvest. If Simargl is a worn Simurgh, and the Sey Div is his folk memory in reverse, then the god who drowned in the Dnieper was the protector of every furrow in Rus'. The hypothesis is ingenious and untestable: no text calls Simargl a seed-guardian, and the Sey Div connection rests on names and functions, never on an attestation. It is cited here exactly as Rybakov framed it — a structure built from parallels, honest about its own materials, and better than any rival precisely because it admits what it is. [Honest Silence] The Sphinx of the Pantheon: Like Stribog, Simargl must be described by what is missing. No treaty swears by him; the Malalas gloss that rescued Dažbog passes him by; no saint inherits his day; South Slavic folklore preserves no Dajbog-like fossil of his name; and no archaeological find — not the Zbruch idol, not the axe-amulets, not the Peryn' enclosure — can be tied to him with any confidence. What remains is structural: a pantheon needs a vegetation-guardian, the name is Iranian, and the Iranian original is the greatest plant-guardian of the Near Eastern myth-world. Modern scholarship has filled the gap with a functional god; modern paganism has filled it with a feathered angel of gardens. Both are guesses at a shape the sources never drew. Simargl is the Kyiv pantheon's sphinx: a riddle posed in a foreign accent, guarding a seed no one has ever seen.

instruction: Tell me a myth about "Lada".
output: No medieval Slavic text tells a myth of Lada . What survives is a trail of witnesses — a funeral play, a chronicler's glosses, Renaissance mythography, and living spring songs — from which scholarship must carefully separate memory from invention. Her 'mythology' is therefore the history of how a song-cry became a goddess, and an honest temple must tell it that way. [The Oldest Witness] The Refrain in the Round Dance: The oldest trace of Lada is not a story about her but a word sung in her place. In the spring round-dances of the South Slavs on Jurjevo — St George's Day, 6 May, when the grazing season opens — the cry Lado! punctuates the melody: greeting, praise, chorus, or the goddess herself, the sources never say. Young people cut the green oak, the zelenika , dance around it, and carry it to the pasture; nineteenth-century ethnographers among Croats, Serbs, and the Balkan Roma recorded the songs with the refrain intact. Farther north the same word softens into endearment: in Polish and Ukrainian wedding songs ladko and lado mean simply 'dear one.' The earliest stratum of the evidence is thus not narrative but music. If Lada was ever a full goddess, her first body was a song — which is why she has survived every empire that buried her chroniclers. [The School Play] Lada, Lel, and Polel on the Stage: The first text to list Lada among the gods is a joke at her expense. The Kraków school drama Pogrzeb świętej Roksany ('The Funeral of St. Roxane'), composed around 1500 and printed in 1535, brings together three students — a German, a Czech, and a Pole — to argue over whose hero deserves burial. The Pole defends his own ancestors: our gods, he insists, were Lada, Lel, and Polel , and our songs still remember them. The comedy mocks him for clinging to heathenry; but mockery preserves what reverence forgot, and the schoolboy's boast is now our earliest catalogue of Slavic divine names. The sources disagree even here: the play pairs Lada with Lel and Polel, while later writers split the twins differently and added genealogies no one attests. A goddess remembered in ridicule is still remembered — the play is less evidence of cult than of a name refusing, two centuries after conversion, to disappear. [The Chroniclers] The Glosses of Długosz and His Successors: Jan Długosz, the fifteenth-century Polish annalist, inserted into his Annales (Book I) marginal glosses on the old religion: the pagan Poles, he claims, used Lado for God himself, and among their goddesses he names Lada — glossing her, erratically, as Venus. The glosses, transmitted in the copy made by Stanisław Komasius, equate the native names so inconsistently that no modern scholar trusts the identifications. Later Renaissance mythography repeated and inflated them: Marcin Kromer's Polonia (1555), Maciej Stryjkowski's Kronika (1582) — which makes Lada a goddess of love — and Stanisław Sarnicki (1585) and Szymon Starowolski (1615), who repeat the lore with growing confidence. None of them cites a source older than folk memory. The chroniclers did not record Lada; they manufactured her — a caution this temple must carry at its threshold. [The Debate] Goddess or Refrain?: The nineteenth century decided the question by enthusiasm. Alexander Afanasyev's Poetic Views of the Slavs on Nature (1865–1869) enthroned Lada as a great goddess of spring and love, flanked by her twin sons Lel and Polel; Šafařík and Krek spread the picture across Slavdom, and Romantic art gave her a face. Twentieth-century scholarship pulled back hard: Michał Gieysztor's Mitologia Słowian (1982) keeps her cautiously, while Leszek P. Słupecki's Religia Słowian (2018) and other critics argue that the attestations are too late and too folkloric — that lado may never have been more than a refrain-word, with Lada its feminine form, like the wedding cry ladno still heard in Serbia. Comparatists set her beside the Greek Horai and the Latvian Laima, but no genetic link can be proven. The tradition is fragmentary and the sources openly disagree — and the debate itself, still alive, is the closest thing Lada has ever had to a cult.

instruction: Tell me a myth about "Morana".
output: Slavic paganism wrote almost nothing down, so Morana's mythology survives as a rite, a name, and a constellation of village customs across Poland, Bohemia, Moravia, Slovakia, and the Balkans — read together, they amount to a complete theology of winter's death and spring's return, kept alive by practice rather than by any book. [Attestation] A Goddess between the Lines: Morana reaches us obliquely, through the margins of other people's books. Her earliest written trace is a fifteenth-century Latin–Polish school glossary, the so-called Medulla Grammatice, where the Latin word mors — 'death' — is glossed with the Polish morana; schoolboys were being taught the goddess's name as the plain word for dying. Sixteenth-century writers then describe the rite itself: Marcin Siennik complains of peasants who fashion a straw woman at winter's end and drown or burn her in the name of Marzanna, and Maciej Stryjkowski's chronicle records the custom in the villages of Mazovia. No epic survives in which Morana acts, and no chronicler retells her deeds. What survives is a name, a meaning, and a crowd of village rituals that kept both alive. The myth tells us how this tradition stored its goddess: not in pages, but in practice — in a rite repeated so faithfully that five centuries of theologians could not kill it. [Ritual] The Drowning of Marzanna: On the fourth Sunday of Lent — or on the spring equinox in the older reckoning — the village takes a figure of straw and rags dressed as a woman and carries it in procession to the riverbank: Morana's Polish ritual self, Marzanna. The girls who carry her sing farewells to winter; then the effigy is doused with water, drowned, and often burned where it lies. Her Moravian and Slovak cousins carry the Morena doll out on 30 April and throw it into the stream while the children cry that Morena should carry winter out of the village with her. The Church denounced the custom for centuries as a pagan survival; Communist-era ethnography filed it under folklore; neither suppressed it, and after 1989 the rite returned openly to Polish schools. Today children across Poland still drown and burn Marzanna every spring. The rite enacts the year's great transaction: winter is not begged to leave — it is killed, and spring arrives as the corpse sinks. [Season myth] The Bride of Winter and the God of Spring: Modern scholarship has tried to give Morana the love-story the medieval sources never recorded. The Indo-Europeanists Vyacheslav Ivanov and Vladimir Toporov reconstructed a full seasonal cycle: Morana, winter's queen, is wooed and wed in spring by the vegetative god Jarilo; he abandons or dies with the autumn, she murders him in revenge, and the world freezes in her grief until the returning sun avenges him in spring. The reconstruction rests on comparative folklore and seasonal rite rather than on any surviving Slavic epic, and specialists debate its every stage — but it has been embraced by Slavic Rodnovery communities, for whom the wedding, betrayal, and killing of Morana and Jarilo form the turning myth of the liturgical year. The uncertainty itself is instructive: folklore supplied the rite, and scholarship supplied the plot. Whatever its age, the cycle says what the drowning already implies — winter is not weather but a person, who loves, mourns, and can be made to die. [Name magic] The Root of the Nightmare: The name tells the whole story by itself. Proto-Slavic *morà meant at once death, pestilence, and the crushing demon of bad dreams — and its daughters still do the same work: Polish zmora is the night-hag that paralyses the sleeper, Serbo-Croatian mòra the fever-vision that rides the chest, Russian mor the plague that empties villages. The word is an inheritance, not an invention. Greek has μόρος, doom; Latin has mors, death; Sanskrit has mṛtyú; Lithuanian has mirtìs — linguists read the family back to an Indo-European root *mer-, 'to die' (Beekes, EDG s.v. μόρος; ESSJa s.v. *morà). To name the goddess is therefore to invoke a constellation in which winter, disease, and nightmare are one phenomenon: the cold weight that settles on the world and on the sleeping body alike. Slavic folklore never separated them, and its goddess keeps all three meanings folded into a single name.

instruction: Tell me a myth about "Zmey Gorynych".
output: The crown of the Dobrynya cycle: how a hero's mercy gave the dragon a second life, and how the second battle was won by a wet hat, not a sword. The byliny are oral epic, recorded from living singers in the eighteenth and nineteenth centuries. [The bylina] Dobrynya Rides to the Mountains: In the bylina of Dobrynya Nikitich and Zmey Gorynych, recorded by the nineteenth-century collectors of the Kireevsky circle, the hero's mother warns him never to ride to the Sorochinsky mountains, for the fire-breathing serpent holds them. The young hero rides anyway. From a dark cloud the dragon descends with three heads, and fire pours from each mouth. They fight for three days — Dobrynya's arrows spent, his clothing burnt, the earth scorched black around them. At last the dragon begs for mercy: let me go, brave Dobrynya, and I will never again carry off Christian people. The hero remembers his mother's teaching — she who spared the serpent brought grief upon herself — but he sheathes his sword and lets the dragon go. The bylina's first lesson is mercy; its second, still to come, is what mercy costs when it is spent on a dragon. [The bylina] The Second Battle and the Wet Hat: The dragon keeps neither his word nor his fear. He seizes Zabava, niece of Prince Vladimir, and carries her to his mountain. Dobrynya rides after him, but at the serpent's river his horse stumbles and refuses the water — an omen he cannot ignore. The second battle is worse than the first: flame no shield can face. Dobrynya survives by his mother's counsel — he soaks his women's hat in the river and fights beneath the dripping hood, the wet wool hissing where the fire strikes it. When the dragon weakens, Dobrynya cuts off all three heads, then gathers the severed stumps and burns them, for a zmei's heads grow back if they are allowed to rejoin; finally he bathes in the dragon's blood and returns Zabava to her uncle's hall. The detail every singer kept is the wet hat: the weapon that wins the second battle is not steel but preparation — soaked wool against dragonfire, and the patience to finish what mercy left unfinished. [The fairy tales] The Tribute of Maidens: Outside the bylina, in the fairy-tale corpus gathered by Afanas'ev in the nineteenth century, the three-headed zmei belongs to a darker economy. He descends on a town and names his price: maidens, nine at a time, year after year, and the townsfolk pay, because the alternative is fire. These are anonymous tales of the ATU 300 dragon-slayer type, and the dragon's hunger here is less personal than the bylina's — he is not anyone's nemesis, he is the thing the community feeds. A peasant's third son, the fool of the family, marks his arrows and climbs to the lair. In these tales the dragon-slayer is almost never the expected one: not the king's champion but the youngest brother, the one nobody fed to the serpent. The tribute myth turns the whole village into an accomplice, and the slayer into the one who finally refused to pay — the point being that dragons are affordable only until someone counts the cost. [The collectors] The Epic as Archive: The bylina itself had to be saved as often as the princess. It survived in the mouths of peasant singers in the Russian north until the mid-eighteenth century, when the compiler Kirsha Danilov set down the earliest known collection of byliny, and again in the 1860s when P. V. Kireevsky's expeditions took the songs from living performers whose grandmothers had sung them. Folklorists from Veselovsky to Propp argued over the dragon's ancestry: a pagan storm-serpent, they proposed, overlaid with the Christian St George — the folk hero Dobrynya standing in for the saint, the dragon for the devil of the iconostasis. Propp, in his Russian Epic Studies, read the dragon fight as a seasonal spring rite pressed into epic form. Whatever the origin, the song outlived every theory about it. The epic is the only weapon in the cycle that never had to be reforged: as long as someone sings it, the dragon stays slain and alive at once.

instruction: Tell me a myth about "Xōlōtl".
output: Xōlōtl's myths run on twoness: twin of the morning star, guide of the dying sun, the god who is always the second of a pair — and always the one who goes down into the dark. [The Guide] Across the Nine Waters: The Aztec dead journeyed four years through Mictlān's nine levels, and at the deep river it was the dog — Xōlōtl's creature — who swam them across: a soul whose family had mistreated dogs in life found no ferryman, while one buried with his red dog had a guide already in the grave (Sahagún, Florentine Codex, trans. Anderson & Dibble — the funeral rites of the dead's journey). The funeral rite killed a dog 'the color of fire' and laid it with the dead to carry its master home. Among the world's psychopomps, he is the only one who comes as a pet — the escort you raised from a pup, not a paid professional of the crossing, and the myth's quiet claim is that loyalty outlasts the life that earned it. [The Sacrifice] The God Who Hid: At the creation of the fifth sun the gods gathered at Teotihuacan to sacrifice themselves and set the new sun moving (Leyenda de los Soles, Codex Chimalpopoca). Xōlōtl refused to die: he fled, weeping so hard his eyes fell from their sockets, and hid — as the twin-stalked maize, as the doubled maguey, and at last as the axolotl in the lake. They found him even there, and he died like the rest. The myth is the Aztec anatomy of the price of survival — and of the god who begged to live and serves death anyway: the one who ran is precisely the one the dead meet at the river, as if the underworld drafted its guide from the only god who had tried, with everything he had, to stay on this side of it. [The Twins] Venus Split in Two: Quetzalcōātl is Venus as morning star, herald of the light; Xōlōtl is Venus as evening star, which follows the sun into darkness (Sahagún, Florentine Codex, Book 7 — the star cycles and the binding of the years). The astronomy is exact — one planet, two appearances — and the myth makes it biography: one twin leads the dawn out of the night, the other escorts the day into it. Together they keep the star's whole circuit, and the world's whole hope: nothing in the Aztec sky set unaccompanied, and no light went down into the dark without the god of guides riding it. [The Descent] The Bones of the Fathers: When the fifth age needed people, Quetzalcōātl descended to Mictlān for the bones of the dead, and the later tellings send Xōlōtl with him as the one who knows the road — past Mictlāntēcutli's traps to the underworld council, where the lord of the dead set impossible conditions: sound my conch, which no breath will blow, and circle my realm four times without setting the burden down (Leyenda de los Soles; cf. the Histoyre du Mechique). The bones, ground in a bowl and sprinkled with the gods' own blood, became humankind — every Aztec child made of the dead, carried up past the watchful lord by knowledge of the road back. That the tellings choose the dog-brother for the escort is the myth's own logic: who better to know Mictlān's way than the god who ferries it daily?

instruction: Tell me a myth about "Tlāltēcuhtli".
output: Tlāltēcuhtli appears in several Mesoamerican creation accounts as the earth monster who must be defeated and dismembered before the present world can exist. The most detailed Nahuatl version survives in the Histoyre du Méchique , a sixteenth-century colonial manuscript; the Leyenda de los Soles and the Florentine Codex supply parallel doctrines. These sources are fragmentary and written after the conquest — the tradition itself says so, and this temple reports them as such. [Creation myth] The Dismemberment of the Earth Monster: Our fullest Nahua creation account survives in a sixteenth-century French manuscript, the Histoyre du Méchique (associated with the cosmographer André Thevet) — colonial, fragmentary, and precious for exactly that reason. It tells that the gods Quetzalcōātl and Tēzcatlīpōca, seeing a great monster in the form of a caiman called Tlāltēcuhtli floating on the primordial waters, transformed themselves into two great serpents and seized her, one by the right hand and foot, one by the left, and tore her in two. From one half they made the earth, from the other the sky; from her hair they made trees, plants, and flowers, from her eyes wells and springs, from her nose rivers and valleys, from her shoulders mountains. The victim did not die quietly: she cried out in the night for the hearts of men, and the gods consented to feed her. The Leyenda de los Soles tells a parallel creation. The myth's meaning is contract, not conquest: the world exists because a being was broken, and it keeps existing only while the debt of flesh is paid. [Solar myth] The Sun's Nightly Journey: The Florentine Codex — the encyclopedia compiled under Bernardino de Sahagún from Nahua elders in the 1540s–1570s — describes the sun's nightly passage in the plainest physical terms: at evening the sun enters the gaping mouth of the earth in the west, passes through the body of Tlāltēcuhtli, and is delivered again at dawn in the east. To the sources this is no metaphor: the earth has a mouth, jaws, and hunger, and the day itself is a meal it cannot be allowed to refuse. Nahuatl vocabulary underwrites the image — the earth is tlālli , and Tlāltēcuhtli is that land made lord. The doctrine that night is the sun passing through a body made every evening an act of digestion and every morning a birth: in this cosmology time does not flow above the world but through it, and the calendar keeps its count in the gut of the ground. [Ritual foundation] Offerings to the Hungry Earth: Sahagún's informants describe a relationship of payment. Before a house was built, a field planted, or a body buried, the earth was addressed and fed — food, flowers, copal incense, and in the highest rites blood — because unfed earth refuses its function (Florentine Codex, Books 1 and 11; Durán, Book of the Gods and Rites ). The Codex Magliabechiano illustrates precisely such offerings set before a crouching earth figure. The archaeological correlate is overwhelming: the Templo Mayor excavations have recovered dedicatory caches buried as gifts to the earth at every stage of construction, some containing the remains of sacrifice. Colonial friars read this as devil-worship; the Nahua informants present it as ordinary courtesy. Both testify to the same theology: the ground under Mexico City was never inert — it was a creditor holding the mortgage on every foundation stone. [Modern discovery] The Red Monolith Beneath the Cathedral: On 2 October 2006, in a trench at the foot of the Templo Mayor, Leonardo López Luján's team uncovered a slab that made international news: a monolithic Tlāltēcuhtli more than four metres across, carved crouching with claws extended, a skull at the waist-buckle, death's eyes in its sockets, and traces of red and yellow pigment still in the stone. López Luján associated the monument with the nearby cremation deposits of Mexica rulers — above all Ahuitzotl, who died in 1502 — reading it as the earth lord summoned to receive a king. The find completed a five-hundred-year symmetry: the colonial city was built over the earth's face, its cathedral stones cut from the temples of the precinct; the excavation put the face back into the light. The earth, the Aztecs said, always gets what it is owed — even if payment comes in the currency of archaeology, and five centuries late.

instruction: Tell me a myth about "Ọrúnmìlà".
output: Ọrúnmìlà's mythology lives in the thousands of Ifá verses (òdù Ifá) that record his journeys, judgments, and interventions — wisdom's biography told as scripture. [Cosmogony] The Witness at the Foundation of the World: According to Ifá tradition, Ọrúnmìlà was the only orixá present when Olódùmarè created the earth. He observed the placing of the rivers, the rising of the mountains, and the distribution of destinies, and the corpus never stops drawing authority from that attendance (Abimbola, Ifá: An Exposition of Ifá Literary Corpus , 1976; Bascom, Ifa Divination , 1969). The other orishas received domains; Ọrúnmìlà received the memory of everything. Because he witnessed the beginning, he can trace any present trouble back to its origin and prescribe the sacrifice that will set it right. The Ifá verses return to this scene whenever authority is questioned, and it has silenced sceptics for centuries. The myth defines knowledge as witnessing rather than power: the one who watched the world being made became the one to whom the world turns when it forgets what it is for. [Origin] Àgbọnnìrègún, the Medicine That Never Fails: Before descending to earth, Ọrúnmìlà received from Olódùmarè the gift called àgbọnnìrègún — the sixteen sacred palm nuts and the science of reading them, glossed in the corpus as 'the medicine that never fails' (Bascom 1969; Idowu, 1962). The myth has a practical moral: the other orishas came down with powers over fire, water, and iron, but Ọrúnmìlà came down with a method. Wherever he travelled — and the verses send him wandering through every kind of settlement — he could answer any question put to him by casting the nuts and reciting the odù that fell. That is why the nuts are addressed with the respect due a founder, and why their loss ends a priest's career. The story makes divination a deliberate endowment, not an improvisation: heaven equipped its witness with the one tool the world would never stop needing. [Destiny] The Man Who Chose a Bad Head: A celebrated òdù narrative tells of a man who, before birth, knelt impatiently in heaven and seized the first head Àjàlá the potter offered — a cracked, ill-fired orí. On earth his life collapsed: his farms failed, his wives left, his name soured. At last he consulted Ifá, performed the prescribed sacrifice, and in a dream journey returned to the house of Àjàlá, where he exchanged the ruined head for a sound one; he woke on earth a different man (Abimbola 1976; the Orí cycle of narratives). The story is the corpus's most beloved parable of hope: destiny chosen cannot be unchosen, but heaven keeps a pottery, and sacrifice is the road back to it. Ọrúnmìlà's role is never to mock the careless chooser — only to chart the road back. [Counsel] The Client Who Would Not Sacrifice: Countless òdù verses end the same way: a person consults Ifá, receives a precise prescription — offer this, avoid that — and ignores it; ruin follows exactly as the odù said it would (Bascom 1969 catalogues the motif). Sometimes the refuser is a king who will not humble himself, sometimes a trader who counts the ẹbọ too dear. Ọrúnmìlà never punishes; the ignored counsel simply unfolds, the way an unread letter still contains its bad news. The motif is the corpus's pedagogy of practice: divination is not knowledge for its own sake but knowledge tied to an act. A verse unperformed is a door left shut, and a sacrifice owed is a debt the world always collects. The god of wisdom measures understanding the way a doctor measures recovery — not by what you heard, but by what you did.

instruction: Tell me a myth about "Ọṣọọsì".
output: Ọṣọọsì's mythology lives in praise-poetry and divination verse — the oríkì that greet him, the Ifá corpus that ranks him among the orisha, and the itan, the sacred stories of the diaspora houses that still tell of the one arrow. [Oríkì] The Hunter Who Kills Once: His praise-poems are the hunt distilled: the oríkì greet Ọ̀ṣọ́ọ̀sì as the hunter who kills with a single arrow — the archer whose patience is so complete that the forest gives him what it denies the noisy and the hasty. In the Candomblé houses of Brazil the same idea opens his festivals: Oxóssi, rei das matas, king of the forest, the provider whose one shot feeds the whole town. The oríkì tradition is not ornament here; it is the liturgy of competence. [Ifá Corpus] The Orisha of the Odù: In the Ifá divination corpus — the 256 odù and their thousands of memorized verses — the divine hunter walks as provider and strategist: the orisha who knows the paths of the bush as the babaláwo knows the paths of the palm nuts. Bascom's fieldwork in Ife and among Cuban practitioners recorded his place in the diviners' world; Idowu's theology of the orisha sets him among the ministers Olódùmarè appointed over creation's wild half. Wherever Ifá is consulted, the forest has a spokesman. [Lukumí] Among the Warriors: In Cuban Santería, Ochosi stands with the Guerreros — the Warriors: Eleguá who opens the road, Ogún who clears it with iron, Ochosi who hunts its game, and Osún who keeps watch — the first orishas a practitioner receives. His Cuban face is the justice-bringer: devotees call on him in court cases and wrongful accusations, the hunter whose arrow finds the truth the way it finds the heart of the deer. The hunt and the lawsuit are one skill: tracking. [Candomblé] Oxóssi of the Twentieth of January: In Brazil, Oxóssi was paired with São Sebastião — the Roman soldier shot through with arrows for refusing to renounce his faith, his iconography a perfect mirror for the archer orisha — and the saint's feast of January 20 became Oxóssi's own. In Umbanda his name heads the whole linha de Oxóssi, the line of the caboclo spirits, the indigenous forest guides. Three nations, three spellings, one bow.

instruction: Tell me a myth about "Aganjú".
output: Aganjú's myths are less numerous than those of Ọṣun or Ṣàngó, but they centre on a single theme: the earth as a living, burning body that carries human life without belonging to it. Where other orishas crowd the town and its markets, Aganjú's dossier is written at the boundary — volcano, desert, quarry — and in the diaspora's discovery that the wilderness god was carrying the world all along. [Lineage] Son of Odùduwà and Ọbatalá: Aganjú's birth is a statement of his character: he arrives from the union of the two powers that divide the Yoruba cosmos. In many lineages he is counted a son of Odùduwà, the royal ancestor who founded the earth's cities, and of Ọbatalá, the white-clothed sculptor of human bodies; the genealogies vary — oral tradition keeps several versions, and no single Ifá corpus settles the question. What the variants agree on is the outcome. This child of kingship and craft refuses both inheritances and chooses the uncultivated bush, the lava field, the place no farm can claim. Where Ọbatalá shapes and Odùduwà rules, Aganjú simply burns and bears. Divination verses recorded by Bascom and others keep him at the world's edge, immense and mostly silent, invoked when the earth itself must be addressed — droughts, eruptions, the cracking of foundations. The myth means that every order rests on an unowned force it cannot command: the volcano is the family member the palace never invited home. [Kingship] The King Who Became the Volcano: A second tradition makes Aganjú not a god from birth but a king who became one. Samuel Johnson's History of the Yorubas (1921), the great early record of Oyo tradition, preserves the memory of an Aláàfin — a king of the old Ọ̀yọ́ empire — remembered as Aganjú, whose rule ended in apotheosis: his name passed to the orisha of the wilderness, and the royal cult and the wilderness cult folded into one figure. Johnson is a single, late, colonial-era source, and modern scholarship treats the deified-king account cautiously — it may be a rationalization, or a genuinely remembered apotheosis of the kind Yoruba kingship often produced. But the tradition matters even if it is embroidery, because it explains why Aganjú carries both a king's gravity and a volcano's indifference to law. The myth means that the wilderness god may once have worn a crown — and that a king too fierce for the palace could still find a temple. [Diaspora] Aggayú Solá Carries the World: In Cuban Santería, Aganjú crosses the Atlantic and grows. As Aggayú Solá — the name already swelling with the sea-voyage — he is imagined as a giant so tall that rivers reach his ankles and palm trees are grass under his feet; he walks through lava as others walk through sand, and the earth rides on his shoulders like a load. When he possesses a devotee in ceremony, the person's whole gait changes: the step becomes heavy, swaying, patient, as if the ground under the dancer has remembered it is alive. Verger, who documented the orisha cults on both sides of the Atlantic, records that the diaspora re-centered Aganjú from the edge of settlement into the very center of the ritual house, pairing him with Ṣàngó as earth-fire to sky-fire. The transformation is the myth's meaning: a god of the uninhabited place became, in exile, the god who carries the inhabited one. The wilderness orisha ends up holding the whole world. [Cult] The Desert and the Town: Aganjú's cult geography is a map of the human boundary. His offerings — palm wine, smoked fish, red palm oil — are carried to the edge of towns, to road-cuts and quarries, to the last wall before the bush begins; in Candomblé houses his assentamento of iron-rich and volcanic stones sits low and grounded, as close to the floor as a god can get. Unlike Ọṣun, whose rivers run through the marketplace, Aganjú keeps the places where people stop and wilderness resumes. Mason's studies of New World Yoruba ritual describe the deliberate slowness of his rites: nothing about him is quick, because nothing about volcanoes is quick. The theology is stated by the offering site itself — civilization rests on older, hotter forces and owes them a share. The myth means that the wall around the city is a courtesy the wilderness extends, not a victory it has conceded.

instruction: Tell me a myth about "Ọbalúayé".
output: Ọbalúayé's mythology is not a heroic cycle but an oral canon — Yoruba praise poetry carried across the Atlantic and kept in patakís , the teaching stories of Santería and Candomblé. The versions disagree in detail and agree in meaning: affliction is real, the earth sends it, and survival rightly borne becomes holiness. [Patakís] The King Cast Down: In the most widely told patakís of the Cuban canon, Babalú-Ayé was not always a beggar. He was a king — some say the proudest of the orixás — who grew contemptuous of the sick, or hoarded the secrets of healing, until Olodumare's judgment fell on him: sores from the soles of his feet to the crown of his head, and exile from every door. Only the dogs stayed, licking his wounds, and in their rough tenderness lay the first medicine. Cast out, he walked the earth as the poorest of the poor, and the humiliation remade him: the god who had despised affliction became its master and its cure. His modern collectors — Mason in Four New World Yoruba Rituals , Murphy in Santería: African Spirits in America — record versions that differ in detail; all agree on the moral: the healer must know the body from inside affliction, and pride is the first disease he treats. [Yoruba ground] The Dogs and the Hidden Path: Dogs belong to Ọbalúayé on both continents because they live at the boundary he owns — between the village and the bush, the healthy and the sick, the living and the earth that takes them. In Yoruba teaching the dog runs ahead on paths men cannot see; in diaspora patakís it is the dog who leads the sufferer to the stream where the healing leaves grow, or who carries the message between the sick person's door and the orixá's. His devotees keep the image literally: two dogs stand beside the old man on crutches in every altar figure, and dog imagery runs through his beadwork and his cloth. The myth encodes the practical work of healing in an epidemic age — one must follow signs that do not speak in human language, keep low to the ground, and trust the guide that never strays far from the earth that sends both the sickness and the herb. [Diaspora] At the Crossroads of Saint Lazarus: In Cuban Santería, Babalú Ayé appears as an old beggar at the crossroads, leaning on crutches, accompanied by dogs — and the image is liturgical as much as narrative. His feast falls on 17 December, the Catholic day of Saint Lazarus, and on that night tens of thousands of Cubans make the pilgrimage to the shrine of San Lázaro at El Rincón, many crawling the last distance on their knees, leaving offerings of roasted corn, dry wine, and herbs: the largest religious procession in the country. The beggar's shape is theology: illness can reduce anyone — king or scholar — to dependence, and dependence rightly borne is a form of holiness. The crossroads is his because sickness is a crossroads, the body at the point where the road forks toward death or back toward life, and his dogs are posted there to guide the choosing. [West Africa] Sọpọnná and the Name Not Spoken: In Yorubaland the smallpox deity was spoken of with greater care than any other orisha. The safe title was Ọbalúayé — 'master of the world' — while the name Sọpọnná, attested in the Ifá corpus and early ethnography, was dangerous to say aloud during an epidemic, since naming the disease might summon it (Idowu, Olódùmarè ; Bascom, Ifá Divination ). When mission churches and colonial medical authorities attacked 'smallpox worship' in the early twentieth century, the cult went underground and re-emerged across the ocean, re-dressed as Babalú-Ayé beneath the cloak of Saint Lazarus. The concealment is itself the theology: the god of invisible killers keeps his name hidden, and survives by being renamed — a deity whose power is secrecy learned, under persecution, to live by it across an ocean.

instruction: Tell me a myth about "Baiame".
output: Baiame's mythology is preserved in the oral traditions of the Wiradjuri, Gamilaraay, and neighbouring nations. The stories are not free-floating entertainment: they are title deeds to country, instruction manuals for law, and maps of the sky. What follows are widely reported themes; local elders hold the authoritative versions of each nation's stories. [Creation] The Making of the World: In the beginning Baiame shaped the land. He formed the hills and rivers, planted the trees, and made the animals. Then he made the first people and gave them their languages, their countries, and the laws by which they should live — the earliest ethnographers of the Euahlayi, above all K. Langloh Parker in The Euahlayi Tribe (1905), record the Baayami of creation as the maker whose work is the country itself. Every mountain, waterhole, and plain became a reminder of his creative act, and every clan received the responsibility to care for the part of country made for it (Parker 1905; Berndt and Berndt 1964). Creation here is not a finished product handed over but a continuing arrangement: the world is a country made by an ancestor and entrusted to his descendants, and the deed of trust is the story itself. [Sky] The Retreat to the Sky: When the work of creation was finished, Baiame rose into the sky and made his camp there. From that distant place he watches over the world he made — remote, but not absent, his presence announced by the dark lanes of the Milky Way, which are said to be his camp or the tracks of the emu he placed there, and by the stars themselves, the campfires of the ancestors who went before. The early recorders of the southeast (Parker; Elkin 1938) heard the same withdrawal in many nations: the Sky Father who made the world does not govern it day by day, because the law he gave does that work for him. The withdrawal is the gift: a maker who stayed would be a ruler, but a maker who leaves behind law becomes an ancestor. Distance is how the Sky Father turns creation into inheritance. [Law] The Son Daramulum: Baiame's son Daramulum moves between earth and sky as a messenger and teacher. Often associated with the rainbow and with thunder, Daramulum taught the people the secrets of initiation and the songs that must be sung at each stage of life; it is his voice that the bullroarer carries at the bora ground, and his figure that the initiated recognize in the images kept from the uninitiated. Through him, Baiame's law is passed on without the Sky Father needing to descend himself (Parker 1905; Elkin 1938). The arrangement is precise: the father's law, the son's voice. A law that can only be delivered by the lawgiver in person would die with him; a law carried by a messenger becomes a tradition. [Sky] The Emu in the Sky: The dark shape of the emu stretches across the Milky Way — the great bird read not from stars but from the dust lanes between them, its head in the Coalsack, its body along the galactic plane. It is both a constellation and a story: the emu in the sky tells the people when to collect emu eggs, when to hold ceremonies, and how to read the seasons, and Aboriginal astronomers and their collaborators have shown the reading is practical — the constellation's turning marks the breeding season of the emu on the ground. Baiame placed it there as a calendar and a memory, so that the connection between sky and country would never be lost (cf. Fuller, Harney and Norris on Aboriginal astronomy). The bird above and the bird below are one fact in two places: the sky is not a separate world but the same country seen at night, and the calendar is written in darkness rather than light.

instruction: Tell me a myth about "Bunjil".
output: Bunjil's stories belong to the Dreaming of the Kulin nations — the Woiwurrung, Boonwurrung, Wathaurong, and their neighbors — recorded by A. W. Howitt, Aldo Massola, and the communities themselves. They explain how Country was made, how law was given, and how the creator withdrew into the sky so that he might continue to watch over the world. [Creation] Shaping the Land and the Law: In the Dreaming, Bunjil travelled across what is now central Victoria and shaped Country into its living form: he raised the mountains, traced the courses of the rivers, named the plants and animals, and taught each where it belonged. Then he did what a mere landscape-maker would not: he gave law. The Kulin peoples remember him establishing the rules of kinship and marriage, the obligations between clans, and the duties each people owes to its Country — seasonal burning, careful taking, respect for the places where spirit beings remain. His two wives, the black swans, and his son Binbeal the rainbow accompanied the work. Crucially, the stories insist that Country and law were made together : the mountains are not scenery but scripture, and the river's bends are not geography but instruction. (Howitt 1904; Massola 1968) The tradition encodes a complete environmental philosophy — creation, tenure, and responsibility in a single narrative. [Deluge] The Sea That Would Not Stop Rising: In the telling recorded from Boonwurrung elder Carolyn Briggs, the Kulin nations fell into conflict and began to neglect family and Country, and the sea rose in anger and would not stop. The people gathered and asked Bunjil to intervene. He agreed — but on a condition: they must change their ways and return to the law. He walked to the water's edge, raised his spear, and commanded the sea to stop, and the sea stopped. (Briggs, 'Boon Wurrung Story', Yarra Healing 2000) The story is told as a moral charter, but it carries what may be a far older memory: at the end of the last Ice Age, rising seas flooded the Bassian Plain and cut Tasmania from the mainland — an inundation the ancestors of the Kulin peoples witnessed over generations, and which Australia's oral traditions are now famous for preserving with geological accuracy. The myth's force lies in its bargain: the sea keeps its bounds only while the people keep their obligations — a covenant, not a one-time miracle. [Ascent] Lifted into the Sky: When his work was finished, Bunjil called his family together and asked Waang, the crow, to release the winds — which Waang kept tied in skin bags — so that they might all be carried to the sky. Waang opened the whirlwind, and the wind lifted Bunjil and his wives and son upward. Bunjil became the bright star Altair ; his two wives, the black swans, became the stars on either side; and some tellings say he departed from the island of Deen Maar, off the coast of what is now south-western Victoria, which remains a sacred place of the Gunditjmara and Eastern Maar peoples. (Howitt 1904; Mudrooroo 1994; NIAA, Deen Maar Indigenous Protected Area) The departure is not an abandonment: the eaglehawk still circles above Country, and the star still marks the season. The creator withdrew so that the creation could belong to the people — and he stayed close enough to watch what they do with it. [Sacred site] Bunjil's Shelter: In Gariwerd — the country now known as the Grampians — Bunjil took shelter in a cave in the Black Range, and there, in red ochre, his image was painted: the creator figure flanked by two dingoes, gazing out over the valley. The site known as Bunjil's Shelter is one of the most important Aboriginal rock-art places in Victoria, protected under the Aboriginal Heritage Act 2006 and visited only under the protocols its Traditional Owners set. It is not treated as a relic of a finished religion. For the Jardwadjali and Djab Wurrung peoples, and for the wider Kulin community, the shelter is a place where the ancestor's presence is understood to remain — a working site of memory, education, and obligation, cared for rather than merely conserved. (Parks Victoria 2009) The painting turns myth into address : whoever stands before it is standing where the creator once stood, being looked at by the one who is supposed to be watched for.
