instruction: Tell me a myth about "Taliesin".
output: Taliesin's dossier divides into two figures the Welsh tradition never quite separated: the historical poet of sixth-century Rheged, and the wonder-child of the cauldron whose story is medieval but survives whole only in sixteenth-century manuscripts. The first is attested within three centuries of his life; the second is the fullest legendary biography any Celtic poet ever received. Between them the name becomes a theory of poetry itself. [Historia Brittonum §62; Book of Taliesin] The Poet of Urien: The Historia Brittonum (c. 829) names five poets famed in the days of Ida of Bernicia, in the mid-sixth century: Talhaearn Tad Awen, Aneirin, Cian, Blwchfardd — 'and Taliesin, who is renowned in British poetry'. The Book of Taliesin preserves the substance behind the notice: a core of praise-poems to Urien of Rheged and his son Owain, court verse of the Old North, singing the wars of Rheged against the Bernician Angles. Ifor Williams's scholarship established the canon: a dozen poems of the Book stand as plausibly the work of a real Taliesin, court bard of Urien in the generation before Rheged fell. This is the oldest Taliesin the record offers — not a wonder-child but a professional of the northern courts, remembered three centuries later as the very type of the famed poet. The legend did not invent him; it annexed him, and gave the court bard of Rheged a second birth out of a goddess's cauldron. [Hanes Taliesin] The Cauldron and the Chase: Ceridwen, dwelling by Lake Tegid in the land of Gwynedd, had two children: Creirwy the fairest of maidens and Afagddu, called Morfran, the most ill-favored of men. To compensate her dark son she set a cauldron of inspiration and science to boil for a year and a day, put blind Morda to tend the fire, and set the boy Gwion Bach to stir. On the last day three drops of the charmed liquor flew from the cauldron onto Gwion's thumb; scalded, he put it in his mouth — and at once knew all things past and to come. The cauldron split, and all its virtue was spent on the wrong child. What follows is the great transformation chase of Celtic literature. Gwion fled as a hare; Ceridwen pursued as a greyhound. He became a fish in the river; she came after as an otter. He rose as a bird; she stooped as a hawk. At last he dropped as a single grain onto a winnowing floor, and she came as a black hen and swallowed him. Nine months she bore him, and could not kill so fair a child when he was born; she sewed him in a skin coracle and cast him into the sea on the eve of May Day. [Hanes Taliesin] The Weir and the Court of Maelgwn: The coracle drifted into the salmon weir of Gwyddno Garanhir at the mouth of the Dyfi, where Gwyddno's son Elffin — the luckless, whose every venture failed — drew it from the water. Opening the skin, he saw a child's forehead shining from the folds and cried: 'behold a radiant brow!' — tal iesin — and so named him. The infant, not yet weaned, answered with his first poem, the Consolation of Elffin, and from that day Elffin's luck turned. Years later, when Elffin boasted at Maelgwn Gwynedd's court that he had a wife more virtuous and a bard more skilled than any there, Maelgwn cast him into prison with thirteen locks and sent Rhun to test the wife; Rhun returned with a drugged servant-maid's finger and ring as false proof of her fall. Taliesin came to court, sat in a corner, put a finger to his lips and blew — 'blerwm blerwm' — and all the king's bards could only drone the same, save Heinin their chief. Then the child stood and sang, summoned a wind that shook the court and terrified the king, exposed the false finger, vindicated Elffin's wife, and sang the locks open. Elffin walked free, and Taliesin foretold the very end of the world. [Book of Taliesin: Cad Goddeu; Preiddeu Annwfn] I Have Been in Many Shapes: The legendary poems of the Book give Taliesin the widest voice in Celtic literature. In Cad Goddeu, the Battle of the Trees, he boasts of a hundred existences — sword in hand, rain in the sky, string of a harp, word among letters, eagle on the tide — while Gwydion enchants the trees of the wood to march and fight for the sons of Dôn. The poem's refrain is the poet's creed: I have been in many shapes before I attained a congenial form. In Preiddeu Annwfn, the Spoils of Annwn, he is the one survivor who can tell of Arthur's raid on the Otherworld for the cauldron of the Head of Annwn — the cauldron kindled by the breath of nine maidens, rimmed with pearls, that will not boil a coward's food. Three full shiploads went into Annwn; save seven, none returned. The poet who has been everything is the one who may speak of everything — and the two poems together are why medieval Wales called him not merely bard but Chief of Bards.

instruction: Tell me a myth about "Myrddin".
output: Myrddin's dossier divides in two, and the tradition itself knew it: the northern prophet who went mad at Arfderydd and fled to Coed Celyddon, preserved in the Welsh Triads, the Annales Cambriae, and the Black Book poems; and Geoffrey of Monmouth's Merlinus, who carried the wild man into Latin and grafted him onto the Arthurian world. Gerald of Wales already separated them in the twelfth century: Merlinus Ambrosius, the boy prophet of Vortigern's tower, and Merlinus Celidonius — Sylvester — the wild man of the Caledonian forest. [Annales Cambriae / Trioedd Ynys Prydein] The Battle of Arfderydd: The Annales Cambriae enter under the year 573 the battle of Arfderydd, fought in the north between the sons of Eliffer and Gwenddolau son of Ceidio — a historical-seeming conflict of the British Old North. The Welsh Triads count it among the futile battles of the Island of Britain, brought about, in the triad's famous understatement, for a lark's nest; and the triad records the consequence that matters here: Gwenddolau fell, and Myrddin became mad. From that seed the whole legend grows. Myrddin son of Morfryn, his lord dead and his side defeated, flees the world of the mead-hall into Coed Celyddon, the Caledonian forest, and becomes Myrddin Wyllt — the Wild — living from the forest's gifts and speaking only in verse and prophecy. [Black Book of Carmarthen] The Apple Trees and the Oianau: The earliest Welsh manuscript, the Black Book of Carmarthen (c. 1250), preserves the poems that give the wild man his own voice. In Yr Afallennau, 'The Apple Trees', Myrddin addresses the sweet apple tree that shelters him: he laments Gwenddolau, slain in the bloodshed of Arfderydd; he grieves that he endures want while once he rode at the head of warriors; he hides from Rhydderch's men; and the refrain returns to the tree, his one companion and hiding-place. The companion poem, Yr Oianau, keeps the same voice — the outcast prophet calling his mournful 'oian' through the forest, mourning his dead, marked out by madness as the gods' or fate's chosen sufferer. These are not narrative poems but laments with prophecy threaded through them; together they made Myrddin the patron and mouthpiece of the whole Welsh prophetic genre. [Red Book of Hergest] The Conversation of Myrddin and Gwenddydd: The Cyfoesi Myrddin a Gwenddydd ei chwaer — 'The Conversation of Myrddin and His Sister Gwenddydd' — is the tradition's most human document. Gwenddydd, wife of Rhydderch and sister of the wild prophet, questions her brother across the gulf his madness has opened: she mourns the warrior he was, the mead-feasts he no longer honours, the lord they both have lost. Myrddin answers her with prophecy — the fate of Wales, the coming of its deliverers — but the prophecy keeps breaking against grief. The dialogue fixes what the poems imply: the wild man is not forsaken but watched from the world he left. Gwenddydd survives in Geoffrey of Monmouth's Latin as Ganieda — Rhydderch's queen, Myrddin's sister, and, at the end of the Vita Merlini, his successor in prophecy itself. [Vita Merlini] The Threefold Death and the Life of the Forest: Geoffrey of Monmouth's Vita Merlini (c. 1150) is the wild man's fullest biography. Merlinus — poet, prophet, and king in Geoffrey's telling — loses his reason at a battle among the northern princes and flees to the Caledonian wood, where he lives as a silvester homo, a man of the forest, feeding on roots and fruit, snow on his shoulders, unknown to his own court. Rhydderch's men find him and drag him back; at court he laughs at things no one understands, and his laughter is always a prophecy. To a boy he foretells a threefold death: from a rock, in a tree, and in the water — and the boy, falling from a cliff, is caught by a tree with his head in the stream, dying all three deaths at once, as no human prudence could have guarded against. The poem lets him go home to the forest at last. He appears riding a stag, driving the woodland herds before him like a shepherd of the wild; [[taliesin|Taliesin]] — Telgesinus in the Latin — comes to him, and the two seers discourse at length on the winds, the waters, the fishes, and the making of the world. In the end Merlin gives his observatory to his sister Ganieda, who takes up the prophetic gift, and retires to the forest for good — the mad king become the wise wild man, the only sovereignty he can still keep. [Historia Regum Britanniae / Historia Brittonum] The Boy at Vortigern's Tower: Geoffrey's other Merlin came from another book. The ninth-century Historia Brittonum of Nennius tells of the boy Ambrosius — a child without a father — brought to King Vortigern to be sacrificed so that his collapsing tower at Dinas Emrys might stand; the boy instead reveals the pool beneath the foundations and the two dragons, red and white, whose battle is the prophecy of Britain: the red dragon of the Britons, the white of the Saxons. Geoffrey took Nennius's boy and gave him Myrddin's name: Merlinus Ambrosius. The graft made one figure of two traditions — the royal prophet of the tower and the mad prophet of the forest — and Gerald of Wales, a generation later, was already insisting they were two. The composite Merlin who results is the one the world inherited: prophet to Vortigern, architect of kings, and, in the romances that followed, counsellor of Arthur himself.

instruction: Tell me a myth about "Gawain".
output: Gawain's dossier runs from a Welsh triad to a fourteenth-century masterpiece: in every century someone is testing him, and the test is always the same — not whether he can fight, but whether he will keep faith. He passes every quest and fails one truth; the tradition has been debating which matters more for seven hundred years. [Culhwch ac Olwen] The Knight Who Finished the Quest: The oldest Arthurian tale in Welsh names him in its great muster at Arthur's court: Gwalchmei mab Gwyar — Gwalchmai son of Gwyar — 'because he never returned home without achieving the quest he had gone to seek; he was the best of walkers and the best of riders; he was nephew to Arthur, the son of his sister, and his first cousin.' In a catalogue of hundreds of warriors, giants, and wonders, that is the whole of his entry, and it is the whole of his character: the Welsh tradition remembers him not for a single exploit but for completion itself — the errand that always comes home. Centuries later, when Chrétien and the Gawain-poet needed a knight whose courtesy could carry an entire narrative, they were still writing in the shadow of that one sentence. [Trioedd Ynys Prydein] One of the Three Well-Endowed Men: The Welsh Triads — the medieval memory-system that files the Island of Britain's heroes in threes — name Gwalchmai son of Gwyar among the Three Well-Endowed Men of the Island of Britain, beside Llacheu son of Arthur and Rhiwallawn Broom-Hair (Triad 4). Rachel Bromwich's edition of the Triads is also the standard witness for his name: Gwalchmai, gwalch 'hawk' + Mai 'May', the 'hawk of May' — a name that stands in Welsh, glossed and explained, generations before any French romance ever sang of Gauvain. Bromwich notes that the second element has also been compared to the British god Maponos, the 'Divine Son' of the spring, so the name may carry a youth-and-season resonance older than the month itself. To be filed in a triad is to be fixed in memory: the Welsh gave him no long tale, but they gave him a slot no one else could fill. [Historia Regum Britanniae] The Nephew of the King: Geoffrey of Monmouth's Historia (c. 1136) made him Latin and sent him across Europe: Walganus, son of Loth of Lodonesia and Arthur's sister Anna, given as a boy to the service of Pope Sulpicius in Rome, recalled to Britain to be knighted, and made the steel edge of Arthur's Roman campaign — the knight who cuts through the emperor's host and slays the nephew of Lucius. When Mordred's treason calls the army home, Walganus falls at the landing, in the first fighting on the shore, and is buried as the chronicle says. A generation earlier, William of Malmesbury had already written him down as Walwen — and reported his tomb, found at Rhos in Pembrokeshire, fourteen feet long. Geoffrey's Walganus is grave, dutiful, and doomed: already the nephew whose loyalty is his tragedy, three centuries before Malory would make that loyalty the hinge of the whole downfall. [Chrétien de Troyes] The Measure of Courtesy: In the romances of Chrétien (c. 1160–1190), Gauvain is not the hero of any single quest but the standard against which all the heroes are measured: Erec et Enide ranks him first of the knights of the Round Table, and through Cligés, Lancelot, Yvain, and the Conte du Graal he moves as the court's fixed point — courteous without effort, brave without boasting, the knight whose speech is as ready as his sword. Chrétien lets Perceval's innocence test him and the world test them both; the Continuators of the Perceval give him stranger gifts — a strength that doubles as the sun climbs to noon and fails as it falls — the trace that later scholarship would read as the memory of a solar hero. Where other knights must learn courtesy, Gauvain simply is it; that is precisely why he is so hard to write a story about. [Sir Gawain and the Green Knight] The Bargain of the Green Chapel: At Camelot's New Year feast a giant all in green rides into the hall and offers a Christmas game: any knight may take one stroke at his neck with the great axe, on condition of receiving one in return, a year and a day hence, at the Green Chapel. Gawain takes the challenge, strikes the head clean off, and the Green Knight rides out holding it, reminding him of the tryst. The year turns, and Gawain rides north to keep his bargain. At Hautdesert, Lord Bertilak proposes an exchange of winnings: each evening they will swap whatever the day has gained. Three days the lord hunts; three days his lady tests Gawain in his chamber; and each evening Gawain faithfully renders the kisses he has received — but on the third day he keeps back the green girdle the lady swears will save his life. At the Green Chapel the axe falls three times: twice withheld, and once, for the kept-back lace, a nick in the neck. The Green Knight is Bertilak, sent by Morgan le Fay; the girdle was the whole point. Gawain wears it home as his 'token of untruth' — and Camelot laughs, and binds green laces on every shoulder. The poem's subject is not whether a knight can fight but what truth costs, and whether one small love of life can be forgiven . [Le Morte Darthur] The Last Letter: Malory's Sir Gawaine is the courteous knight grown tragic: head of the Orkney clan, Arthur's dearest nephew, whose feud with Lancelot — after Gareth and Gaheris are slain in the fire of Guenevere's rescue — drags the fellowship to ruin. Wounded at Dover by Lancelot in the last single combat, he dies of the reopened wound, writing with his own hand the letter that calls Lancelot 'flower of all noble knights' and begs him to come see his tomb. And on the eve of Salisbury Plain he returns in Arthur's dream with a troop of ladies, warning the king not to fight Mordred on the morrow — the nephew still trying, from beyond death, to bring his uncle's last errand home. It is the pattern's final turn: the knight who always finished the quest dies writing an errand he will not live to see delivered, and begs the one man he fought to come anyway.

instruction: Tell me a myth about "Bedwyr".
output: Bedwyr belongs to the oldest stratum of Arthurian tradition: the Welsh heroic material that predates Geoffrey of Monmouth and the whole romance edifice. His dossier is compact and precise — a poem's roster, a tale's three great episodes, two triads — and across all of it one fact never varies: where Cei goes, Bedwyr goes, and the one-handed man is never the lesser of the pair. [Pa gŵr? · Black Book of Carmarthen] The War-Band Remembered: The poem known from its opening line as Pa gŵr yv y porthaur? — 'What man is the gatekeeper?' — is the oldest Arthurian poem in Welsh: preserved in the thirteenth-century Black Book of Carmarthen, and itself composed perhaps centuries earlier. In it Arthur, halted at a fortress gate by the porter Glewlwyd Gafaelfawr, recites the roll of his companions to win entry, and Bedwyr stands in that roll beside Cei and Arthur's son Llacheu — already, in the earliest witness, one of the names Arthur speaks to prove his company. The poem is fragmentary — it breaks off mid-recitation — but its testimony matters beyond its length: it shows a Welsh Arthurian war-band whose heroes had their own deeds long before Geoffrey of Monmouth drew Arthur into Latin history, and Bedwyr is fixed in that founding generation. [Culhwch ac Olwen] The One-Handed Spearman: Culhwch ac Olwen, the earliest full Arthurian prose tale, gives Bedwyr his formal introduction when Arthur calls the companions for the quest of Olwen: Arthur called Bedwyr, 'who never shrank from any enterprise upon which Kai was bound. None was equal to him in swiftness throughout this Island except Arthur and Drych Ail Kibddar. And although he was one-handed, three warriors could not shed blood faster than he on the field of battle. Another property he had: his lance would produce a wound equal to those of nine opposing lances.' The great court-list earlier in the tale quietly extends the household: Amren son of Bedwyr stands among Arthur's huntsmen, and Eneuawc daughter of Bedwyr among the golden-chained maidens of the Island — the one-handed spearman with a son and daughter woven into the fabric of the court. [Culhwch ac Olwen] The Beard of Dillus the Bearded: No leash in the world could hold Drudwyn, the whelp of Greid son of Eri, save one made from the beard of Dillus Farfawc — and the beard was useless unless plucked from him alive with wooden tweezers, for once dead the bristles would turn brittle. As Cei and Bedwyr sat on a beacon cairn on the summit of Pumlumon, 'in the highest wind that ever was in the world', they spied smoke that did not bend with the wind, and found the greatest robber who ever fled from Arthur scorching a wild boar at his fire. They let him eat his fill and sleep; they shaped the wooden tweezers while he slept; Cei dug a pit beneath him, struck him into it, and together they plucked the beard clean and slew him. The leash was made and delivered to Arthur at Celli Wic — and Arthur answered with an englyn mocking Cei's deed, at which Cei's wrath was so great that the warriors of the Island could scarcely make peace between them, and Cei never again came to Arthur's aid. The episode that shows Bedwyr and Cei at their closest is the tale's own explanation of their company's end. [Culhwch ac Olwen] The Sword of Gwrnach and the Cauldron of Diwrnach: For the sword of Gwrnach the Giant, from whose castle no guest had ever returned alive, Cei went in alone under a false craft — the best burnisher of swords in the world — and won Bedwyr admission by a sign: the head of his lance would leave its shaft, draw blood from the wind, and settle on its shaft again. Inside, Cei polished the giant's sword, talked him out of his scabbard, and struck off his head with his own blade; the company despoiled the castle and bore the sword to Arthur's court by the beginning of the year. In Ireland, for the cauldron of Diwrnach Wyddel, the embassy's request was refused outright — and then Bedwyr arose and seized the cauldron and set it on the back of Hygwyd, Arthur's cauldron-bearer, while Llenlleawg Wyddel caught up Caledfwlch, and they slew Diwrnach and his company and fought their way back to the ship Prydwen, carrying the cauldron off full of Irish treasure. The two episodes are the pair's whole method: Cei's cunning at the gate, Bedwyr's hand on the prize. [Trioedd Ynys Prydein 21 · 26] The Diadem Above the Three: The Welsh triads keep the tradition's compressed memory, and they name Bedwyr twice — both times beside Cei. The triad of the Three Battle-Diademed of the Island of Britain names Drystan son of Tallwch, Hueil son of Caw, and Cei son of Cynyr — and then adds: and one was battle-diademed above all three of them, and that was Bedwyr son of Bedrawc. In the tradition's own arithmetic, the one-handed man outranks the three crowned warriors it had just named. The second naming is the triad's own joke at the war-band's expense. In the triad of the Three Powerful Swineherds, Drystan son of Tallwch kept the swine of March son of Meirchyawn while the swineherd carried a message to Essyllt — and Arthur and March and Cei and Bedwyr were there, all four, yet did not succeed in getting so much as one pigling, neither by force, nor by deception, nor by stealth. The greatest names in the Island, together, defeated by one watchful man and a herd of pigs. [Historia Regum Britanniae IX] Beduerus at Soissons: Geoffrey of Monmouth, drawing the Welsh heroes into his Latin history of the kings of Britain (c. 1136), makes Bedwyr into Beduerus: Arthur's cupbearer and constable of Normandy, one of the two companions — with Caius the seneschal — closest to the king. In the war against the Roman emperor Lucius, Beduerus falls in the fighting before Soissons — Geoffrey names his killer the giant Ritho of Mount Aravius, whom Arthur afterwards slew in single combat — and Arthur has him carried to Bayeux in Neustria, a city his own ancestors had built, and buried there with great lamentation. Geoffrey's account is pseudo-history, not Welsh tradition — but it fixed Bedwyr in the Latin chronicle line that Wace and Layamon would follow, and it is the hinge on which the Welsh Bedwyr turns into the Bedivere of European romance: the companion who dies in Arthur's service, far from home, mourned by the king he served.

instruction: Tell me a myth about "Kai".
output: Kai's mythology lives in the oldest stratum of Welsh Arthurian tradition: Culhwch ac Olwen gives him the tale's largest dossier after Arthur himself, and the fragmentary dialogue poem Pa Gur remembers exploits the prose never told. The later Latin and French traditions kept the man and quietly spent the magic. [Culhwch ac Olwen] The First Companion: When Culhwch comes to Arthur's court to win Olwen daughter of Ysbaddaden Chief Giant, Arthur grants him help, and the first companion named is Cei son of Cynyr. The warrior-list fixes his peculiarities in one breath: nine nights and nine days he could be under water; nine nights and nine days he could go without sleep; a wound from Cei's sword no physician could heal. Cei the Tall — when it pleased him he could make himself as tall as the tallest tree in the forest. And the list adds the attribute the whole fellowship depended on: when the rain was heaviest, whatever he carried in his hand stayed dry for a handbreadth above and below, so great was his heat; and when the cold was hardest on his companions, he was fuel to them to light their fire. The list also preserves his mother's prophecy that his heart would be cold — the oldest trace of the coldness the later romances turned to mockery. [Culhwch ac Olwen] The Salmon and the Sword: Two of the hardest anoethau — the 'things hard to get' that Ysbaddaden sets as the bride-price — fall to Cei. To free Mabon son of Modron from his prison at Caer Loyw, the company follows the oldest animals to the Salmon of Llyn Llyw, and Cei and Bedwyr ride up the Severn on the salmon's shoulders; while Arthur's men assault the fort from the front, Cei carries Mabon away on the salmon's back. And when Arthur's band comes to the hall of Wrnach the giant, whose sword is needed to hunt the boar Twrch Trwyth — no guest had ever left that hall alive — Cei claims to be a master polisher of swords. Admitted, he burnishes the giant's blade, asks to hold it to test the work, and strikes Wrnach's head off with his own sword; the company destroys the fortress. The wonder-hero's greatest feats in the tale are won with a craftsman's hands, not a charge of horse — a hint of how the tradition will later make him the man who keeps the tools, not the one who swings them. [Culhwch ac Olwen] The Beard of Dillus and the Englyn: The beard of Dillus the Bearded was wanted to make a leash for the whelp Drudwyn, and Cei and Bedwyr found the giant alone. Cei dug a pit, tricked Dillus into it, plucked his beard out with wooden tweezers, and killed him afterward — and Arthur, watching, sang an englyn mocking Cei for making a leash from a living beard he could never have taken from a healthy man. Cei answered nothing, but the tale records the consequence in a line: because of that englyn there was enmity between Cei and Arthur ever after. The tale gives him no further feat of note; the fellowship's first companion becomes its first estrangement. The closing tally keeps the ending: Gwyddog son of Menestyr slew Cei, and Arthur slew Gwyddog and his brothers to avenge him — the rift repaired only in vengeance, and too late for either of them to enjoy it. It is the oldest Arthurian story about how a court breaks: not by siege, but by a joke aimed at the wrong man's pride. [Pa Gur / The Welsh Triads] Nine Witches and the Cat of Anglesey: The fragmentary dialogue poem Pa Gur yv y Porthaur?, preserved in the Black Book of Carmarthen, shows Arthur and the gatekeeper Glewlwyd Mighty-grasp trading boasts, and the boasts are Cei's: Cei pierced nine witches, and Cei the Fair went to Anglesey to destroy the monster the Welsh called Cath Palug — the gigantic cat that the triads say was born of the sow Henwen and raised by the sons of Palug as one of the island's plagues. The poem breaks off in the middle of that account, and scholars read the torn ending as the oldest trace of Cei's own death-fight. The early verse remembers him where the prose does not: as the champion sent against the things no one else would face — witches in their coven, a cat the size of a calf on an island shore. Behind the steward of the romances stands this older figure, the one whose dossier needed only a fragment to prove it: where the road was worst, the tall man went first. [Historia Regum Britanniae] Caius Dapifer: Geoffrey of Monmouth, writing about 1136, Latinizes him as Caius dapifer — Kay the steward — and gives him the seneschal's office and the province of Anjou at Arthur's plenary court at Caerleon, while Bedwerus the cupbearer receives Normandy. In Geoffrey's Roman war Kay fights as duke, is killed in the great battle against Lucius, and dies; Geoffrey says he was buried at Chinon, the castle he himself had built, mourned by the whole army. The magic is gone — no nine days' breath, no fire in the hands — but the office Geoffrey fixed to the name proved more durable than any peculiarity: from this book onward, Kay is the steward of Arthur's court in every language that tells the story. What the Welsh gave as a wonder, the Normans received as a job title — and the job title is what survived, in French, English, German, and every retelling since, a thousand years of comic stewards standing on the shoulders of the tall man who kept the fire.

instruction: Tell me a myth about "Don".
output: Dôn has no myth of her own — no tale, no speech, no deed the sources record. What she has is a family, and the family is the mythology: the Fourth Branch of the Mabinogi unfolds among her children and her brother Math, and the oldest Arthurian tale cannot finish its tasks without two more of her sons. Every witness names her the same way — as the mother in the matronymic — and the Welsh tradition built its northern divine house around exactly that: Plant Dôn , the Children of Dôn. [Math fab Mathonwy] The Sister-Sons at Math's Court: The Fourth Branch opens at the court of Math fab Mathonwy, lord of Gwynedd — who cannot live unless his feet rest in a virgin's lap, except when war is in the land — and it introduces the great men of that court by their mother's name: Gwydion and Gilfaethwy, sons of Dôn, Math's own sister-sons, his nephews and his company. Gwydion is 'the best teller of tales in the world'. It is these two who set the branch's whole tragedy in motion: Gilfaethwy desires Goewin, the maiden of the foothold, and Gwydion engineers the remedy — a war against Pryderi of Dyfed, bought with conjured stallions, hounds, and shields that vanish after a day, so that the king marches south and the rape can happen. Through all of it — the war, the crime, the three years of animal-shape punishment — the mother never appears. Dôn is present in the text exactly as a name inside other names: uab Dôn , son of Dôn, the matronymic the tale attaches to her children every time it introduces them. The most consequential family in Welsh prose walks the stage under her name, and she never once walks it herself. [Math fab Mathonwy] Arianrhod ferch Dôn and the Wand: When Math needs a new footholder after Goewin, Gwydion proposes his own sister: 'Seek for you a maiden... here is Arianrhod daughter of Dôn.' The maiden is summoned and asked if she is a virgin; she answers that she does not know but believes she is. Math makes her step over his magic wand, and as she steps she drops a fine yellow-haired boy — Dylan, who at once makes for the sea and takes the sea's nature, Dylan Eil Ton, son of the wave — and, all but unnoticed, 'something small' that only Gwydion marks, wraps in a cloth, and hides in a chest at the foot of his bed. From the chest comes the boy who will be Lleu. Arianrhod, shamed before the whole court, refuses the boy and lays upon him the three tynghedau — the fated destinies — that he shall have no name until she names him, no arms until she arms him, and no wife of any race then on earth. The rest of the branch is Gwydion undoing his sister's curses by craft. Dôn's daughter is the Fourth Branch's proudest and most wounded figure — and Dôn is present, once again, only in the patronymic: uerch Dôn , daughter of Dôn. [Culhwch ac Olwen] The Ploughman and the Smith: The oldest of the Arthurian tales sends Culhwch to win Olwen, daughter of the chief giant Ysbaddaden Bencawr, who answers the suit by naming the anoethau — the long roll of impossible tasks the suitor must perform before any wedding. Two of Dôn's sons stand inside that list, because the tasks cannot be done without them. Amaethon fab Dôn must be fetched to till the giant's ground: no ploughman alive can work that land but him. And Gofannon fab Dôn, the smith of the divine house, must be brought to the work of the headlands — the craft that prepares the ground is his. The passage is the Welsh tradition's clearest statement of what the Children of Dôn are: not a royal house in the ordinary sense but a house of powers — enchantment, the plough, the forge — each child a function the world cannot do without. Agriculture and smithcraft, the two oldest arts of civilization, belong to the matriarch's sons. [Welsh Triads / Kat Godeu] The Futile Battle: The Welsh triads keep a battle for the house of Dôn. Among the Three Futile Battles of the Island of Britain stands Cad Goddeu, the Battle of the Trees, fought — the triad says — on account of a bitch, a roebuck, and a lapwing that Amathaon fab Dôn brought away from Annwn, the Otherworld. A theft of three creatures, and a war. The Book of Taliesin's poem Kat Godeu remembers the same war from the other side of the family: it is Gwydion who enchants the trees of the forest into an army — alder at the front, oak in the thick of it — against Arawn of Annwn. One son's theft begins the quarrel, another son's enchantment fights it; and behind both, again, the mother who gives the house its name and never raises a hand in it. [The Welsh Genealogies] Plant Dôn: Welsh tradition organized its divine and heroic world by the mother's name. Plant Dôn , the Children of Dôn, stands beside Plant Llŷr as one of the two great kindreds of the Mabinogi world, and the genealogical tracts give the matriarch a lineage: Dôn daughter of Mathonwy — which makes her sister to Math fab Mathonwy and explains why her children move so freely in his court. The name-list of her children runs across the sources: Gwydion, Gilfaethwy, and Arianrhod in the Fourth Branch; Gofannon and Amaethon in Culhwch ac Olwen. Later genealogies lengthen the list and supply what the tales omit — a husband, Beli Mawr — but the Mabinogi itself gives Dôn neither husband nor a single word of speech. She is the only major figure of the Four Branches who never appears, and the only one whose name all the others carry. The house is hers because the names are hers; nothing more was ever written, and nothing more was needed.

instruction: Tell me a myth about "Beli".
output: Beli has no adventure of his own: his story is his house. The Mabinogion knows him as the dead king whose four sons inherit Britain, France, and the quarrels of the next generation; the pedigrees know him as the root; and Geoffrey of Monmouth knows him as Heli, father of the builder of London. [Mabinogion (Lludd a Llefelys)] The Four Sons of Beli: The tale of Lludd and Llefelys opens with the settlement of the island: Beli the Great, son of Manogan, was king of this island, and he had three sons — Lludd, Caswallawn, and Nynniaw — and, as the story tells, a fourth son called Llefelys. When Beli died, the kingdom of the Island of Britain fell to Lludd as the eldest, and Lludd ruled it prosperously, rebuilding the walls of London and living there for most of the year. Llefelys, the youngest, went to France, won the love of the old king's only daughter, and inherited that kingdom in his turn. What follows — the three plagues that fall on Britain, and Llefelys's counsel from the middle of the Channel — belongs to the sons' temples. Beli's part is finished in the opening lines, and that is precisely his function: he is the point from which legitimacy flows, the dead father whose reign makes his sons' divided world one family. [Mabinogion (Branwen ferch Llŷr)] Caswallawn's Veil: The Second Branch remembers Beli's house at the moment it takes the crown. While Brân the Blessed marched into Ireland to avenge Branwen, he left seven men as regents in Britain, his son Caradog at their head. Caswallawn son of Beli marched against them wearing a veil of illusion, so that no one could see him — only his sword killing. He slew the seven, and Caradog died of a broken heart at the sight of the slaughter and the knowledge of who held the island now. Caswallawn son of Beli became king in London. The branch never explains or excuses the usurpation; it simply registers that while the children of Llŷr spent themselves overseas, the children of Beli took the island — the two great houses of Welsh tradition passing the crown between them without a battle anyone could see. [Harleian Genealogies] The Root of the Royal Trees: Outside the tales, the record that made Beli matter was parchment of a drier kind. The Harleian genealogies — the collection of Welsh royal pedigrees preserved in British Library, Harley MS 3859 (c. 1100) — carry the lines of the British kingdoms back generation by generation until they reach Beli mawr, who stands near the root of the trees. To claim a throne in early Wales was, in part, to publish a pedigree, and the pedigrees converge on him. The convention was old and remarkably tenacious: centuries later, the genealogical tracts still counted descent from Beli the Great as the deepest legitimacy a Welsh royal house could print. He is the standing proof that in the British tradition, ancestry is not mere decoration on kingship — it is the thing itself. [Geoffrey of Monmouth] Heli, Father of Lud: Geoffrey of Monmouth's Historia Regum Britanniae (c. 1136) took the Welsh Beli into Latin and made him a chapter of world history. As Heli he reigns after King Cligueillus, a man of forty years' rule, and fathers three sons: Lud, Cassibelaunus, and Nennius. Lud succeeds him and rebuilds the city of Trinovantum with noble walls, surrounding it with countless towers and renaming it Kaerlud, Lud's City — whence, Geoffrey says, its later name London, and the memory of the king in the gate called Ludgate. Through Geoffrey, Beli's house entered the bloodstream of European letters: the Historia was one of the most copied books of the Middle Ages, and the sons of Heli — Lud the city-builder, Cassibelaunus the enemy of Caesar — carried their father's ancestry wherever Latin was read. [Tertullian / Herodian] The Bright One Behind the King: Older than any Welsh manuscript is a continental witness the scholars keep setting beside Beli's name. Around the year 200, Tertullian lists the local gods of the provinces and gives the Noricans Belenus (Apologeticum 24); a generation later, Herodian tells how, at the siege of Aquileia in 238, the citizens credited their deliverance to Apollo, the god the people of that region worshipped under the name Belis. The altars agree: dedications Belino Augusto sacrum cluster at Aquileia and across the eastern Alpine provinces. Whether the Welsh ancestor-king descends from this 'bright, shining' god is the standing question of Beli scholarship. The names are close, the traditional gloss fits, and a euhemerized god makes a plausible root for a genealogy — but no text performs the identification, and the honest verdict is the one the handbooks give: a venerable possibility, unproven. This temple holds the question open.

instruction: Tell me a myth about "Omononushi".
output: Ōmononushi's mythology is preserved in strange, archaic tales of snakes, possession, and oracles — the Kojiki's strangest marriage, the constitution of Japan's sovereignty, and a shrine with no god-house, because the mountain is the god. [Kojiki] The Serpent Husband of Ikutamayori: A maiden named Ikutamayori was visited each night by a beautiful man who came unseen. When she bore his child, her parents demanded to know the father. She had him leave a needle threaded with red silk in the hem of his garment; in the morning she followed the thread, and it led to the foot of Mount Miwa and vanished into a cave — where the visitor declared himself: he was Ōmononushi , the great lord of the mountain, and he appeared in serpent form. The child of this union was Kotoshironushi, the god who would one day counsel the peaceful surrender of the land to the heavenly grandson (Kojiki; cf. Nihon Shoki, Aston's translation). The tale binds three things into one knot — mountain, snake, and the Miwa priestly line, whose descent from the kami's human bride it exists to explain. [Kojiki · Nihon Shoki] The Oracle of the Land: When the heavenly emissary Takemikazuchi descended to demand the land from the earthly god Ōnamuji (Ōkuninushi), Ōnamuji consulted his children. Kotoshironushi, away at Cape Miwa, answered that resistance to the heavenly grandson was hopeless — and then all eyes turned to the mountain. Ōmononushi was consulted, and his oracle settled the matter: 'Let the land be given over in peace,' he declared; the land was yielded, and he withdrew into a hidden realm, promising that his favor would attend his proper worship. The Nihon Shoki tells the same event differently, folding the mountain god into Ōnamuji himself: Ōnamuji, it says, is also called Ōmononushi (Kojiki; Nihon Shoki, tr. Aston, I). Here the god is pure voice: sovereignty changes hands in Japan not by conquest but by consultation — and the mountain kami's consent is the constitution. [Kojiki] The Bride of Miwa: Ōmononushi took as wife Seyadatarahime, daughter of his own son Kotoshironushi by Ikutamayori — and their child was the princess Himetataraisuzuhime. She became the consort of Emperor Sujin and bore the future Emperor Suinin: the serpent-god of Mount Miwa thus entered the imperial genealogy itself, the god's line becoming grandmother to the next sovereign. The Kojiki's genealogy is compressed and the texts do not spell every step out plainly, but the dynastic point stands: the mountain married into the house that received the mountain's realm. The marriage also sealed an alliance between the Miwa priestly house and the court — the god who gave the land away kept his blood beside the throne. The Kojiki records the whole sequence without wonder, as plain genealogy: which is how one knows the text was compiled on the winning side. [Kojiki · Nihon Shoki] The Plague and the Possessed Princess: In Emperor Sujin's reign plague and disaster struck the land, and divination named the cause: the great kami of Mount Miwa, never yet given a shrine, was angry. The god made his will known by possessing a princess of his own line and speaking through her: worship me, he demanded, and I will cause the land to flourish. Sujin founded the rites; the pestilence lifted. The Nihon Shoki's parallel account likewise has the god speak through a human mouth, claim credit for guiding the cession of the land, and demand his due — the god of Miwa and the god of the land-transfer asserted as one and the same (Kojiki; Nihon Shoki, Aston I). Myth here explains a liturgy: Ōmiwa's worship began, the texts insist, when the neglected mountain finally raised its voice. [Cult] Worship without Image: Ōmiwa Shrine, at the foot of the mountain in Nara prefecture, is one of Japan's oldest shrines and one of the strangest: it has no honden , no inner sanctuary housing a divine image, because the god is not symbolized by anything — the god is Mount Miwa. Worshippers pray toward the peak across a unique three-pillared torii, the Miwa-torii; before the worship hall stand sacred sake casks, for Ōmononushi is patron of the brewers of Miwa, and his serpent form — a great snake said to coil in the mountain's caves — was traditionally offered sake. First listed among the great shrines in the Engishiki (927 CE), the site preserves a stratum of Japanese religion older than images: the mountain itself as shintai , the deity's body. The absent statue is the theology: what has no face cannot be owned, and what cannot be owned cannot be conquered.

instruction: Tell me a myth about "Sukunahikona".
output: Sukunahikona's dossier is small but perfectly formed: the Kojiki (712) and the Nihon Shoki (720) tell how a kami no bigger than a child crossed the sea in a bark boat, partnered the great Ōkuninushi, taught medicine and sake, and sailed away to the Everlasting Land. The lesson the sources keep pressing: size and power are not the same thing. [Kojiki] The Little Prince from Across the Sea: The Kojiki ('Records of Ancient Matters', 712) tells how Ōnamuchi — the god later called Ōkuninushi, 'Great Renowned Lord' — stood on a beach in Izumo when a strange little boat came gliding over the sea. In it sat a kami small in body, and his boat was woven of muku bark. Ōnamuchi asked his name, and the small one answered: he was the son of Kamimusubi, one of the three creation deities, and his name was Sukunahikona, the Little Renowned Prince. Then came the exchange that defines the whole partnership: Ōnamuchi, who had struggled alone to make the wild land fit for people, asked, in effect, whether anyone would be his companion in that work — and Sukunahikona answered that this was why he had come. The meeting is the myth's thesis: the great lord had strength without knowledge, and the little prince had knowledge without strength; the land needed both. The Nihon Shoki ('Chronicles of Japan', 720) tells a parallel version with details of its own. (Kojiki, trans. Philippi, 1968; Nihon Shoki, trans. Aston, 1896.) [Kojiki] Shaping the Land Together: Together the two set about the work the Kojiki calls making and pacifying the land. Ōnamuchi brought the authority — he had survived Susanoo's trials by fire and serpent and the malice of his eighty brothers — and Sukunahikona brought knowledge: the two traveled the islands fixing boundaries, subduing hostile kami, and settling where rivers, rocks, and forests would belong to people. The Kojiki gives the partnership no single set-piece battle; its point is duration — the long, unglamorous labour of turning wilderness into a country. When the work was done, the land had shrines where none had been and fields where none had grown. Later ages read the pair as a charter for Japanese rule: sovereignty as collaboration between visible majesty and hidden craft, the great lord above and the little prince below — a division of labour the Kojiki quietly credits with everything that made Japan habitable. [Kojiki] The Physician and the Brewer: Before he left, Sukunahikona gave the two arts for which he is still worshipped. The Kojiki credits him with teaching humanity the way of healing disease and the way of brewing sake — medicine and wine, the twin consolations of the mortal condition. Sake in particular became the bridge between worlds: the offering that eases speech between humans and kami. His medical patronage deepened in later centuries, when epidemic disease, above all smallpox ( hōsō ), made his name a household word; the tiny prince who came in a bark boat became one of the kami most often petitioned when illness struck, and his Ōsaka shrine in the old medicine quarter of Horie still draws those praying for health. The pairing is older than any shrine: a god who heals and a god who brews are one god, because both trades turn perishable things — grain, herbs, time — into comfort. [Kojiki] The Departure for the Everlasting Land: The Kojiki closes the partnership with a farewell. Sukunahikona climbed into his little bark boat and sailed away over the horizon to Tokoyo-no-kuni, the Everlasting Land across the sea, the country from which he had come. Ōnamuchi watched him go and grieved aloud: with his companion gone, how could he alone complete the work of the land? In his loneliness he built a palace for the absent prince and enshrined him there, so that departure became enshrinement — the myth's own explanation of how a god who left Japan can still be worshipped in Japan. Every reading must face the quiet poignancy of the scene: the helper deities of the age of the gods do not stay; they equip the land and withdraw, leaving mortals to carry on with what they were taught. That withdrawal is the hinge between myth and history.

instruction: Tell me a myth about "Tajikarao".
output: Tajikarao's mythology is a single great scene — the Ama-no-Iwato , the Heavenly Rock-Cave — yet it is among the most retold scenes in Japanese religion. When Amaterasu hid herself and night swallowed the world, the eight hundred myriad kami tried persuasion, dance, and mirrors; only when the strong-handed kami acted did the sun return. His entire dossier is those few seconds at the cave mouth (Kojiki; Nihon Shoki). [Kojiki] The Sun Withdraws into the Rock: The crisis begins with Susanoo's rampage. The storm god, granted leave from heaven, trampled down the ridges of Amaterasu's rice-paddies, filled in her irrigation ditches, and finally flayed the heavenly piebald colt and hurled its carcass through the roof of the sacred weaving-hall, so that a weaving-maiden, struck by the flying shuttle, died at her loom (Kojiki). Amaterasu, in grief and fear, 'went into the Rock-Cave of Heaven and fastened its Rock-Door'. At once the Plain of High Heaven went dark and the Central Land of Reed-Plains — Japan itself — fell into long night; the eight hundred myriad kami wailed, and calamitous deities swarmed like summer flies. The myth's architecture is precise: the sun's absence is not night but negation — nothing in the world works until the goddess is brought back out. [Kojiki] The Laughter at the Cave Door: The assembled kami answered with misdirection. The goddess Ame-no-Uzume bound up her sleeves with a heavenly vine, took a bundle of sasaki grass for a headdress, overturned a tub before the cave, and stamped out a lewd, rattling dance upon it, baring herself to the roaring laughter of the whole assembly. Amaterasu, hearing the uproar, wondered how the gods could make merry while the world lay dark. When she cracked the Rock-Door to ask, Ame-no-Uzume answered that a goddess greater than she had come — and the kami had already hung the polished mirror Yata-no-Kagami and the curved jewel on the branches of a sakaki tree beside the door, while Ame-no-Koyane intoned the first ritual words. The mirror did the persuading; the dance bought it a crack of light. Cunning opens the door a finger's width — no more. [Kojiki · Nihon Shoki] The Strong Hand: Leaning out to see the 'new goddess', Amaterasu saw her own blazing reflection — and as she stood amazed, Ame-no-Tajikarao seized her by the hand and pulled her bodily out of the cave (Kojiki). The Nihon Shoki's parallel gives him the rougher deed: he tears the Rock-Door itself from its hinges and casts it away. Either way, dawn broke instantly over heaven and earth; Ame-no-Futotama stretched the great sacred rope, the shimenawa , across the cave mouth so the goddess could not withdraw again, and Susanoo was banished in payment. Of all the kami in the scene, only Tajikarao performs no ruse and speaks no word — he acts . The myth's balance sheet is exact: Uzume's wit creates the opening, the mirror supplies the reason, and strength finishes the work. Each is necessary; only one of them is over in a single motion. [Togakushi] The Door That Flew to Shinano: Medieval tradition follows the door. The Nihon Shoki's account of the cave already records that the Rock-Door, once torn free, was hurled far away; shrine legend at Togakushi — the name means nothing other than 'the hidden door' — in the mountains of Shinano (present-day Nagano) holds that it landed there, on the forested slope where the Upper Shrine stands to this day. The five shrines of Togakushi grew around the spot, and the Middle Shrine enshrines Tajikarao himself, worshipped as the kami of strength, decisive action, and the opening of what is shut; pilgrims still climb the avenue of giant cryptomerias to the Oku-sha through snow and mist. No text records where he went afterward; the mountain is his whole biography. A kami who exists for five seconds of myth acquired, through the object he threw, a mountain for a memorial.

instruction: Tell me a myth about "Toyotama".
output: Toyotama's cycle, told in the Kojiki's Hoori narrative, is the story of a sea princess who marries into the land — and of the promise whose breaking closes the road between the realms forever. She is at once bride, mother, and exile: the ocean's gift to the imperial genealogy, and its loss. [Kojiki] The Bride of the Sea Palace: Hoori — Hikohohodemi-no-mikoto, the hunter prince — came to the seashore weeping over a lost fishhook and a broken brotherhood. Guided by the old man of the sea, Shihotsuchi, he descended to the palace of Watatsumi, the dragon god of the depths. The palace walls were fish-scaled, its lanes alive with every creature of the sea, and the god received the prince with ceremony, presenting him to his daughter Toyotama-hime: 'I give you this maiden; dwell in our midst as long as heaven endures.' For three years Hoori lived in the sea palace, and there he recovered the hook, mastered his elder brother Hoderi, and won his bride (Kojiki, Hikohohodemi-no-mikoto; trans. Philippi). The marriage is the myth's hinge: the land's prince, powerless on land, is made whole by the sea's alliance — an oceanic bride as the seal between the hunting shore and the deep. [Kojiki] The Vow at the Birth-Hut: When Toyotama was with child, she told Hoori: 'In our country, when our kind give birth, we do so in our true form; do not look.' She built a parturition hut, sealed its entry, and withdrew. But longing overcame the prince: he stole to the hut and peered inside, and there he saw no woman but a great eight-fathom sea-dragon — a wani , sea-serpent or crocodile — coiling about the child. Ashamed to be seen in her true shape, Toyotama abandoned the newborn, left the hut, and returned to her father's palace; and the road between the sea and the land, she declared, was closed, because he had broken his promise (Kojiki). The sources preserve the detail without comment, and its force needs none: in the economy of this myth the gaze is the one theft the sea cannot forgive. What Hoori took by looking, the lineage paid for in a mother lost. [Kojiki] Tamayori Raises the Child: Toyotama did not leave the child wholly orphaned. From the sea palace she sent her younger sister, Tamayori-hime — 'the jewel-adorning princess' — to nurse the boy at the shore. The Kojiki names him Ugayafukiaezu, 'he of the unfinished roof': when the birth-hut was built, its thatching was left incomplete, and the name fixed the broken moment in the child himself. He grew at the edge of the sea he could never enter, married Tamayori — the aunt who had stood in his mother's place — and by her had four sons: Itsuse, Inahi, Mikenu, and the youngest, Kamuyamato-Iwarebiko. The pattern is an old one, attested across Japanese and continental tradition: what the mother could not stay to finish, the maternal kin complete, and the lost woman returns to the lineage through her sister. From that fourth son the chronicles will draw the first emperor. [Kojiki] Why Birth Is Hard: The Kojiki closes the episode with an aetiology that turns a private shame into the human condition. Toyotama, departing, declares that she had meant to give birth easily — in the manner of her own kind, smoothly and without pain — but because Hoori had broken his promise, from that time forward women would suffer in childbirth. The sea princess thus bequeaths to every mother of the land the cost of a father's curiosity. The same chapter makes her the grandmother of empire: her youngest son's son took the name posterity knows as Emperor Jimmu, and Jimmu's eastern expedition, told later in the Kojiki, carries the sea's bloodline to Yamato and the throne at Kashihara. Read whole, the myth binds the two great facts of Japanese kingship into one sentence: the imperial line descends from the ocean, and it descends through a broken promise.

instruction: Tell me a myth about "Ugayafukiaezu".
output: Ugayafukiaezu's mythology is the final chapter of the Hoori–Toyotama cycle and the prologue to the reign of Jimmu: one night on a seashore, one unfinished roof, one farewell poem, and a lineage that steps out of the hut into history. [Kojiki I] The Cormorant-Feather Hut: The Kojiki (age of gods) tells how the sea princess Toyotama-bime, daughter of Watatsumi the sea god, came up from the deep to bear the child of the land-hunter Hoori. On the seashore she built a hut and thatched its roof with cormorant feathers, and as her hour came she warned her husband: do not look inside. Hoori waited, but when the cry came he could not hold back; he peered through the wall and saw his wife transformed into a great sea-creature — the Kojiki says an eight-fathom shark — coiled in labor. Toyotama knew herself shamed. She left the newborn where he lay, in the hut whose cormorant thatch had never been finished, and the compilers give the child his name from the shelter itself: Ugayafukiaezu, 'Cormorant-Thatching-Unfinished' . The scene survives because a roof was never completed: a goddess of the sea delivering on land, and a lineage beginning in the gap between the elements. [Kojiki I] The Farewell Song: Before she returned to the sea, Toyotama spoke the poem the Kojiki preserves as one of its most celebrated archaic songs: had you not shamed me, I would have come and gone by the sea-road, and for ever eased the way of the ships; but now that you have looked, the crossing will be hard — the precise wording varies in translation, but Philippi's rendering keeps its reproach intact. She left the child in the care of her younger sister Tamayori — 'Good Jewel' — who came up out of the water to suckle him. In a text crowded with genealogies, the poem is the rare moment the myth turns elegy: a mother who could have made the sea a road for her son instead leaves him a song — and the imperial line inherits, with its treasures, a story about the price of looking. [Kojiki I] The Aunt Who Stayed: Tamayori raised the boy of the unfinished hut, and when he was grown the Kojiki says she became his wife; the compilers record the union without comment, the sea line marrying back into itself. Four sons were born: Itsuse, Inahi, Mikeiri, and the youngest, Kamuyamato-Iwarebiko. The Nihon Shoki's parallel account of the succession tells how the three elder brothers marched east against the defiant chiefs of the land and failed — Itsuse fell at Kusaka, his army repulsed — while the youngest, guided by the three-legged crow Yatagarasu sent down from heaven, found the road through the mountains, defeated Nagasunehiko, and planted the Yamato line. The child of the roofless hut becomes the hinge on which the narrative turns from gods to kings : from this point the chronicles stop telling of the divine age and begin, almost, to tell of a realm. [Nihon Shoki] The Treasures Cross the Water: The Kojiki and Nihon Shoki agree on the cargo of the line Ugayafukiaezu completes: the imperial regalia — the mirror, the sword Kusanagi, and the jewel — descended from Amaterasu with Ninigi, passed down through Hoori's house, and went east with Jimmu on the expedition, the divine mirror and sword carried against the rebels of the land. Later tradition placed the unfinished hut's son at the exact point where the age of the gods closes: everything celestial has now crossed into a single human lineage. The Nihon Shoki's more sober parallel strips away wonders and keeps the genealogy, which is testimony of its own kind — whether read as myth or as charter, the story exists to make one claim: that the family of the unfinished roof was entrusted with heaven's treasures , and did not drop them.

instruction: Tell me a myth about "Hoderi".
output: Hoderi's story in the Kojiki is a tale of sibling rivalry, the exchange of gifts, and the transfer of sovereignty from the sea to the land. He is the elder son, the firstborn of Ninigi, destined to be bypassed — and Japan's two oldest histories tell his falling-short with different temperaments, and the difference is itself instructive. [Kojiki] The Exchange of Gifts: When Ninigi's sons grew up, he divided the world's livelihood between them: to Hoderi, the elder, he gave the fishhook that rules the sea; to Hoori, the younger, the bow and arrow that rule the mountains ( Kojiki , age of the gods). Hoori proposed that they exchange — he would try the sea, Hoderi the chase — and Hoderi agreed. But the sea resisted the stranger: Hoori fished for days and caught nothing, and in a fury he flung the precious hook into the waves. Hoderi's response was absolute: he would sooner lose a kingdom than his hook, and he demanded its return on pain of their brotherhood itself. Cornered, Hoori walked into the sea to answer for the loss. The exchange looks innocent but is the hinge of the whole cycle: a fisherman's tool, lost and owed, becomes the lever that moves sovereignty from elder to younger, from sea to land. [Kojiki] Hoori's Triumph: Beneath the waves Hoori found not punishment but fortune: the palace of the sea god Watatsumi, and marriage to the god's daughter Toyotama-hime. From the sea's depths he sent the lost hook back to land — recovered, in the Kojiki 's wry detail, from the throat of a sea bream — bearing a curse that turned against its owner: whatever it touched would fail and wither. Struck by the curse, Hoderi saw his stores dwindle and his luck collapse, until he came barefoot to his younger brother, begging terms. Hoori took the submission and the precedence; Hoderi gave him his daughter and his allegiance, and the elder line bent to the younger. The myth's meaning is economical and severe: legitimacy in the age of the gods does not follow birth order but the flow of fortune, and the sea, for all its plenty, could not hold the future that was gathering on the land. [Genealogy] Ancestor of the Hayato: The Kojiki closes Hoderi's line not with extinction but with a dignified office: his descendants are the Hayato , a people of southern Kyūshū remembered in early Japanese records as warriors and as ritual specialists at the imperial court. Historically the Hayato appear in the eighth-century chronicles as a military people whose sons served the throne — an echo, scholars have long suspected, of a pre-Yamato population of the south absorbed into the imperial order on terms its own myth explains. The genealogy does double work: it gives the defeated elder brother a posterity, and it gives the victorious court a way to honor the people it absorbed, as ritualists rather than rebels. In Hoderi's house the myth means: the bypassed line is not erased but employed — the memory of the elder brother kept on the payroll of the younger's descendants. [Nihon Shoki] The Tide Jewels of the Other History: The Nihon Shoki (720 CE) tells the same feud with different names and sharper weapons: the brothers are called Umisachihiko, Sea-Luck Lad, and Yamasachihiko, Mountain-Luck Lad, and the sea god arms the younger with the two tide jewels — one that floods, one that ebbs. When the elder attacks, the flooding jewel drowns him; when he begs, the ebbing jewel spares him, and he swears service to his brother's line, becoming — the genealogy agrees — ancestor of the Hayato. The Shoki's variant notes are harsher still: in one alternate account the elder brother does not survive the feud at all. Two official histories, two temperaments: the Kojiki converts defeat into service, the Shoki leaves the sea prince gasping on the tideline. Read together they show the early court arguing with itself about what to do with the elder line — absorb it lovingly, or drown it and call it law.

instruction: Tell me a myth about "Hoori".
output: Hoori's mythology is the bridge between the heavenly descent of Ninigi and the earthly reign of Emperor Jimmu: a story of exchanged tools, a lost hook, a voyage to the dragon palace, a broken promise, and a line of kings. It is told in the Kojiki and repeated, with variations, in the Nihon Shoki. [Kojiki] The Exchanged Tools: The youngest son of Ninigi and Konohana-Sakuya-hime received from his father the bow , while his elder brother Hoderi received the fishhook — one son of the mountains, one of the sea, mirroring the division of the land itself (Kojiki I). Hoori proposed that they exchange tools for a single day: he would try his brother's fortune with the hook, Hoderi the mountains with the bow. The day went well for no one. Hoori, inexpert at the shore, lost the borrowed hook in the sea, and when he dived and dragged the bottom it could not be found. Hoderi refused every substitute — first his own sword, then five hundred mother-of-pearl hooks, then a thousand — demanding back the one original hook, the single object through which a man's fortune was thought to run. The impossible demand drives the younger brother out of the human world and down into the sea: the quarrel over one small thing is what opens the door to the gods. [Kojiki] The Dragon Palace of Watasumi: Following the counsel of an old man on the beach — one of the passing kami who advise heroes at their lowest hour — Hoori sat on the bough of a tree that bent over the waves until the tide carried him down through a gateway into the undersea palace of Watasumi-no-kami , the sea deity. There he was welcomed, bathed, feasted, and married to the sea god's daughter Toyotama-hime , the 'Abundant-Jewel Princess' (Kojiki I). When Hoori confessed why he had come, Toyotama's brother searched the sea and recovered the lost hook from the throat of a red sea-bream. Watasumi then gave his son-in-law two treasures — the tide-flowing jewel and the tide-ebbing jewel, with which any sea can be raised or stilled — and taught him the ruse by which a proud man is broken: do not answer rage with rage, but mock it gently as it rages , and its strength will spend itself against your calm. The palace gives the exiled brother everything his own shore withheld: a wife, the hook, and a strategy. [Kojiki] The Mocked Brother and the Covenant: Hoori returned to land and waited on the beach. When Hoderi came raging across the strand, Hoori sang a mocking song — as the Kojiki has it, like the bushes on the shore his brother's beard was tangled, like the drifting seaweed his rage floated aimlessly — and Hoderi attacked. Hoori raised the tide-flowing jewel, and the sea rose to Hoderi's neck; Hoderi begged and wept, and Hoori raised the ebbing jewel and spared him (Kojiki I). The brothers made peace on a new order: Hoderi would keep the watery ways, and his descendants would serve Hoori's line forever. Thus the sea-fortune and the mountain-fortune were divided as they still are in Japan — and the humbler brother, who had lost everything in the water, came home owning both the land and the sea's obedience. The myth's arithmetic is deliberate: the borrowed hook cost nothing to replace, but the brotherly covenant it purchased was the real prize. [Kojiki] The Broken Taboo and the First Emperor: Toyotama came up from the sea to bear her child, but first she built a parturition hut roofed with cormorant feathers and laid down the law that Hoori must not look inside. Curiosity — the flaw and the engine of this whole cycle — overcame him. He peeked and saw his wife in her true shape, a great sea-dragon coiled in the hut; mortified, Toyotama abandoned the land and the newborn, sending her sister Tamayori-hime in her place with a parting song. The child, Ugayafukiaezu , was raised by his aunt, married her in time, and their son was Kamuyamato-Iwarebiko — better known as Emperor Jimmu , first emperor of Japan (Kojiki I; Nihon Shoki I). Hoori's one act of disobedience costs him his wife, yet it leaves the imperial line on land, guarded by sea and mountain at once. The sources read the episode without apology: the line of emperors begins exactly where the promise was broken.

instruction: Tell me a myth about "Nishinakahime".
output: Nishinakahime's mythology is two sentences long in the Kojiki — and they are among the most striking in the whole canon. Everything else the tradition knows about her is in her name: hani, potter's clay, and yasu, the yielding. The potters of Japan's ancient kiln towns supplied the rest of her story — a thousand years of practice laid at her feet. [Kojiki] The Dying Goddess Bears the Clay Kami: Izanami gave birth to the fire god Kagutsuchi, and the fire burned her so badly that she sickened and lay dying. From her body in its extremity came the last kami of the living generation: from her vomit, the metal-mountain deities Kanayamahiko and Kanayamahime; from her urine, the water goddess Mizuha-no-me; and from her bowels, the brother and sister of clay — Hani-yasu-biko and Hani-yasu-hime (Kojiki, birth of Kagutsuchi; the Nihon Shoki gives her the parallel names Haniyama-hime, 'Clay-Mountain Princess,' and Haniyasu-no-kami). The texts state this with the same flat calm as everything else in the divine genealogies, yet the implication is immense: the kami of humanity's three great materials — metal, water, clay — are born from the mother's death-agony. In Shinto's most radical birth story, the technologies that make civilization possible are not stolen from heaven or won by conquest; they are what a dying goddess leaves behind. [Name] A Name That Means 'Clay That Yields': Hani-yasu is a name that explains itself, the way kami names so often do. Hani (埴) is potter's clay, the earth dug from the subsoil that holds water and takes any shape; yasu (安/易) is 'easy, gentle, workable.' The goddess is, literally, the clay that yields — earth soft enough to form. The great Kokugaku scholar Motoori Norinaga, in his Kojikiden , glossed the name as hani-neyasu : clay kneaded and worked until its stiffness softens and it becomes obedient to the hand. The spelling is itself a lesson: the Kojiki's characters 波邇夜須 are phonetic choices made for sound rather than sense, which is why later writers preferred the semantic form 埴, 'clay,' that the Nihon Shoki uses in Clay-Mountain Princess. Shinto rarely makes abstract theology; here the theology is a craft instruction. The name is a recipe: work the clay until it yields — and to read the name correctly is already to know what she is. [Kojiki] Three Gifts of Civilization from One Body: Read together, the kami born from Izanami's failing body form a complete inventory of material culture. Kanayama-hime, from the vomit, is metal — ore, smelting, the smith's art. Mizuha-no-me, from the urine, is water — wells, irrigation, the pure stream. And Hani-yasu-hime, from the feces, is clay — the kiln, the pot, the fired vessel that outlives its maker. Japan confirmed the inventory in its shrines: the clay siblings are enshrined in pottery districts as the kiln ancestors ( tōso ), and the Kanayama kami at mines and smithies. The distribution of a goddess's dying body across human technology is unique in the Kojiki: no other birth narrative so completely fuses physiology and craft. Her mythology is her etymology writ large — from the body of the mother earth-goddess comes the very substance that, worked by human hands, holds grain, sake, and the ashes of the dead. [Folk Tradition] The Kiln Ancestors: The imperial chronicles give Hani-yasu-hime two clauses; Japanese potters gave her a thousand years. The great ceramic towns — Bizen, Shigaraki, Echizen, Seto, Tanba, Tokoname, the six ancient kilns ( rokkoyō ) — enshrine the clay kami as patrons and founders of their craft, under the titles Clay-Mountain Princess and Clay-Mountain Prince, and kiln observances still open with offerings to the earth the pots are made from. The tradition's material memory runs deeper than the shrines: the haniwa , the 'clay rings' and hollow figures set on the great tombs of the Kofun age (3rd–6th centuries), carry her element hani in their very name — clay that was never forgotten as sacred stuff. A goddess born in a moment of utmost indignity became the quiet patron of Japan's most refined art: the tea bowl's wabi, the Bizen jar's unglazed fire-marks — all of it earth-plus-fire, her two inheritances in one vessel.

instruction: Tell me a myth about "Kingu".
output: Kingu enters the Enuma Elish not as a primordial element like Apsû or Tiāmat, but as a response — the consort Tiāmat chooses after her first partner is destroyed. He is chaos with a general's mind: the one who turns Tiāmat's grief into organized war. His story moves from elevation to defeat to transformation, because in Mesopotamian cosmology the slain enemy does not simply disappear; he is reworked into the world. [Elevation] Tiāmat Makes Kingu Her Consort: The epic's first tablets set the stage in catastrophe. Apsû, the primordial freshwater, cannot sleep for the noise of the young gods and plots to destroy them; Ea preempts him, wraps Apsû in sleep, and kills him, building his own sanctuary on the still waters (Enuma Elish I). Tiāmat, the salt sea, endures this in silence — until her own offspring drive her to fury. She raises an army of monsters, 'the viper, the dragon, and the lahmu-hero, the great storm-demon, the mad dog, and the scorpion-man' (Enuma Elish I, trans. Foster), and to lead them she takes a new consort: Kingu. 'She exalted him among the assembly of the gods... set him to arms, let the host go at his side' — a figure promoted precisely because he is not one of the old order, and therefore cannot be expected to spare it. Kingu is chaos given a chain of command. [Authority] The Tablet of Destinies: To legitimate Kingu's command, Tiāmat performs the epic's most consequential gesture short of battle: she fastens the Tablet of Destinies — the ṭuppi šīmāti, the inscribed register by which fates are decreed and confirmed — upon his breast. To hold the tablet is to hold the power to bind and loose the destinies of gods and worlds; Kingu is thus briefly made a rival sovereign, and the younger gods are thrown into terror, because fate itself seems to have defected to chaos. In Mesopotamian thought the tablet was no metaphor: legitimate kingship meant the gods' confirmation of a ruler's decrees, and its seizure marks every true transfer of power in the mythic record — as the Anzu poem shows when the lion-headed bird steals the same authority from Enlil. Kingu's elevation is therefore legible to every Babylonian listener as a constitutional crisis: the wrong being now held the seal of heaven. [Conflict] Marduk Defeats Kingu: The divine assembly, helpless, offers kingship to any god who can answer the threat — and Marduk of Babylon answers, on a chilling condition: 'When I speak, let my word be confirmed; the command I utter, let the gods fulfill it' (Enuma Elish III). The gods test him by destroying a garment and commanding him to restore it; he does, and they arm him with the flood-weapon and the storm-wind. In single combat Marduk splits Tiāmat with an arrow, fashions heaven and earth from her body, and then turns to her army. Kingu is seized, bound, stripped of the Tablet of Destinies, and counted among the dead — 'Marduk took the Tablet of Destinies from Kingu and fastened it upon his own breast' (Enuma Elish IV). The usurper's badge becomes the victor's legitimacy, in one motion: Babylon's god now confirms fates, and the poem that sings it was recited in Babylon's New Year festival to say exactly that. [Transformation] The Creation of Humankind: With Kingu dead, the gods face a quieter problem: who will do the world's work? They have built the cosmos, but its service is unending, and they complain of their toil (Enuma Elish VI). Ea proposes the solution, and Marduk adds the justice of it: the rebellion had a first cause, and the first cause should pay. The assembly convenes, and Kingu is condemned — 'the one who made war, suborned Tiāmat, and prepared the onslaught: he shall be given over to slaughter' — and from his blood, mixed with clay, Ea fashions humankind. The charge laid on the new species is the service of the gods, that the divine assembly may rest. Few cosmogonies are so unsentimental: humanity is not fashioned from the victor's generosity but from the rebel's sentence, and our mortality is the leftover of a war we did not fight. The myth's ending is the epic's warrant — the gods divide the offices of heaven and earth, and Marduk's fifty names close the hymn.

instruction: Tell me a myth about "Lahmu".
output: Lahmu is not a protagonist of long narrative cycles; his power is concentrated at origins and thresholds. He appears at the very beginning of the Babylonian cosmos, and he endures at the edges of the ordered world as a guardian. [Cosmogony] Firstborn of the Primordial Waters: The Enuma Elish opens with Apsû, the freshwater abyss, and Tiāmat, the salt sea: 'when sweet and bitter mingled together, no reed was plaited, no rushes muddied the water' ( Enuma Elish , Tablet I, lines 1–20). From the mingled waters the gods were born in pairs — first Lahmu and Lahamu , then Anshar and Kishar, then Anu, and finally Ea, the line that ends in Marduk. Lahmu is therefore the first divine body to emerge from chaos, the earliest shape the cosmos takes after the waters meet. The interpretive claim of the genealogy is deliberate: the gods do not precede the deep — they arise out of it, in twos, and the very first of them is already a threshold-being, standing where the two waters become one. [Apotropaic cult] The Hairy Doorkeeper: In ritual texts and iconography Lahmu is a protective demon stationed at doorways. His shaggy body and beard were believed to frighten away evil. Clay figurines and glazed reliefs show him as a muscular, bearded male with curled hair, often flanking an entrance; ritual texts prescribe the burial of such figures beneath thresholds and beside door sockets, so that the passage between street and sanctuary is permanently guarded (Wiggermann, Mesopotamian Protective Spirits ). To pass his gate was to move from dangerous outside into protected inside. The choice of a hairy body is practical magic: in Mesopotamian thought the monstrous face the demon turns toward the world of demons is the very thing that keeps them at bay — the guard must be as frightening as what he guards against. [Iconography] The Six-Curled Guardian: Lahmu is recognizable in Mesopotamian art by his long beard arranged in six or seven rounded curls, a naked or lightly clad hairy body, and an aggressive stance. He sometimes grasps a weapon or a gatepost, and on glazed brick reliefs from palace façades he stands in profile between real and painted doors, so that the image itself performs the warding. These attributes made him instantly readable as an apotropaic figure: the hair that named him became the visual sign of his power. The standardized curls are the mark of an established craft tradition — the guardian's face was drawn, moulded, and glazed by workshops who knew exactly which god they were posting at the king's door, even when no caption named him. [Paired cult] Lahmu and Lahamu: Lahmu is paired with Lahamu, a feminine counterpart whose name shares the same root. In the Enuma Elish the pair is born together from the mingled waters, before Anshar and Kishar, and they grow up to bear the next generation; in ritual art they appear as matching figures on either side of a door, male and female aspects of a single protective function. The pairing is not decorative but structural: the threshold is the most charged line in the Mesopotamian house, and a line needs two sides. Where one guardian would personify defence, the twin pair personifies completeness — the whole doorway, both jambs, both directions of passage. It is the oldest architectural theology in the world: the door as a place, and the place as a couple.
