instruction: Tell me a myth about "Tvaṣṭṛ".
output: Tvaṣṭṛ's cycle is the Vedic meditation on craft and consequence: the hands that make the weapons, the cups, and the children are the same — and what is made can turn on its maker's world. [The Weapon] Forging the Vajra: When the dragon Vṛtra held the waters captive, Indra needed a weapon worthy of the deed: Tvaṣṭṛ forged the vajra, the bolt that smashed the ninety-nine fortresses and split the dragon's jaw. The Ṛgveda repeats the attribution like a signature — "the bolt that Tvaṣṭṛ made for thee" — the smith's name stamped on the pantheon's supreme weapon. [The Son] Viśvarūpa's Three Heads: Tvaṣṭṛ's son Viśvarūpa — three-headed, six-eyed — served as priest of the gods while secretly feeding the anti-gods' share of the offerings. Indra struck off the heads; from them sprang the partridge, the sparrow, and the quail. The smith's grief at his son's death is the hinge of the whole cycle: the forge turns from weapons for the gods to a weapon against them. [The Avenger] The Making of Vṛtra: Taittirīya Saṃhitā tells the terrible sequel: Tvaṣṭṛ performed a rite to create an avenger — but the accent of the mantra slipped. He meant "slayer of Indra" (indrā-śatru, with the accent of possession); the words came out "Indra-slain" — and Vṛtra, the monster he raised, was doomed by grammar to die by Indra's hand. The smith fashioned the weapon; the language fashioned the outcome. [The Daughter] Saraṇyū and the Shadow: His daughter Saraṇyū married the Sun and, unable to bear his blaze, left her own shadow-image in her place and fled as a mare. The Sun discovered the substitution, followed as a stallion, and of their union were born the twin Aśvins. Tvaṣṭṛ's household thus generated the gods of healing and dawn — the fashioner's line shaping light itself.

instruction: Tell me a myth about "Mèngpó".
output: Mèngpó's myth is a single scene, retold for centuries: the old woman, the bridge, the bowl — the gentlest moment in the whole machinery of the afterlife. [The Office] The Last Station: Chinese folk cosmology orders the underworld like an administration: Yánluó's ten courts judge the deeds of the life, assign the punishments and the repayments — and then send the soul to Mèngpó. At the Nàihé Bridge she ladles her tea of five flavors; the soul drinks, and the record of the life — the loves, the hatreds, the unfinished business — dissolves. Only then is it fit to be reborn. [The Legend] Why She Serves: Folk tellings give her a biography: she was, some say, a woman of the mortal world who grieved her dead so deeply that heaven gave her this office — that no other soul need carry grief across the boundary. Others make her a wind-spirit of antiquity, or a servant of the underworld's lord promoted for her gentle hand. The variants agree on the point: the one who erases memory does it out of mercy, having known what memory costs. [The Refusal] Those Who Will Not Drink: The tales always leave a door: a soul that refuses the tea, or spills it, carries fragments across — and is born with a birthmark, a déjà vu, a face it cannot forget. Chinese fiction is full of such revenants: lovers recognizing lovers across lifetimes, enemies resuming ancient quarrels, all because one soul at the bridge would not finish the bowl. Memory, in the folklore, is a debt carried by the stubborn. [The Jade Record] The Bureaucratic Underworld: Her clearest dossier is late and popular rather than canonical. The Yùlì bǎochāo (玉曆寶鈔, 'Jade Calendar,' a morality tract circulating from the Ming and printed widely in the Qing) maps the Chinese underworld as a ten-court bureaucracy under Yánluó, and its woodblock illustrations place Mèngpó last of all — past the judgments, past the Wheel, at the bridge where her booth does its quiet work, small and busy among the magistrates, ladle in hand. Earlier traces are thinner, and the scholars are honest about it: she belongs to the folk stratum that writing caught late, flourishing in storytellers' retellings, underworld scroll-paintings, and the pilgrimage landscape of Fēngdū, where the Nàihé Bridge was built in stone and crossed by the living. Being undocumented is almost her theology: the one who erases the records left none of her own.

instruction: Tell me a myth about "Pángǔ".
output: Pángǔ's myth exists in two sentences of immense consequence, recorded by Xú Zhěng in the 3rd century CE — and expanded by a civilization into its canonical account of how the world began. [The Egg] Three-Five Calendar Record: Xú Zhěng's Sānwǔ lìjì (3rd century CE, preserved in later encyclopedias) gives the founding text: 'Heaven and earth were chaos like a hen's egg, and Pángǔ was born within it. After eighteen thousand years, heaven and earth opened: the bright, light qì rose to become heaven; the dark, heavy qì sank to become earth. Pángǔ stood between them, changing nine times daily — heaven rising ten feet a day, earth thickening ten feet, and Pángǔ growing ten feet — for eighteen thousand years more, until heaven stood ninety thousand li above the earth.' The arithmetic is the myth's own poetry: the world is not spoken into being but pushed apart by increments, against a measurable resistance — creation as the first and longest labor, and the giant as the one who never stops growing because his work is never done. [The Death] The Body Becomes the World: When the separation was fixed, Pángǔ died — and the transformation began, in the same text's most famous lines: his breath became wind and cloud, his voice thunder, his left eye the sun and his right the moon, his four limbs the four sacred mountains, his blood the rivers, his veins the roads, his flesh the soil, his hair the stars, his skin and body-hair grass and trees, his sweat the rain — and, in the most anthropologically piquant line, the fleas and lice of his body, quickened by the wind, became the black-haired people. Nothing in the list is wasted and nothing is decorative: the myth insists that geography is biography — that every mountain is a limb and every river a vein — so that to wound the landscape is to wound the body one lives inside. It is the world's most complete statement of the sacredness of place. [The Late Arrival] China's Youngest Creator: The myth's strangest fact is its date: no pre-Han text mentions Pángǔ, and the Sānwǔ lìjì itself has to be reconstructed from quotations in medieval encyclopedias, for the original is lost. Scholars trace his entry through southern traditions — the Yao and Miao genealogies of the dog-ancestor Pán Hù, phonetically adjacent, from the very region the later sources call Pángǔ country — absorbed and cosmicized in the Wei-Jin centuries, when the north's older creation-by-culture-hero had left a vacancy at the very beginning. China's canonical creation is thus a relative newcomer, adopted so completely that every schoolchild now learns it as the oldest story — a case of a myth winning by arriving last, exactly when the civilization needed a single name to put at the head of time. [The Variants] Folk Versions and a Southern Country: By the sixth century the giant had accumulated regional tellings, and Rèn Fáng's Shùyì jì ('Records of Strange Matters', c. 500 CE) preserves the collated harvest. The folk versions map his body onto the sacred mountains with cheerful disagreement: in one, his head became the Eastern Marchmount, his belly the Central, his limbs the Southern and Northern, his feet the Western; in another, his tears became the rivers, his breath the wind, his voice thunder, his pupils lightning — and his moods the weather, his gladness clearing the sky and his anger clouding it (Shùyì jì, quoting what it calls Qín-Hàn popular sayings). The most remarkable entry records that in the southern sea there was a Pángǔ country whose people bore Pángǔ as their surname — a whole people claiming descent from the giant. And in the Wú-Chǔ region south of the Yangtze, the tellers made him a married pair: Pángǔ and his wife, 'the beginning of yin and yang.' The creator was still growing new versions four centuries after his first written breath — evidence that China never finished deciding what its youngest god meant.

instruction: Tell me a myth about "Honshū".
output: Honshū's mythology is the national charter itself: the Kojiki's island-birth, the sun goddess's gift of the land, and the descent of her grandson to rule it. [The Birth] The Islands from the Spear: The Kojiki opens on the heavenly bridge: Izanagi and Izanami stir the ocean with the jewelled spear, and from the brine dripping from its point the first island coagulates. Descending, they wed and give birth to the islands of Japan — the "great eight islands" culminating in Ōyashima — and then to the kami of wind, sea, mountain, and tree. The archipelago is not created but born: the land is kin. [The Sun] Amaterasu's Realm: When the sun goddess Amaterasu withdrew into the Heavenly Rock-Cave — outraged by her brother Susanoo's rampage — the world went dark until the gods' comic dance lured her out. Her mirror, hung outside the cave, caught her own light back to her; that mirror rests at Ise on Honshū's Kii coast, and her shrine there has been ritually rebuilt every twenty years for thirteen centuries: the island's heartwood, renewed. [The Descent] Ninigi and the Rice Land: Amaterasu sent her grandson Ninigi down from heaven to rule the "Land of Fair Rice-ears of the Fertile Reed-plain" — the Kojiki's name for Honshū's heartland — bearing the three regalia. His great-grandson Jimmu conquered eastward to Yamato and became the first emperor: the mythic bridge from island-birth to imperial genealogy, anchored to real ground in Nara's basin. [The Yielding] Ōkuninushi Surrenders the Land: One more myth fixes Honshū's western half to the imperial story. When Amaterasu sent her grandson down to take the land, its ruler — Ōkuninushi, the great land-master of Izumo — was first challenged through his sons, each defeated in turn, and then visited by the divine negotiators with a counter-offer: yield the visible world to heaven's line, and in exchange heaven would build him a shrine 'with its pillars thick at the base and high at the head' and house his spirit there ( Kojiki , age of the heavenly grandchild). Ōkuninushi accepted. The Nihon Shoki remembers the bargain as a settled diplomatic exchange — Japan's mythic account of how the western realms joined the Yamato order without a war of conquest. Izumo Taisha, on Honshū's Sea-of-Japan coast, stands where the deal was struck, and the vast pillars its ancient halls once held were, by tradition, exactly the size the god stipulated. The myth is a charter for peaceful annexation: the land yields, the god is honored, and both houses — Izumo's shrine and the imperial palace — stand on the same island.

instruction: Tell me a myth about "Kyūshū".
output: Kyūshū claims the mythology of beginnings: the chronicles land the sun goddess's grandson on its peaks, send the first emperor out from its shores, and let its storms write themselves into the national soul. [The Descent] Ninigi on Takachiho: The Kojiki and Nihon Shoki bring the heavenly grandson Ninigi down to earth on the peak of Takachiho — placed by tradition in Kyūshū's mountains — where he marries the blossom-princess Konohanasakuya-hime. She proves her divine conception by setting fire to the birthing hut and delivering three sons amid the flames; their line leads to Jimmu, the first emperor. The imperial charter myth is, geographically, a Kyūshū story. The shrine at Takachiho still marks the descent-spot, and the Ama-no-iwato cave in the gorge beside it — where the sun goddess Amaterasu once hid — anchors the whole island as the stage of the Age of the Gods. The myth means Japan's sacred geography begins not at the capital but at the gateway: the gods landed where the continent first appears. [The Founding] Jimmu's Departure: The chronicles begin Japan's history on this island. Jimmu, the great-grandson of Ninigi, tired of ruling only the Hyūga coast and resolved on the eastern expedition to Yamato: 'the land to the east is fair... let us go to the land of the rising sun.' His first fleet was wrecked, his brother Itsuse died of a wound, and the way was cleared only after the vanishing sacrifice of the empress — but the divine crow Yatagarasu, three-legged, was sent to guide him, and after the mountain campaign against Nagasunehiko he founded the dynasty at Kashihara, in 660 BCE by the chronicles' reckoning. Myth means history here in the full sense: Japan's imperial charter is a Kyūshū story of leaving Kyūshū. The gateway completes its service by producing the one who crosses it. [The Storm] The Divine Wind: Twice the Mongol-Chinese fleets of Kublai Khan reached Kyūshū — 1274 and 1281, the second numbering thousands of ships — and twice, after hard fighting on the Hakata beaches, typhoons destroyed the armadas. The shrines had prayed for deliverance, and the nation named the storm kamikaze , 'divine wind': weather as providence, and the coast of Hakata Bay as the sacrificial altar of the largest seaborne invasions the world had yet seen. Later tradition credited the prayers of Iwashimizu and Hakozaki shrines, and modern underwater archaeology at Takashima has raised the fleets' own testimony — anchor stones, ceramic bombs, and hulls preserved in Imari Bay. The myth means providence has a shoreline: the same straits that carried every gift from the continent also carried the storm that saved the island from it. [The Hidden Faith] The Kirishitan Century: Francis Xavier landed at Kagoshima in 1549; within decades Kyūshū had a quarter-million Christians, daimyō baptized with their domains, and seminaries at Arima and Azuchi. Then came the turn: persecution, the crucifixions at Nagasaki, the Shimabara-Amakusa rising of 1637 — and 250 years of hidden Christians keeping Latin prayers in corrupted Japanese, baptizing in secret, venerating statues of Kannon as the Virgin. Their revelation in 1865, when farmers of Urakami knelt before a French priest at the Ōura Cathedral overlooking the harbor, stunned the mission world. The Ōura church still stands, and the villages of the Amakusa islands and the Nagasaki coast are UNESCO-listed as the 'Hidden Christian Sites in the Nagasaki Region.' The myth means the gateway keeps what it takes in even when the door is slammed: a faith survived two and a half centuries on this shore purely by being hidden in plain sight.

instruction: Tell me a myth about "Tūmatauenga".
output: Tūmatauenga's cycle is the Polynesian account of how humanity got its arts: not by gift but by conquest — the war-god subduing his elemental brothers and distributing the spoils to his mortal children. [The Separation] The Sons of Ranginui and Papatūānuku: In the beginning the Sky Father Ranginui and the Earth Mother Papatūānuku lay locked together in an embrace, and their children lived crushed in darkness between them. Among the sons was Tūmatauenga , fiercest of them all. When the brothers debated what to do, it was Tū who urged the final solution — kill the parents and have done. The others recoiled at the thought of slaying their own father and mother, and the gentler counsel of Tāne prevailed: the parents would be forced apart, not slain (Grey, Polynesian Mythology , the legend of the children of Rangi and Papa). Rongo, Tangaroa, Haumia, and Tū himself tried to push the parents and failed; then Tāne set his head on the earth, his feet against the sky, and tore the parents open. Light came into the world — and Tāwhirimātea, who had loved the darkness, went to war over it. The myth is exact about its genealogy of war: strife is not an intruder into creation but a sibling of the light itself, born the moment separation was chosen. [The Storm] The One Who Stood: Tāwhirimātea, god of winds and storms, had opposed the separation of his parents, and now he took war to his brothers in revenge, riding the weapon-winds of his storm-army. Tangaroa fled to the sea; Tāne withdrew into the forests; Rongo and Haumia thrust themselves into the earth — but Tūmatauenga alone stood fast on the open plain , unbowed under the tempest (Grey, Polynesian Mythology ). When the storm at last spent itself, the standing one turned on his fleeing brothers and made their domains his own: he wove nets and took Tangaroa's fish, set snares for Tāne's birds, and dug into the earth for Rongo's kūmara and Haumia's fern-root. His name is the doctrine: tū means 'to stand'. War, in the Māori telling, is first of all a posture — the refusal to move when everything else runs — and only secondly a weapon; the whole later tradition of the haka, the pūkana, and the pa is that posture made communal. [The Spoils] The Arts Won by Conquest: By subduing his brothers, Tūmatauenga made their realms noa — common, usable — and so gave humankind its technologies: the net and hook for the sea, the snare for the forest, the digging-stick for the garden. The karakia of planting, fishing, fowling, and war all carry his name, for every tapu those arts break was broken first by him; Best and Tregear record his invocation where food is made safe to eat. The cycle thus makes the fiercest god the culture-bringer: not Tāne the gentle separator but Tū the stander, who gathered what the storm scattered and portioned it out. The distribution is the myth's second doctrine. What war wins must be handed on; the conqueror who keeps everything for himself defeats the purpose of standing, and the tribe that forgets how to feed itself has lost the spoils twice. [The Descent] The Children of Tū: The tradition gives the war-god a family larger than any brotherhood: humankind itself. Tregear records the phrase he tamaiti nā Tū — 'a child of Tū' — as a way of naming a human being ( The Maori-Polynesian Comparative Dictionary , s.v. Tu), and the southern branches of the family tell the same descent as genealogy: in Tahiti, Tū is not only the war-god but the first ancestor, the root of the human line (Henry, Ancient Tahiti ). The Māori cycles draw the moral plainly. The brothers who fled or hid left their domains to be taken; the one who stood gave humans his own nature — fierceness, endurance, and the habit of war. To be human, in this theology, is to have inherited the furious face; the arts of peace, Rongo's garden and Tangaroa's sea, are the domains of humankind's gentler uncles, conquered and kept only because their fierce brother stands guard over them.

instruction: Tell me a myth about "Guāndì".
output: Guāndì's myth is history sanctified: the Records of the Three Kingdoms gave him a life, the Romance gave him a legend, and eight dynasties gave him a godhood — loyalty tested by gold, exile, and death, then canonized rank by rank until the executed general stood beside Confucius. What is worshipped is the word that outlasts its usefulness. [The Oath] The Peach Garden: The Romance of the Three Kingdoms (ch. 1) opens not with a battle but with an oath: in the blossom of Zhang Fei's peach garden, the three — Liu Bei the petitioner, Guan Yu the bearded giant, Zhang Fei the hot-tempered butcher — kneel before heaven and earth: "We ask not to be born on the same day, but we beg to die on the same day." The history behind the novel, the Sanguozhi (ch. 36), knows no oath; it records only that the three were close as brothers and shared everything. The oath is the Romance's invention, and it is one of the most consequential inventions in Chinese literature: for six centuries sworn brotherhood (結義) has been the template for loyalty between men who are not kin, quoted at initiations, in opera, film, and lodge ceremonies alike. The myth teaches that the deepest bonds are chosen, witnessed, and paid for in the same coin — a day of death, whenever it comes. [The Capture] Three Conditions, One Horse: Captured with Liu Bei's household when Xiapi fell, Guan Yu dictated his own terms of surrender ( Romance , ch. 25): he would yield only to the Han emperor, not to Cao Cao; the two sisters-in-law must be guarded with full propriety; and the moment his brother was found he would leave. Cao Cao tested the terms with gifts — gold, silks, ten beauties, and finally the Red Hare, the empire's finest horse. Guan Yu bowed twice for the horse alone: "once I hear where my brother is, I can reach him in a day." He repaid the courtesies in full — riding alone into a hundred thousand men to take the enemy general Yan Liang's head at Baima (ch. 26) — then hung his seal, left letters of thanks, and rode a thousand li through five passes and six of Cao's garrisons to rejoin a lord far poorer than his captor (ch. 27). Honor, the novel says, answers courtesy with interest — and keeps accounts with everyone. [The Apotheosis] From General to Emperor: The historical Guan Yu died badly in 219 CE — abandoned by allies, surrounded at Maicheng, captured at Linju and executed by Sun Quan's men ( Sanguozhi , ch. 36). His head was sent to Cao Cao at Luoyang and buried with the honors of a prince — the grave at Guanlin that is still his shrine — while Wu buried the body at Dangyang in Hubei, where his cult first took root. Deification took eight centuries and is the slowest canonization in Chinese religious history. A Sui-era legend, preserved in Song Chan transmission records, converts his vengeful ghost at Mount Yuquan into a Buddhist protector; the Song court titled him Duke (1102) and later Prince; the Wanli emperor of the Ming raised him to Emperor — Guan Sheng Dijun — in 1614; and the Qing added the word Sage, pairing him with Confucius as the martial co-sage of the empire. No other Chinese figure rose from executed general to peer of Confucius. Rank upon rank, earned by the same oath. [The Guardian] Sangharama at the Gate: Buddhism adopted its most unlikely guardian: the general who died over a broken oath became Sangharama , protector of the monastic precinct. In Chan halls his statue stands opposite Weituo's, the two flanking the Buddha's gate — the monk's army and the monk's police. The choice is theologically pointed. The religion of impermanence stations at its door the god of the promise that does not change, and communities that release men from family duty still require a witness against oath-breaking. His night patrol survives in legend: on the last night of the year he walks the world's courts, righting verdicts that living judges got wrong — a task the opera stage gave its fullest form, where Guan Yu's shade intervenes for the falsely condemned. Daoism claimed him too, as Xietian Dadi. But the deepest adoption is this: in Hong Kong, the police-station altar and the lodge shrine burn incense to the same red face, because both sides require a god whose displeasure is worse than the law.

instruction: Tell me a myth about "Gaurī".
output: Gaurī's myths are the Great Goddess's domestic epic: the mountain-daughter who becomes the universe's mother through patience — Satī reborn, Śiva out-waited, two sons made, and a calendar of festivals that still re-enacts her story in millions of homes. [The Birth] Daughter of the Mountain: The Purāṇas remember her previous body: Satī, daughter of Dakṣa, who burned herself in the sacrificial fire when her father insulted her husband Śiva — and whose scattered limbs became the Śakti-pīṭhas, the goddess's seats of power spread across the subcontinent. Reborn as Pārvatī, daughter of Himavat the mountain-king, she was Gaurī from the first: the golden girl of the peaks, destined from birth for the ash-covered wanderer who had forgotten how to love. Her name is older than her story — in the Ṛgveda gaurī is simply the feminine of gaura , the golden one of the herds — and the Purāṇas' point is that the name waited: the cow-gold of the dawn hymns becomes, in time, the skin of the Mother. The myth means the goddess keeps her bodies the way a lineage keeps its house: burned down and rebuilt, but never homeless. [The Penance] Winning the Unwinnable: When beauty and Kāma's flower-arrows failed to move Śiva in his grief for Satī, she chose tapas : years of austerity in the forest — leaves for food, rain for bath, standing on one leg through the seasons. The Śiva Purāṇa tells the test: Śiva came disguised as a stammering young brahmin and mocked her wasted devotion and her emaciated god; offered instead his own beautiful form; everything but her vow was negotiable, and she would not be dissuaded. Conquered by patience, the ascetic asked for her hand, and the gods gathered at Kailāsa for the wedding the Purāṇas tell as the universe's own — Himavat giving the bride, the Ganges and the moon attending, the mountains dancing. The myth means that in the Śākta world the courtship is reversed: it is the goddess who woos, the god who is won, and the victory belongs to work rather than grace. [The Mother] Two Sons, One Lap: Of her own body she shaped Gaṇeśa — the gatekeeper-son molded from the turmeric-and-sandalwood paste of her skin while she bathed — and of the gods' combined fire came Kārttikeya (Skanda), the war-son she raised as her own. The elephant-headed and the six-faced, the remover of obstacles and the destroyer of demons: both call her Mātā, and the texts make her maternity the point of the household's theology. Her Gaṇeśa story is hers most of all: when the boy barred Śiva from her bath and the gods fell on him, Śiva's stroke took his head — and the goddess's grief, in which the worlds shook, moved the gods to restore him with an elephant's head, the first head that came to hand. A son made without any male, defended by a mother against all heaven: the Purāṇas say her lap is where the world's two busiest gods still rest. The myth means motherhood here is sovereign — the children are made, not granted, and the making is worship. [The Festival] Gaurī Vṛata: Her living myth is the calendar: the Tṛtīyā fasts and the Gaurī festivals of Maharashtra and the South, where married women pray for their households' wellbeing and unmarried girls for good husbands — honoring the goddess who won the ideal marriage by her own effort. The rite is precise: the golden image is made, worshipped, and fed for three days; then it is carried to the river and immersed — the mother received as a daughter and released as a goddess, like a bride returning to her husband's house. In its theology the vrata re-enacts her penance in miniature: the fasting women of the festival perform, for three days, the austerity by which she performed the impossible. The myth means devotion is biography read aloud — her story, told yearly to the next generation of daughters, with turmeric for ink and the household for its page.

instruction: Tell me a myth about "Śani".
output: Śani's myths are about the impossibility of escaping consequence — even for gods, and especially for kings. [The Birth] The Shadow of the Sun: The Purāṇas make him the child of a substitution. Sūrya's wife Saṃjñā, unable to bear the sun's fierce radiance, left her shadow-double Chhāyā ('Shade') in her place and returned to her father's house; of Chhāyā were born Śani and his siblings. When the truth came out, the sun's household split forever: Śani, the shadow's son, cast so baleful a gaze that his own father's countenance darkened at their meeting — the Purāṇas explain the sun's dimming and the rift between father and son with the same myth. The estrangement is permanent and instructive: the planet of justice is the sun's shadow-child, and no brilliance in the family exempts it from audit. Every solar dynasty — every royal line claiming descent from Sūrya — carries a slow auditor in its own blood. [The Gaze] Even the Gods Are Judged: His stories form a single syllabus of the gaze. When Śani's eye fell on gods and heroes, even the great bowed: the Purāṇic and epic cycles send the afflicted into wandering, beggary, and exile, until the debt is paid in full. The Hanumān legend gives the tradition its one counter-story and its favorite: when the slow planet pressed his power on Hanumān, the mighty one simply pinned him — under foot, in some tellings under his tail — and Śani, begging release, swore never to afflict Hanumān's devotees. The tale sets the exact boundary of his empire: devotion freely given (bhakti) is the one force he will not audit. He is the one god who bows to love — and the tradition treasures the exception precisely because everything else about him is exceptionless. [The Season] Sade Sati: The living myth is the calendar. Saturn takes some two and a half years to cross each zodiac sign; when he transits the sign before, of, and after your natal moon, astrologers warn of Sade Sati — the seven-and-a-half-year season of testing. Careers stall, elders ail, patience thins; marriages and ventures are postponed; and the remedy prescribed is the same from Maharashtra to Tamil Nadu: sesame-oil lamps lit before his image, iron worn or donated, crows fed before breakfast, and the Saturday fast kept. Varāhamihira had already codified the planet's stern nature in the sixth century, and the observance has only grown since. The most-followed planetary cult in India is his, and its genius is this: fear of the slow planet has been converted into a weekly discipline — a hygiene of humility that outlasts any single transit. [Late kathā] King Vikramāditya's Seven and a Half Years: A late kathā cycle — preserved in the sthala-māhātmyas and oral tellings rather than the early Purāṇas — sends Śani to test the one king no planet should touch. Vikramāditya, whose judgment was proverbially just, once slighted the slow planet, and Śani sat upon his fortunes for seven and a half years: the king sold himself, lost his kingdom, was boiled in oil (saved by the goddess), cut limb from limb in the tale's grisliest episodes, and emerged at the end of the period with his justice intact and his kingdom restored, having learned what the poor learn daily. The tale is folklore, not scripture, and the scholarship says so; but its structure is exact Śani doctrine: even the best man owes a term of patience, and the account closes precisely on schedule. It is the one Śani story India tells with a smile.

instruction: Tell me a myth about "Ọrun".
output: Ọrun's myths are the architecture of Yoruba cosmology: how heaven was connected to earth, how every soul is commissioned before birth, and how the traffic between the two realms has never once stopped. [The Descent] The Chain to Earth: In the beginning there was only sky. Below Ọrun lay the primeval waters, and on the water floated nothing but the command of Olódùmarè. The creation account recorded across Yorubaland — set down by the Rev. Samuel Johnson in the early twentieth century and analyzed by Bolaji Idowu — tells how Olódùmarè sent the orisha down a golden chain from heaven with a hen, a chameleon, and a handful of sand. Where the sand fell and the hen scratched, a mound rose from the flood: Ilé-Ifẹ̀, 'the house that spreads', the navel of the earth. The chain did not come back up; it anchored heaven to the new ground, and orisha, ancestors, and newborn souls have traveled it in both directions ever since. The myth means that Yoruba cosmology is a story of migration. Every birth repeats the first descent, and the road between Ọrun and ayé has never once been closed. [The Choice] The Choosing of Orí: Before a child is born, the Ifá corpus teaches, its soul kneels in Ọrun at the workshop of Ajala, the celestial potter, to choose its orí — the inner head that is its personal destiny. The odu narratives (see Abimbola, Ifá: An Exposition of Ifá Literary Corpus, and Bascom, Ifá Divination) tell of souls who chose carelessly, who bargained, or who arrived too late and had to take whatever heads remained. The choice is then sealed and the memory wiped: the child is born carrying an unread contract, and life is the slow reading of it. This is why Yoruba religion lavishes its attention on the head itself — offerings are made to the orí, the physical crown of the body, the one shrine every person carries everywhere. The myth means that destiny is chosen, not imposed — but chosen by a self you no longer remember being. [The Traffic] Souls on the Road: The Yoruba cosmos runs on commuting. Orisha descend to mount their priests in trance; ancestors return as Egúngún masquerades; the dead are reborn, and the abíkú — 'born to die' — are the children who keep commuting, slipping back to Ọrun young and being sent down again until their earthly parents find a charm to bind them to stay. The Ifá verses speak of these journeys as ordinary travel — dangerous, expensive, but routine — along the same chain-road the first orisha descended (Abimbola; Bascom; Drewal). The dead do not leave the world; they change direction. The myth means that Ọrun is not a distant heaven but an adjacent one — the next town, not the next world — and the border is crossed so often that every lineage keeps stories of the crossing. [The Return] The Egúngún Come Back: The most dramatic proof that the dead commute is the Egúngún: the masked, robed masqueraders who appear at the great festivals and are understood — not metaphorically but literally — as ancestors returned from Ọrun for a visit. The cloth-wrapped figure may never be touched or unmasked, for the cloth is both its embassy and its disguise; its voice is disguised, its blessing is sought by the whole lineage, and its displeasure is feared more than any chief's (Drewal, Pemberton and Abiodun, Yoruba: Nine Centuries of African Art and Thought, 1989). The Egúngún societies keep the costumes as lineage treasures handed down the generations, and the appearance of the ancestors is the high point of the ritual year. The institution means that heaven maintains a postal service: the dead can still speak, still bless, still scold — they simply cannot stay, and the message always comes wrapped in cloth.

instruction: Tell me a myth about "Xiuhtēcuhtli".
output: Xiuhtēcuhtli's myths are the calendar's: the fire that must be renewed, and the darkness that waits if it is not. [The Cycle] The Drilling of the New Fire: At the close of each 52-year cycle (the xiuhmolpilli, the 'tying of the years'), the Aztec world extinguished every flame: households went dark, pots were smashed, debts were settled, and the people waited on their rooftops, fasting, watching the sky. Sahagún's informants told him the terror plainly — if the Pleiades ( tianquiztli ) had not yet crossed the zenith by midnight, some said, the sun would not rise and the demons of darkness would come down to eat the last men (Florentine Codex, Book 7). When the star-merchants passed, the fire-priests climbed Huixachtlan, the Hill of the Star, and drilled the new flame on a captive's chest with the fire-sticks. The fire caught; a runner carried it down to the Templo Mayor; relays carried it to every city, and every hearth in the empire was relit from the one flame. Time is a fire that must be relit by hands — a civilization whose calendar had an ignition switch, and one night in fifty-two years when everyone held their breath. [The Elder] Huehueteotl, the Old One: Under his other name he is the oldest thing in the cosmos: Huehueteotl, 'the Old, Old God,' the wrinkled figure who carries the fire-bowl on his bent back, present before the suns were set in motion. Sahagún lists him among the primordial gods (Florentine Codex, Book 1), and the tonalamatl — the book of days — set him at the head of the first trecena, 1-Cipactli: the count of time begins under his sign. The Aztecs put him at the center of the world's four directions, the fire-pillar between the levels, and every domestic hearth was his shrine: the three stones of the kitchen, the offering of copal before the pot went on. It is the smallest and the greatest cult at once — the god of the kitchen who is also the god of the calendar, worshipped in the millions of hearths no army could ever close. The Old God never needed a temple because he had already been given one: the floor of every house. [The Nourishment] What Fire Asks: The codices and the friars' informants record his contract: fire feeds the world and feeds on it. Offerings of copal, of the first fruits, of the tongue and the heart — the great feeding of the flames at state ceremonies, and the fire-priests' own austerity, searing and fasting before the brazier (Florentine Codex, Books 1–2; Durán, Book of the Gods). Xiuhtēcuhtli's priests walked barefoot through fire and passed the year keeping his vigil; in the empire's hard logic, the highest offering was the heart, because fire is the one creditor who always collects. The theology is a merchant's ledger with cosmic stakes: light, heat, and the year on one pan of the scale; copal, bread, and life on the other — and the god, being fire, cannot be cheated, only fed. To cook dinner was to pay him; to let the hearth die was to default. His is the oldest bargain in the Americas, and it is still open. [The Double] The Turquoise Serpent: Fire made animal: the xiuhcoatl , the 'turquoise serpent,' is Xiuhtēcuhtli's nahual — his animal double — and the burning weapon of the sun itself (Florentine Codex, Book 7, where the fire-serpent blazes among the sky's omens). In stone he appears as a rattlesnake with a snout of flames, poised to strike: on the great imperial monuments, on sacrificial vessels, in the frieze of burning tails that runs along the precinct walls. When the sun wages war on the moon and the stars at the beginning of the age, it is the xiuhcoatl he throws — a serpent of fire that slices the night open. Iconography does what myth sometimes cannot: the serpent is what movement looks like when it burns, fire given a spine, a rattle, and a will. The Old God carries the bowl; the serpent is what spills out of it when the world needs burning rather than warming.

instruction: Tell me a myth about "Plūtō".
output: Plūtō's Roman myths retell the Greek cycle with a merchant's accent: the underworld as treasury as much as tribunal. Ovid gives the rape of Proserpina, Virgil and Ovid the one descent that moved him, Apollodorus the thieves who failed, Hesiod the older wealth-god beneath the name, and Rome's own calendars the gate that opened three days a year. [The Taking] Proserpina in the Meadow: Ovid tells the Roman rape with a landscape's grief (Metamorphoses 5.385–571). In the meadow below Henna, Proserpina gathers flowers — violets, lilies, crocuses — and laughs when the narcissus springs up, a trap set by Venus for the sake of her son Cupid's empire. The ground opens; Plūtō, 'the lord of the dark', carries her down through the pool of Cyane, whose waters, forbidden to speak, dissolve the nymph herself into a spring. Cerēs searches with torches lit at Etna's flame; she turns the mocking boy Ascalabus into a spotted gecko, and opens the cattle of the old man who sheltered her until he curses his own gift. Jupiter arbitrates: the girl who has eaten is bound to the deep. Six pomegranate seeds — or one, in the older Greek telling — divide the year between mother and husband, spring and summer above, autumn and winter below. The myth is Rome's charter for the agricultural year: what is buried is not lost, and what returns must first have descended. [The Musician] Orpheus Charms the Deep: When Orpheus lost Eurydice to a snake, he did what no mortal does: he went down singing. Virgil's account (Georgics 4.453–527) makes the underworld itself soften — the Danaids' urn rests, Ixion's wheel stands still, Tityos' vultures pause — and Ovid adds (Metamorphoses 10.1–85) that even the king and queen of the deep wept, a first for both. The condition was set: lead her up, and do not look back until you stand in daylight. At the very border, love or doubt turned his head, and she was reclaimed — a second death, and this one his own doing. The Romans read the myth as Plūtō's one audited exception: the deep can be moved, exactly once, and only by the thing it does not possess — a mortal voice persuasive enough to make law pause. Every later descent of European poetry, Dante's, Monteverdi's, Gluck's, walks the same road under the same rule. [The Thieves] Theseus and Pirithous on the Throne of Forgetfulness: Not all who descended came to sing. Pirithous, having rashly sworn to marry a daughter of the highest god, persuaded his friend Theseus to descend with him and carry off Proserpina herself (Apollodorus, Bibliotheca 2.5.12; Epitome 1.24). They sat upon the Chair of Forgetfulness and could not rise, their limbs bound by serpents, until Heracles — come below on his own errand for the hound — wrenched Theseus free and left Pirithous fixed in the stone of the deep, where some say he remains. The failed abduction is the myth's own footnote to the wisdom of Solon, who warned Croesus that no man may count himself happy before the end. The moral Plūtō keeps is plain and grammatical rather than cruel: the dead belong below, the living above, and the queen between is not a prize but a treaty. The exceptions are famous precisely because they are singular — one singer admitted, two thieves impaled, and the border back in order by morning. [The Wealth] Plūtus the Giver: His older Greek identity is Ploutos, Wealth — born to Demeter and the mortal Iasion 'in the thrice-ploughed fallow' (Hesiod, Theogony 969–974), and granted by Demeter to bless 'all mortal men' in the Homeric Hymn to Demeter (486–489). The folk logic is geological: wealth — grain, ore, treasure — comes from under the earth, and so the lord of under the earth is its giver. Aristophanes' comedy Plutus made him a blind old steward whose healed sight showers the just with gold — a fantasy Athens understood as precisely that. Rome kept the word's double truth: as Plūtō he is the treasury, as Dis the grave, and the same soil feeds both accounts. No ancient ever mistook him for safe; but properly approached he was the most reliable of gods — the only one whose gifts were audited every harvest and whose invoices were paid in seed corn. [The Gate] The Mundus and the Secular Games: Rome's own door to his kingdom stood at the Tarentum in the Campus Martius, a roofed pit — the mundus — opened by the pontiffs only three days a year, when, as Festus and Servius (ad Aen. 3.104) report, 'the door of the gloomy god is open' and no public business is done. Its greatest rite came in the republic's darkest hour: in 249 BCE the Sibylline books ordered the first Ludi Saeculares, sacrifices and games to Dis Pater and Proserpina to turn the First Punic War (Valerius Maximus 2.4.5; Zosimus 2.1–3). Augustus revived the games in 17 BCE with a liturgy preserved on stone (CIL VI 32323): after the daylight offerings to the Fates, the Ilithyiae, and Earth Mother, the city sacrificed at night, on the Tarentum, to Dis and Proserpina. The gate-myth is the state cult in miniature — Rome does not live with its underworld; it schedules it, opens it three days a year, and closes the door before the business of living resumes.

instruction: Tell me a myth about "Mixcōātl".
output: Mixcōātl's myths are the Aztec origin-story in one figure: the wilderness god who taught the city-builders how to hunt, whose star-road they followed south, and whose household quarrel is written nightly across his own body. The sources are colonial but faithful — Sahagún's informants, the indigenous annals, the picture-histories — and where they disagree, the disagreement is itself instructive. [The Road] The Serpent of Stars: The Chichimec tribes who became the Aztec nobility followed his road: the Milky Way, which the Nahuatl called Mixcōātl, the Cloud Serpent, slithering nightly across the sky. The migrating peoples read their path in his body — the desert crossed by the serpent's light — and when they founded Tenochtitlan they enthroned the wilderness-guide among the city's great gods, the god of where they had come from. The migration theology is the point: an empire founded by wanderers reads its own founding as a following, and the chronicle tradition keeps the memory of tribes who lived by the hunt before they had fields. Mixcōātl's body across the sky is the oldest road-map of Mexican legitimacy — the empire's charter written in stars, followed long before it was written. [The Gift] The Bow of the Chichimecs: As Camaxtle, he gave the wandering tribes the bow and the fire-drill — the two tools of a life in motion. The city never forgot the debt: in the fourteenth month, Quecholli, 'the precious feather', the hunters' own liturgy filled the temple precinct — arrows, nets and deer brought to the god's altar, the rite of the hunt performed at the heart of the greatest city of the valley (Sahagún, Florentine Codex, Book 2). The coronation tradition dressed the new ruler in the insignia of war and the hunt, and the tlatoani's wars opened under the god's banners. The weapons on the altar are the archaeology of gratitude: once a year the city laid down the tools that fed it before it had fields — an empire paying honest tribute to its own wilderness. [The Father] Father of the Four Hundred: In a tradition the later sources preserve, the Centzon Huitznāhua — the Four Hundred Southerners, the star-host — are the children of Mixcōātl with Coatlicue; the mother then conceived Huitzilopochtli from the ball of feathers, and the four hundred, led by Coyolxāuhqui, came up the serpent mountain to kill her. The newborn god emerged fully armed and cut his sister to pieces on the slope of Coatepec (Florentine Codex; Leyenda de los Soles, Codex Chimalpopoca). The sources are not unanimous — the great codices name no father for the four hundred — but where the genealogy holds, its meaning is exact. The god of the hunt is the father of both armies of the night sky: the war the Aztecs fought daily, dawn against stars, is in his household a family quarrel, written nightly across his own starry body. [Genealogy] Father of the Plumed One: The genealogies of the high god are no tidier. In one line of early colonial accounts — the Historia de los Mexicanos por sus pinturas — the wandering hunter Camaxtli, Mixcōātl by another name, is made the father of Topiltzin Ce Ácatl Quetzalcōātl, the priest-king of Tula: the wilderness god fathering the lord of civilization. The Anales de Cuauhtitlān names a different father, Totepeuh, and records the mother's name as Chimalmān. The disagreement is itself the evidence: the Mexica past was a negotiated archive, and each city and each chronicler tied the great names to its own charter. What recurs is the pairing — the hunter and the plumed priest — as if the tradition knew that civilization is always somebody's wandering, settled at last. To stand as even the possible father of Quetzalcōātl is to anchor the entire Toltec inheritance in the hunt; the genealogy is less a family tree than a constitution.

instruction: Tell me a myth about "Ọbà".
output: Ọba's myths are domestic tragedy told as hydrology: the co-wife's war that became a river and a lake. The cycle survives in Yoruba oral tradition — oríkì praise-poetry and the folktale corpus recorded by Bascom and others — and crossed the Atlantic to become the diaspora's parable of the polygamous household. [The oral corpus] Three Wives, One Storm: Ṣàngó, the thunder-king, took three river-wives: Ọba the senior, Ọṣun the beloved, and Ọya the storm-sharer. The cycle survives in the oríkì praise-poetry and the folktale corpus recorded by Yoruba specialists from the mid-twentieth century — Wande Abimbola's editions of Ifá verse, William Bascom's collections of tales — and in the diaspora the three wives became the standard cast of every household drama. The tellings agree on the shape: Ọba, the first wife, watched her husband's love flow downhill to Ọṣun, and love that is watched curdles into jealousy. In the fullest tellings Ọba schemed against Ọṣun — and Ọṣun, the shrewdest of the household, let the scheme come to her first and answered it with one that would end the rivalry. The seniority that should have protected Ọba is exactly what the story burns: in the thunder-king's house, the first wife is the last to be believed, and the household's peace is purchased with her humiliation. [The folktale cycle] The Ear in the Soup: The trap is the cycle's most famous scene, preserved in the folktale collections (Bascom, African Folktales) and endlessly retold in the diaspora. Ọṣun — in some tellings Ọya — let fall that the king loved, above all things, the taste of his beloved's ear in his soup. Ọba, desperate to be loved again, cut off her own ear and cooked it for him. When the bowl came before Ṣàngó and the trick stood revealed, his disgust and rage drove her from the palace; the co-wives laughed, and Ọba fled north weeping, her maimed head hidden under her crown and her hair. The sources disagree on which co-wife set the trap and on how much of the truth Ṣàngó ever learned — the oral tradition keeps the variants alive rather than settling them. What every telling keeps is the ear: the organ of obedience, cut off to buy a love that was never for sale. The myth is the Yoruba anatomy of jealousy — not the villain's punishment, but the victim's self-mutilation, and the crown she designed afterward to live with it. [The lake] The Water of Her Grief: Her tears became her realm. In the tellings, Ọba's flight ended in the water that still bears her name: the Ọba River of Yorubaland, and the lake of her worship, where her priests keep her cult and the faithful mourn with her on her appointed days. The geography is the theology — a goddess exiled from the palace takes the river as her palace, and the quiet water outlasts the thunder. The tradition preserves one firm ritual rule from the household war: Ọba and Ọya, the senior wife and the storm-sharer, can never be honored in the same shrine; some quarrels the orisha themselves decline to reconcile. But her people read the ending differently than the palace did: storms pass, the river stays. The senior wife outlasted the storm-god's louder wives by becoming the thing the storm cannot be — permanent, low, and always arriving. [The diaspora] Obá Crosses the Water: The wives' cycle crossed the Middle Passage with the orisha, and in the Americas it acquired its second life. In Cuba's Santería she is Obá, syncretized with Santa Catalina de Alejandría — whose wheel she shares, and whose feast day, 25 November, became hers; her cult proved strongest in Matanzas province, where her initiates arrange the hair forward over the ears exactly as she arranged hers, the gesture intact across four hundred years and an ocean. In Brazil's Candomblé, Obá keeps her river and her covered ear, and the three-wives drama remains the standard parable told to explain the polygamous household's wars and survivors. Robert Farris Thompson documented how thoroughly the diaspora kept her iconography — the hidden ear is legible in Lucumí altars from Havana to Miami. The crossing is itself the last episode of the myth: the wife the palace expelled became the orisha the ocean could not drown, carried in the hair of women who had lost everything else and still arranged it, forward, covering, dignified.

instruction: Tell me a myth about "Ašavahišta".
output: Ašavahišta’s mythology is the Gathas’ own theology made personal: truth not as an idea but as an immortal who must be fed, fought for, and kept alight. Every fire-temple flame is his dwelling, every honest word his territory, and the final fire of the world’s end his last and clearest sermon. [The Council] The Bounteous Immortals: The Avesta’s great hymn-names them: Vohu Manah (Good Mind), Aša Vahišta (Best Truth), Xšaθra Vairya (Chosen Power), Spenta Ārmaiti (Holy Devotion), Haurvatāt (Wholeness), Amərətāt (Immortality) — the Amesha Spentas, the Bounteous Immortals who are at once Ahura Mazda’s powers and persons, his council and his limbs. Ašavahišta is the second, named beside Good Mind in the Gathas’ own theology: he is the Truth the Good Mind thinks, the order every right word and deed must match. In the earliest stratum he is not one power among others but the standard they all serve — the thing the two spirits contested at creation (Yasna 30.3–5), and the stake of the entire cosmic war between Aša and Druj, Truth and the Lie. Later tradition systematised the six into a household of creation, giving each an element, a metal, a month, a day; but the Gathas already meet him as a presence, not a principle — an immortal who must be fed with rightness and fought for, or lost. [The Element] The Fire of Aša: His element is fire — not the destroyer but the tester. The Avesta gives fire to Aša Vahišta as his very domain: the altar-flame through which prayers rise — the Yasna calls it the most swift and powerful force of Ahura Mazda (Yasna 34.4) — and the ordeal-fire through which innocence is proven. In the Gathas, fire is the wisdom that discerns the true from the false in thought, word, and deed: swift to reward, swift to punish. Every Zoroastrian fire-temple keeps his presence: the flame tended in an urn for centuries without interruption is, in the faith, Ašavahišta made visible — the light that does not lie. Priests feed it five times a day with sandalwood and recite his verse over it; the laity honour it by refusing to defile it with breath, smoke, or the touch of the impure. A god of truth needs no statue: his icon is the one thing every honest eye can audit — a flame. [The Battle] Truth Against the Lie: The Gathas’ whole drama is his: Aša against Druj — Truth against the Lie, order against deceit. “Now the two spirits, the twins known for their two thoughts, words and deeds… the better and the evil,” sing the Gathas (Yasna 30.3–4); at creation the good spirit chose aša and the evil one chose not-aša, and every human being inherits the same choosing, daily, in the only battlefield the cosmos finally has — speech. The righteous advance the world by good thought, good word, good deed; the deceitful tear at the fabric. Ašavahišta is therefore not a passive abstraction but the war’s front line: every true word spoken is his ground gained, every lie his ground lost. This is why Zaraθuštra’s own great crisis, in the Gathas, is not defeat by enemies but doubt among the deceitful (Yasna 46) — and why the creed’s most-recited prayer is his, the ašem-vohū: “Aša is the best, it is happiness — happy is the one who is pure in Aša for the sake of best Aša.” [The Fire] The Final Ordeal: At the end, the texts say, the world is tested by molten metal: a river of fire through which all humanity must pass — to the righteous, warm milk; to the deceitful, burning (Yasna 30.7–8; the Greater Bundahišn). Ašavahišta presides: his fire is the last instrument of the truth he has always been. The fravašis, the guardian spirits of the righteous, prepare the way; the Saoshyant, the coming Saviour, administers the test; and after it the world is made “wonderful” — deathless, without decay. The eschaton is not destruction but assay: the universe finally read for what it is. It is the weighing of the heart written in fire for all souls at once — the same scale, held at last over the whole world. That the final mercy should be molten is the faith’s deepest paradox: the judge of truth and the refiner of metal are one.

instruction: Tell me a myth about "Ádōnis".
output: Ádōnis's myth turns on beauty that cannot be kept. He is desired, born, killed, and divided — a story the Greeks borrowed from the dying-god cults of the Near East and made their own, and a women's rite of lament that gives rare direct voice to female grief in the classical city. [Origin] The Myrrh Tree Splits: Myrrha, daughter of King Kinyras of Cyprus — or of Assyria, in the older eastern versions — conceived a hopeless passion for her own father. Her nurse smuggled her into the royal bed on a night when the king's wife was away at a festival of Demeter; when Kinyras discovered the truth by lamplight he reached for his sword, and the gods transformed the fleeing girl into a myrrh tree (Apollodorus, Bibliotheca 3.14.4; Ovid, Metamorphoses 10.298–502). Ten months later the bark split and the infant Adonis was born — Ovid's loveliest detail has the tree tear 'like a girl's body opening in childbirth'. The tale makes his beauty the fruit of transgression: he is born where the boundary of the family was crossed, and his whole career will be spent on boundaries — between women and men, love and death, the earth and the underworld. [Judgment] Divided Between Two Queens: Aphrodite hid the infant in a chest and entrusted him to Persephone, queen of the dead — but Persephone opened the chest, looked, and refused to give him back. Zeus judged between the goddesses: Adonis would spend a third of the year with Persephone below, a third with Aphrodite above, and a third as he chose — and he chose Aphrodite, for love of her beauty and the living world (Apollodorus 3.14.4). Sappho preserves the women's lament for the dying season — 'tender Adonis is dying, Cyprian; what shall we do?' (fr. 140a) — and a variant has the division decided by lots weighed on a scale, Aphrodite cheating with her girdle to tip the outcome. The myth is transparent seasonal allegory: the year itself divided between the queen of life and the queen of death. Its honesty is the point — desire and mortality get exactly equal terms. [Death] The Boar on the Mountain: Despite Aphrodite's warnings, Adonis hunted a wild boar. The beast gored him in the thigh — some say the boar was Aphrodite's own anger made flesh, or the jealous Ares in animal shape; others blame the youth's recklessness, for he hunted what his protector feared (Ovid, Metamorphoses 10.705–739). He died in Aphrodite's arms, and where his blood struck the earth the anemone sprang up — red, wind-shaken, and short-lived, a flower that nods in the slightest breeze, as Ovid says, 'because it grew from tears'. Persephone received him below, and the goddess's grief became the template for the women's rite. The death of the beautiful hunter is one of antiquity's most retold scenes precisely because it refuses consolation: not resurrection, not apotheosis — only a flower, and a goddess weeping over it every year. [Cult] The Gardens of Adonis: The Adonia was the women's festival of Adonis, attested across the Greek world: at Athens the rooftop ritual mocked by Aristophanes (Lysistrata 387–398); at Alexandria the grand procession of a wax effigy that Theocritus sets in the mouths of two Syracusan women (Idyll 15); and in Syria the temple rites at Byblos that Lucian describes, where the god's death is mourned and his resurrection celebrated (On the Syrian Goddess 6). Its signature rite was the 'gardens of Adonis': lettuces, fennel, and quick-sprouting herbs planted in shallow trays, forced into brief green life, then carried to the rooftops to wither in the sun — miniature lives enacted and lost within days. Plato's Socrates borrows the image (Phaedrus 276b) to dismiss writing itself: the written word, he says, is like a garden of Adonis — pretty, rootless, dead quickly. The cult gives rare direct evidence of women's religious life in the classical city.

instruction: Tell me a myth about "Balor".
output: Balor's dossier is short and total: he exists in the tradition to be the thing that must be brought down. Cath Maige Tuired gives him the war's most famous single stroke, the Lebor Gabála fixes his lineage and his wife's vengeance, and the Donegal oral tradition supplies the prophecy, the tower, and the stolen cow that the medieval manuscripts only glance at. The sources disagree on the details and never on the architecture: a gaze that can only destroy, contained at terrible cost, and turned home at last by his own blood. [Lebor Gabála Érenn] Balor Son of Dot, Grandson of Nét: The book of invasions fixes Balor's place before it tells his deeds: Balor mac Doit meic Néit, 'Balor son of Dot, grandson of Nét', king of the Fomorians — the sea-going race who had pressed on Ireland since the age of the Nemedians, exacting tribute from the outer islands. His wife was Cethlenn of the crooked teeth, whose spear struck the Dagda at Mag Tuired; the Lebor Gabála records that the All-Father afterwards died of Cethlenn's wound — the settled price of Balor's war, long counted in the tally of the battle. His daughter was Ethniu, and by Cian — in the Lebor Gabála's genealogy the son of the healer Dian Cécht — she bore Lugh, the Samildánach, equally skilled in all the arts. Thus the Fomorian king was the grandfather of the Túatha Dé Danann's deliverer: the genealogy on which the whole tragedy of Mag Tuired turns, and the reason no tower, sea, or tax could keep the grandson away. [Cath Maige Tuired] How the Eye Was Poisoned: Cath Maige Tuired explains the weapon before it uses it. Balor had a destructive eye, never opened except on a battlefield, and four men were needed to raise its lid with a polished handle that passed through it; any army that eye looked upon was made worthless, though it were many thousands strong. The poison had a childhood. When Balor was a boy, his father's druids were brewing a charm, and the boy looked in on the work; the fumes of the brew rose and struck the eye, and from that day its gaze was venom. The detail is the tradition's whole theory of the figure in one image: power taken in unguarded, as a child takes in smoke, and carried incurably for a lifetime. What entered by accident becomes the foundation of a tyranny — and a tyranny that must hire four men to open its own weapon has already told you how it will end. [The Oral Tradition (Tory Island)] The Tower and the Prophecy: The manuscripts agree that Ethniu was Balor's daughter and Lugh's mother; how that came to be is told by the oral tradition of the north-west, collected in the nineteenth century on and around Tory Island — Balor's sea-girt fortress off the Donegal coast. A druid foretold that Balor would die by the hand of his own grandson, and the king answered the prophecy with masonry: he locked his daughter Eithne in a tower on the rock, with twelve matrons to keep every man from her sight. The doom came in by the door the theft opened. Balor coveted the Glas Gaibhnenn, the grey-green cow of Cian, and stole her across the water; Cian crossed to Tory for redress, and with the druidess Biróg's aid won into the tower in woman's dress and to Eithne's side. When the child was born Balor had him cast into the sea — but the sea gave him back, fostered and hidden, until a young stranger came to Nuadu's court at Tara and was asked what art he practiced. The question the Fomorians could not answer had been growing up under their own doom all along. [Cath Maige Tuired] The Sling-Stone at Mag Tuired: At the second battle of Mag Tuired the armies broke each other all day, and then Balor came against the Túatha Dé Danann with the Fomorian host, destroying and slaughtering. He commanded that the lid of his eye be raised, so that he might blast the enemy with its look — and the four men set the polished handle to the lid. It was then that Lugh cast a sling-stone at him, which carried the eye backward through his head, so that it was his own host that looked into it. Balor fell on top of the Fomorian fighting-men, and twenty-seven of them died beneath his side. The weapon the Fomorians had built their tyranny on spent its last gaze on its owners — and the battle turned with the eye. The Túatha Dé Danann took back the tribute from the defeated host, and the power of the Fomorians over Ireland was broken for good. A gaze made to wither enemies had met the one thing it could not wither: a small stone, aimed.

instruction: Tell me a myth about "Bhaiṣajyaguru".
output: The stories of Bhaiṣajyaguru are sutras, not epics: scripture built from his twelve vows, his lapis-lit eastern paradise, and the liturgy of healing his name still powers across Asia. [The Twelve Vows] What He Promised Before He Was Buddha: The Bhaiṣajyaguruvaidūryaprabhārājasūtra — in Xuanzang's Chinese translation of 650 CE (T. 450), the standard form in East Asia — first tells what the future Medicine Buddha swore as a bodhisattva: twelve vows. He would make his body shine like lapis lazuli to dispel the darkness of ignorance; he would give beings 'inexhaustible' wealth of goods; he would set those on false paths on the bodhisattva road; he would restore broken precepts and heal 'bodies incomplete' — the blind, the lame, the deaf; he would cure the destitute sick and free the imprisoned from their chains; he would feed the hungry and clothe the naked. One vow — that women who wish it be reborn as men — belongs to its century, and modern translators note it without flinching. The list is the myth: a buddha defined entirely by his promises, and a definition of healing broad enough to include poverty, fear, and error along with disease. [The Eastern Paradise] The World of Lapis Light: Having fulfilled the vows, Bhaiṣajyaguru presides over the eastern pure land the sutras call Vaidūryanirbhāsa — 'Pure Lapis-Lazuli Radiance'. Its ground is vaidūrya itself, transparent as glass; its avenues are bounded by cords of jewels; streams run through it sounding the teaching, and music plays without any musician touching an instrument — Yijing's longer translation of 707 (T. 451) spells the geography out in loving detail. There is no trace of the lower destinies — no hells, no hungry ghosts, no animal births — and beings in difficulty who hear his name and remember it are, the sutra promises, rescued at the moment of death. Devotees who wish it may also choose rebirth in Amitābha's western paradise; the two buddhas are colleagues, not rivals. If Amitābha's west is the sunset of this life's grief, Bhaiṣajyaguru's east is its remedy: a paradise designed like a hospital, staffed like a pharmacy. [The Translations] How the Medicine Master Crossed Asia: The cult rode translation. Xuanzang brought the shorter Sutra of the Merit of the Original Vows of Bhaiṣajyaguru back from India and rendered it in 650, fixing the Chinese name Yàoshī Liúlíguāng Rúlái — 'Medicine Master, Lapis-Lazuli Light, Thus-Come-One.' A generation later, in 707, the pilgrim Yijing translated a longer sibling text (T. 451), the Sutra of the Seven Medicine Buddhas , which surrounds Bhaiṣajyaguru with six other healing buddhas and preserves his healing dhāraṇī — a string of Sanskrit syllables still recited over the sick in Tibetan, Chinese, and Japanese monasteries. From China the sutra passed to Korea and, by the early seventh century, to Japan, where the Medicine Master's name contracted to the two syllables every Japanese still knows: Yakushi. A name's journey is the tradition's own map: Sanskrit to Chinese to Japanese in three generations, with the pharmacy intact at every border. [The Attendants] Two Lights and Twelve Generals: Bhaiṣajyaguru never travels alone. The triad tradition gives him two bodhisattvas — Sūryaprabha, 'Solar Radiance,' and Candraprabha, 'Lunar Radiance' (Nikkō and Gakkō in Japan) — the sun and moon standing at a healer's shoulders. Below them serve twelve yakṣa generals, each commanding seven thousand spirit troops, who swore before the Buddha to protect anyone who keeps the sutra: Kumbhīra, Vajra, Mihira, and nine more, their rolls recited in the liturgy to this day. Iconography fixed the ensemble early: the Medicine Buddha sits in monk's robes, his right hand in the gesture of gift-giving or holding a sprig of myrobalan, his left cradling the medicine bowl — the only major buddha whose standard attribute is a drug. Solar light, lunar light, and a dozen bodyguards: the myth's arithmetic says healing is never a private act — it comes escorted, lit, and guarded.

instruction: Tell me a myth about "Bifrǫst".
output: Bifrǫst is the one road between the worlds of gods and men, and every story told of it is a story about passage: who may cross, what the crossing costs, and what happens when the road itself gives way. Snorri describes it as the strongest of all constructions and yet builds its destruction into the end of the world. The poems of the Codex Regius, which read the name as Bilrǫst , already know that the bridge will break. Around it gather Heimdallr the watchman, the daily assize at Urðr's well, and the solitary figure of Þórr, who is forbidden the span and wades the rivers instead. [Gylfaginning] The Bridge of Three Colors: Gangleri asks how the gods pass from heaven to earth, and Hárr answers that they built Bifrǫst from earth to heaven: a bridge of three colors, very strong, and made with more skill and cunning than any other work. The red in the rainbow, Hárr explains, is burning fire, so that the frost-giants and mountain-giants cannot mount into heaven over the bridge. At the bridge's head, where it reaches the edge of heaven, stands Himinbjǫrg , the hall of Heimdallr, the watchman of the gods. He needs less sleep than a bird, sees a hundred leagues by night as by day, and hears the grass growing on the earth and the wool on the sheep. Beside him waits the Gjallarhorn , whose blast is heard in all worlds. The bridge is the strongest thing in the world, and it is guarded by the one god who never sleeps — the Edda's way of saying that the way between worlds is always open, and never safe. [Grímnismál] The Daily Ride to Judgment: Every day the Æsir ride up over Ásbrú — the Æsir-bridge — on their named horses, to sit in judgment at the ash Yggdrasill. But Þórr does not ride. Grímnismál says that he must wade the rivers Kǫrmt and Ǫrmt and the two Kerlaugar each day on his way to the doomstead, for the Æsir-bridge stands all aflame and the holy waters seethe. Snorri gives the same exception a physical cause: the thunder-god's passage, with the heat and weight of his thunder, would break the span. The strongest of the gods is thus the one who walks — the bridge that carries everyone else cannot carry him. The daily wading is Þórr's liturgy: the god of the common people keeps both feet on the ground, even on his way to judgment. [Ragnarǫk] The Shattering at Vígríðr: When the end comes, Heimdallr stands and winds the Gjallarhorn to wake the gods. Surtr advances from the south with fire, and behind him ride the sons of Muspell toward the field of Vígríðr . They ride over Bifrǫst, and the bridge breaks beneath them. The poets of the Codex Regius knew it already: Fáfnismál says that Bilrǫst breaks as the hosts ride across, and the horses must swim in the surge, and Grípisspá repeats the prophecy. The road between worlds is the first great work of the gods to fall — the connection is severed before the battle is even joined. That the bridge fails before the gods do is the Edda's hardest structural insight: connection is the first casualty of the end, and even Muspell's sons cross it only once. [Völuspá] The Watchman's Hearing: The bridge's safety rests on one insomniac. Völuspá says the seeress knows Heimdallr's hearing, hidden beneath the radiant holy tree, and remembers him drinking the good mead where he stands (stanzas 26–27); Hyndluljóð gives him nine wave-mothers (stanza 35). At Himinbjǫrg he keeps the Gjallarhorn, whose blast runs through all worlds (Gylfaginning). Lokasenna measures the cost of the post: Loki taunts the watchman as the whitest and most doomed of gods, fated to stand drenched and unsleeping at his door forever. Heimdallr answers — and keeps the bridge. The Edda's most eloquent structure is guarded by its least eloquent god: the bridge is only as real as the one who never stops listening for it. His nine wave-mothers make him a child of everything that moves, set to watch over everything that must stay.

instruction: Tell me a myth about "Cáishén".
output: Cáishén's mythology is young and openly composite . The cult is a Song-dynasty growth over older roots, and every avatar brings his own story: a Ming novel supplies the marshal, a Han historian the heartless minister, merchants the retired sage. The tradition never pretends otherwise — and its honesty is part of its power. [The Title] One Office, Many Gods: The two characters 財神 simply mean 'god of wealth' — a title, not a personal name, and the tradition treats it that way. There is no canonical birth-story of Cáishén; instead, the office has been filled, again and again, by figures the culture wished to honor: a loyal minister, a canonized marshal, an honest merchant, even the red-faced war-god Guan Yu in some regions. The clearest early attestations belong to the Song dynasty (960–1279), when China's commercial revolution made wealth a god worth petitioning; the Ming-era compendium Santjiao soushen daquan and the novel Fengshen Yanyi then fixed the cast of avatars. The sources disagree openly about who 'really' holds the office — which is the honest thing for a god of fortune, since every trade, region, and dynasty wants to claim him. A god with many faces is a god owned by many classes; Cáishén's multiplicity is the theology of a civilization that decided prosperity itself was divine. [The Marshal] Zhao Gongming on the Black Tiger: The fullest avatar-story comes from the Ming novel Fengshen Yanyi ( Investiture of the Gods ). During the fall of the Shang dynasty, Zhao Gongming , a hermit of Mount Emei, comes down to aid the doomed house with his black tiger, his iron whip, and his magic pearls; battle after battle turns on his power, until Jiang Ziya's side breaks him with Lu Ya's sorcery — an effigy of straw pierced by arrows. When the war ends and the fallen are canonized, Jiang Ziya invests the dead marshal as the God of Wealth , true lord of the dragon-tiger altar, mounted on his tiger, whip in hand, gold ingot ready — with four assistant deities who manage the welcoming of treasure, the gathering of valuables, the inviting of wealth, and the profiting of markets. The novel turns fortune into a bureaucracy : wealth flows not from luck but from an office, staffed, audited, and answerable — a very Chinese answer to the oldest of prayers. [The Heartless Minister] Bi Gan's Missing Heart: The civil face of the god descends from an atrocity recorded by Sima Qian in the Shiji (c. 90 BCE, 'Basic Annals of Yin'). Bi Gan , uncle and chief minister of King Zhou of Shang, remonstrated against the tyrant's cruelties until the king, goaded on by his favorite Daji, ordered the minister's heart cut out — to test the old claim that a sage's heart has seven openings. Because Bi Gan died heartless , later tradition reasoned, he is beyond greed: no bribe reaches a god who has no heart to desire one. He became the Civil God of Wealth , the form merchants and bankers trust, usually shown in an official's robes holding a ruyi scepter and a scroll. The logic is ruthless and perfectly practical: the only trustworthy custodian of wealth is the man whose desire for it has been surgically removed — a parable about greed built on a mutilation, and one of the darkest etiologies any god carries. [The Merchant] Fan Li, Thrice Rich: A third avatar rises from honest trade. Fan Li — again from Sima Qian — was the strategist who destroyed the rival state of Wu and saved Yue, then refused office and reward, changed his name, and took to commerce; he grew rich, gave it all away, started over, and did this three times , dying in comfort at last under the name Tao Zhu Gong. Merchants made him Cáishén because his fortune was a skill, not a windfall, and because he spent as brilliantly as he earned. Where Bi Gan's wealth is incorruptible and Zhao's is martial, Fan Li's is mercantile : prosperity as craft plus generosity. The choice of a retired official for the marketplace form of the god says something careful about Chinese commerce — that it does not entirely trust itself, and wants its wealth-god to be a man who walked away from power, made money in the open, and let it go. [The Fifth Day] Welcoming Cáishén: The living myth is a calendar custom. On the fifth day of the first lunar month — po wu , 'breaking the five' — Cáishén makes his annual circuit, and every shop and household races to be the first to welcome him . At midnight before, firecrackers tear the dark open; the paper icon that watched over the old year is burned to send the god on his way; dumplings are eaten 'to pinch the villain's mouth' shut. The folk tale behind the noise tells of a merchant so poor his only offering was a single stick of incense — and the god, pleased by the welcome and not the wealth, made his fortune. Businesses time their reopening to the day; the first trade of the year is literally kept by the god's schedule. It is the theology of a merchant culture in one image: fortune is real, it circulates, and it favors the one who stays up past midnight, firecracker in hand, at the door to receive it .
