instruction: Tell me a myth about "Helénē".
output: Helénē's story is told by Homer, Hesiod, Stesichorus, Euripides, and Herodotus — and the tradition argues with itself at every turn: abduction or seduction, guilt or phantom, goddess or woman. She is the most examined face in Greek myth. [The Birth] Leda and the Swan: Zeus desired Leda, the wife of King Tyndareus of Sparta, and came to her in the shape of a swan — fleeing, in the usual telling, an eagle's pursuit, so that the queen received the god under her wing. From her egg, and from a second egg, came the mixed brood of the house of Tyndareus: Helénē and her sister Clytemnestra, and the twins Kastor and Polydeukes, the Dioscuri — only some of them children of Zeus, the tradition says, though which is disputed. The earliest witness is Hesiod's Catalogue of Women (fr. 23a M-W), and Euripides opens his Helen with Leda finding the egg and hatching the child within. Aeschylus' Agamemnon (1455ff.) remembers the swan as a bird that sang for its death. The myth gives Helen a double nature from the first breath: born of a god's disguise and a mortal's bed, sister of the saviors of sailors and of the woman who would murder a king. Beauty, the story says, is never simply born — it arrives already entangled with power. [The Suitors] The Oath of Tyndareus: So renowned was Helen's beauty that suitors came to Sparta from every Greek land — and so dangerous was their number that King Tyndareus feared bloodshed whoever won. Odysseus, himself a suitor in some tellings but wise beyond courtship, proposed the oath that bears the king's name: each suitor swore to defend the marriage-rights of the chosen man, with arms if necessary. Then Helen chose Menelaus, brother of Agamemnon, and the oath bound all of Greece to her marriage. The story is preserved in Hesiod's Catalogue (fr. 198 M-W) and in the Cypria tradition; Homer has Helen on the walls of Troy look down at the Achaean champions and ask, without irony, whom they have left at home for her sake ( Iliad 3.205-224). The oath converts a wedding into a treaty — and a treaty, as the next generation would learn, is only a war waiting for its pretext. [The Judgment] The Apple of the Fairest: When Paris, prince of Troy, was asked to award a golden apple inscribed 'to the fairest,' he chose Aphrodite, who promised him the most beautiful woman alive — Helen, then Menelaus' wife. What followed depends on whom you read. The Cypria tradition (Proclus' summary) makes Paris a guest in Menelaus' house who sails off with the queen while her husband is away in Crete; the Iliad says only that Hera, Athena, and Aphrodite 'came to the shepherd's valley' and that the goddess led her away ( Iliad 24.25-30); Stesichorus and Herodotus insist she never went at all, carried off to Egypt while a phantom burned Troy in her shape. Homer himself refuses to settle it: Helen in the Odyssey (4.261-264) says Aphrodite 'cast in my heart sweet longing' and drove her from her marriage-bed. Abduction, seduction, or frame — the sources disagree, and the disagreement is the myth: an entire war needed a cause, and Greece could never quite decide what Helen's part had been. [At Troy] The Woman on the Walls: Ten years in Troy, and Helénē becomes the war's most unsettled witness. In Iliad 3 she walks the wall with Priam, naming the Greek champions — Agamemnon, Odysseus, Aias, and her own brothers, whom a mist strangely prevents her from seeing. The old king, whose city is dying for her, calls her 'dear child' and refuses blame: 'for my part, I hold the gods responsible' (3.164-165). She watches Menelaus and Paris duel for her, and shudders at Aphrodite's unseen hand when the goddess spirits her stricken husband from the field. And in Iliad 6 she is found at her loom, weaving the battles of Trojans and Achaeans into a purple web — a woman archiving a war fought in her name, while Hector, gentlest of the princes, calls her 'sister' and asks only to be remembered. Homer gives Helen what later retellings often withhold: full consciousness . She is the first to blame herself — 'dog that I am' — in a poem that pointedly refuses to. [The Return] The Phantom and Egypt: How Helen ended the war is disputed; how she came home is, too. Stesichorus of Himera paid the price of telling her story 'wrong' — legend says he went blind — and recanted in the Palinode , preserved in Plato's Phaedrus (243a): 'that story is not true; you never went in the benched ships, nor came to the towers of Troy.' Herodotus (2.112-120), told the same by Egyptian priests, locates the real Helen in the palace of the shape-shifting sea-old man Proteus at Memphis, while a phantom went to Troy. Homer offers the peaceful third act: in Odyssey 4, Telemachus finds Helen and Menelaus at home in Sparta, magnificently reconciled, she dropping the drug nepenthe into the wine to make grief forgetful. Three endings — phantom, hostage, homecoming — and each lets her live. The tradition, unable to convict or acquit her, instead multiplied her until no single Helen could be condemned.

instruction: Tell me a myth about "Iphigéneia".
output: Iphigéneia's story is the price of the Trojan War paid in advance : the maiden summoned to Aulis as a bride, lifted over her father's altar as the fleet's ransom, and — in the tellings that spare her — swept to the far shore of the Black Sea, where the gods set her a second altar and made her its keeper. [Aulis] The Fleet That Would Not Sail: The Cypria , the lost epic of the war's beginnings, told it first: the Greek fleet gathers at Aulis and the winds die. Agamemnon has angered Artemis — in the epic's account by killing a stag in the goddess's grove and boasting he could outshoot her. The seer Kalkhas announces the price: the fleet will sail only when the king gives his daughter Iphigéneia to the goddess. Aeschylus compresses the whole unbearable machinery into the parodos of the Agamemnon (104–257): the portent of two eagles tearing a hare — 'sacrifice a suffering thing' — and the elder king, 'clothed in ruinous frenzy', willing the act with 'a wretched holiness'. What the tradition insists on is not the savagery but the logic: the war against Troy begins by consuming the Greeks' own, at home, before a single ship clears the harbor. Ten years of foreign slaughter are inaugurated by one deliberate domestic one. [The Sacrifice] The Deer on the Altar: Aeschylus stages what the epic only reported, and makes it the most harrowing scene in surviving Greek poetry ( Agamemnon 228–247): the girl, 'gagged like a goat', lifted over the altar by her father's men; 'her saffron robe pouring to the ground'; one glance, one cry for her brother — and her father, 'after that decision, willed it', 'and so the ships sailed'. The Cypria softened the blow for its audiences: Artemis snatched the maiden from the altar, set a deer in her place, and carried Iphigéneia to the land of the Taurians, where she made her immortal. Euripides, in Iphigenia at Aulis , splits the difference and finds the truth inside the contradiction: his Iphigéneia arrives deceived — promised to Achilles — and then, at the last, chooses the sacrifice herself, declaring her death shall be Greece's freedom. The tradition never lets us settle whether she was murdered, rescued, or volunteered; the ambiguity is the point, because all three answers say the same thing about war's arithmetic. [Tauris] Priestess of the Strangers: Euripides' Iphigenia in Tauris finds her years later on the northern Black Sea coast — the Crimean Chersonesos of later geography — priestess of a savage Artemis whose rite demands that any Greek cast ashore be consecrated and slaughtered at the altar. She has become, in her own bitter office, the one who prepares the victims. Her opening monologue is the tradition's most direct audit of the Aulis bargain: she was sacrificed, she says, so that Helen might be recovered and the Greeks might go free — and the brother she died for now stands, in her dream, dead by her own hand at that very altar. The myth's cruelty is precise: the rescued girl is installed as executioner of her own people. Survival, the play suggests, is not the opposite of sacrifice but its continuation — the gods saved her body and spent her life. [The Recognition] The Letter and the Statue: The escape fills the second half of the Iphigenia in Tauris : two Greek captives are brought in, and one is Orestés, sent by Apollo to steal the Taurian image of Artemis. Recognition comes by letter — the play's celebrated scene of Orestés refusing to believe the impossible, and Iphigéneia inventing on the spot the fiction of a ritual purification to save them both. They seize the goddess's statue, flee to the ship, and are caught in the shallows until Athēnâ intervenes, commanding that the image be given a new home at Halai in Attica and that the goddess receive a rite in which a sword is drawn at a man's throat in token, bloodlessly — 'so shall the goddess have her honors'. King Thoas, cheated of his victims, accepts the goddess's will with one of tragedy's most humane exits: if gods they are, they are beyond his vengeance. The ending converts a cult of human sacrifice into a festival of symbolic remembrance — myth rewriting ritual into mercy, and an audience taught to prefer it. [Cult] The Bears of Brauron: The Athenians gave her a home and a function. At Brauron on Attica's east coast stood the sanctuary of Artemis Brauronia, where girls — the famous arktoi , 'bears' — served the goddess before marriage, dancing in saffron robes and dedicating their childhood garments on leaving (Aristophanes, Lysistrata 641–647; the rite's sacred law survives inscribed on marble). Pausanias (1.33.1) saw Iphigéneia's tomb and cult there, and the clothes of women who had died in childbirth dedicated at her shrine; Megara disputed the honor with a rival tomb of its own (Pausanias 1.43.1). Later antiquity multiplied her endings: Antoninus Liberalis (27), after Nikander, reports that Artemis made her immortal as Hekátē; and the tragedians preserve the strangest variant — that she was not Agamemnon's daughter at all but Theseus' child by Helen (Stesichorus; Euripides, Iphigenia at Aulis 509–512), born of a kidnapping before the war ever had a cause. Whichever ending a city preferred, the office is constant: the maiden sacrificed to launch a war becomes the guardian of every girl's passage into adult life.

instruction: Tell me a myth about "Máni".
output: Máni's mythology is brief but exact: he has no hammer-duels and no disguises, only a course to keep and a hunter behind him. The Eddas give him four scenes — a father's fatal boast, the breeding of the wolf that hunts him, two children lifted from a well, and the swallowing that ends the sky — and together they explain both why the moon moves and why it keeps its human face. [Vafþrúðnismál / Gylfaginning] Mundilfari's Boast: In the Vafþrúðnismál , the giant Vafþrúðnir tells Óðinn that Mundilfari is the father of Máni and of Sól alike. Snorri, in Gylfaginning (ch. 11), gives the story its edge: Mundilfari's two children were so fair that he named his son Máni, 'Moon', and his daughter Sól, 'Sun', and married Sól to a man named Glenr. The gods were angered by this ofdramb — this overweening pride — and took the siblings and set them in the heavens. The punishment is an appointment. Sól is made to drive the horses of the sun, Árvakr and Alsviðr, while Máni is charged with steering the course of the moon and ruling its waxing and waning. What a father claimed in arrogance, the gods confirmed in office: the names became the duties, and the children became the sky. The myth is the Eddas' quiet essay on vanity — the one boast the gods could not leave unpunished was a claim of ownership over light. [Gylfaginning / Grímnismál] The Iron-Wood Brood: Why does the moon flee? Because something was bred to chase it. Snorri preserves the genealogy ( Gylfaginning , ch. 12): east of Midgard, in the forest called Járnviðr — Iron Wood — a giantess in troll-woman's shape bore a brood of giant sons in wolf forms, and from that pack come the wolves that hunt the lights. Two of them the Æsir caught and set to their courses: Skǫll runs after the sun, and Hati Hróðvitnisson runs before the moon, and he will catch it — so it must be. The Grímnismál names them in verse: Skǫll follows the shining god, while Hati, Hróðvitnir's son, runs before the bright bride of heaven (st. 39). And the brood is not finished: from the same Iron Wood, Snorri says, will come the mightiest of all, Mánagarmr, the Moon-Hound, who feeds on the lives of the dead; the Vǫluspá laments the coming tormentor in a troll's shape (st. 40). The myth makes the night sky a battlefield of kinship: the lights of heaven are pursued by the children of the giantess, and Máni's speed is the speed of survival. [Grímnismál / Gylfaginning] The Wolf at the Moon's Heels: The moon does not drift; it flees. Snorri explains the physics by the hunter: the wolves run with the lights of heaven, and Hati Hróðvitnisson is the one who runs before the moon and means to take it — and so it will come to pass ( Gylfaginning , ch. 12). From earth, men watching the moon hurry across a winter sky believed the wolf was near; the chase is the Eddic explanation of lunar speed, and of eclipses, when the hound closed its jaws for a moment and the world held its breath. The chase has an ending, and the Eddas do not flinch from it. At Ragnarǫk the Moon-Hound Mánagarmr — fed all his life on the blood of the dying — swallows the moon whole and spatters the sky and the air with blood, so that the sun itself loses its shining and the stars are shaken from the heavens. The image is exact and terrible: time, which Máni measures, is also time, which is eaten. Every month closes because the wolf behind it is a month closer. [Gylfaginning] Bil and Hjúki at the Well: Snorri records that Máni took two children up from the earth, Bil and Hjúki, as they walked from the well called Byrgir, carrying on their shoulders the pail Sægr — often read as a mead-tub — slung from the pole Simul. Their father is named Viðfinnr. 'These children follow Máni,' Snorri adds, 'as can be seen from earth': look at the moon and you will find them there. This is the Norse answer to the man in the moon — not a face but two small figures under a burden, fixed forever in mid-errand. The detail of the well, the pail, and the pole is too homely to be invented ornament; it reads as the residue of nursery-lore older than the manuscript, the kind of story told to children who had already been shown the markings in the moon. Scholars have sometimes linked the pair to the Jack and Jill of English rhyme, but that connection is modern speculation, not attestation. What the myth insists on is gentler: the moon-god's company is not warriors but errand-bearers, and the sky remembers two children on their way home from water.

instruction: Tell me a myth about "Mārs".
output: Mārs enters myth almost entirely as a father — and what he fathers is the city. His stories are told by Rome's historians, not by its Homer, and they all serve one thesis: that Roman power is divine in origin and therefore answerable to ritual . The Vestal and the she-wolf, the shield from heaven, the old king fooled at a wedding: each myth is a charter for a piece of the state cult. [The Vestal and the Twins] Rhea Silvia at the River: Livy opens the Roman story with a vestal crime that is really a divine plan (1.3–4). Numitor, rightful king of Alba Longa, is deposed by his brother Amulius, who forces Numitor's daughter, the Vestal Rhea Silvia, into perpetual virginity so the line cannot challenge him. But the girl, sent to fetch water for a sacrifice, is overpowered in the sacred grove by the god — or so she swears, 'by the god himself, she said that Mars was the author of her seized virginity' — and bears twin boys. Amulius orders them drowned in the Tiber; the river is in flood, the basket grounds at the fig-tree Ruminalis, and a she-wolf comes down from the hills to nurse them in the cave of the Lupercal, while a woodpecker flies food to the infants. The shepherd Faustulus finds them; his wife Acca Larentia raises them; and the twins grow up to restore Numitor and found a city of their own on the Palatine. Livy reports the whole wonder-story and then, with the honesty that makes him Rome's first historian, adds that he gives it as it has come down, 'more adorned with poetry than burdened by proof.' The myth needs no proof: it explains why the war god's temple stands at the heart of the city his sons built. [The Shield from Heaven] Numa and the Ancile: In Numa's peaceful reign — the king who talked Jupiter himself out of human sacrifice with a handful of meal and onions — a shield fell from the sky, the ancile, with a promise that Rome's fate hung upon it. The problem was theft: one true shield, an empire to protect, and every enemy a potential thief. So the king set the cunning smith Mamurius Veturius a test he could not be told about — make eleven copies so exact that even Numa could not pick the divine original — and the twelve ancilia were entrusted to the Salii, the 'leapers,' priests of Mars who danced through the city each March bearing the shields on their left arms and singing a carmen so ancient that even Augustus's scholars confessed they could barely construe it. The smith who made them was driven out, or stoned, or honored — the versions disagree, and Ovid is visibly embarrassed by the tradition — but the ancilia stayed, and were still being carried when the empire was Christian. Mars's shield, like Rome itself, was a copy indistinguishable from the original; that was the whole point. [The Avenger] The Vow at Philippi: The greatest Mars myth is not archaic at all — it is Augustan, and paid for in blood. After Caesar's murder the nineteen-year-old Octavian marched with Antony against the Liberatores, and at Philippi in 42 BC Brutus and Cassius fell, one by the sword, one by his own hand. Octavian had vowed a temple to Mars the Avenger — Mars Ultor — if he should win, and forty years later, in 2 BC, he dedicated it in his new Forum, flanked by colossal statues of the god in crested helmet, spear grounded, breastplate crowded with myth. The temple held the sword of the murdered Caesar and the standards recovered from the Parthians — Crassus's lost eagles finally retrieved by diplomacy and displayed as war won. Ovid, who was there, makes the dedication Rome's birthday party (Fasti 5.545–598): the new theater, the games, the imperial family on the podium, and Mars's godhead finally visible — for until the temple rose, the Romans admitted, no image of Mars had any reliable claim to show what the god looked like. The myth is exactly as blunt as its name: the man who avenged the father became the son of a god, and Mars was the instrument. [The Old King Fooled] Mars and Anna Perenna: Ovid is the only source, and he is delighted to be it (Fasti 3.523–710). Old Mars, he says, had fallen in love — with the warlike maiden Ana Perenna? No: with Minerva herself, who with a goddess's perfect tact referred him onward: 'you are old; she is young' — go woo Anna, 'the years' own goddess.' Anna knew what the old god was after and, on their wedding night, wrapped herself in a veil, went to the bedroom in the dark, and — had placed the aged crone in the bed instead. When Mars at last lifted the veil by the lamp's light, the laugh was heard all over heaven, and Anna was raised to the skies as the river of years. The story is the Fasti's gift to Mars: the most ferocious of the gods made ridiculous by age and desire, and answered not with thunder but with a practical joke — Roman humor at the war god's expense, told in the month of his festival. [The Enemy of Aeneas] Mars for Turnus: In Virgil's Aeneid Mars does for the losing side what he never does for Rome: he loves it. His favorite is Turnus, the Rutulian prince who defends Italy against the Trojan landing, and the god moves through the last books like a pressure behind the war: he sends Allecto, the Fury, to kindle the conflict in Book 7; he strikes Turnus with a courage beyond his own when the prince pursues a phantom Aeneas onto a ship and is carried helpless from the field in Book 9; and in Book 12, when the treaty breaks, Mars arms him for the last duel. Yet Jupiter has already weighed the fates, and not even the war god's advocacy moves the scale. Mars rages; fate is silent and exact. The scene is the Aeneid's quiet commentary on the god Rome trusted most: Mars can arm a hero, but he cannot assign the victory — and when Rome itself is at stake, the poet reminds us, the god of war fights on the other side too.

instruction: Tell me a myth about "Medb".
output: Medb's dossier is the Táin Bó Cúailnge, the longest and greatest tale of the Ulster Cycle — and unlike every other great name in Irish myth, she is not a goddess remembered as a woman but a queen the tradition may once have worshipped as a goddess. The tale itself never says which. [Táin Bó Cúailnge, Recension I] The Pillow-Talk: One night at Crúachan, when the royal bed had been made for Medb and Ailill, they fell into a 'bolster-conversation' — comrac chind cherchailli — and Ailill boasted that the woman married to a wealthy man is well off. Medb answered that she was well off before him: daughter of Eochu Feidlech, high king of Ireland, and the wealthier of the two. To settle it they had every treasure counted — cups, rings, cattle, sheep, horses — and the tally came out exactly even, save one item: the great bull Finnbennach, born in Medb's herd, had scorned to be counted a woman's chattel and walked over into Ailill's, where he stood as the White-Horned of Connacht. That one beast broke the equality Medb would not live without. Her steward Mac Roth found the match: the Donn of Cúailnge, the Brown Bull of Cooley, kept by Dáire mac Fiachna in Ulster. Medb sent for a year's loan of him at princely terms — fifty heifers a year, a stretch of the plain of Aí, her own chariot, and the friendship of her thighs — and Dáire agreed. But the messengers drank and boasted that had the loan been refused they would have taken the bull by force, and Dáire swore that only by force would he ever be taken. The embassy came home empty, and Medb resolved on war. [Táin Bó Cúailnge, Recension I] The Bride-Gift Speech: The Táin lets Medb state her own terms, and the speech is the charter of her queenship. Daughter of the high king, wooed by the kings of Ireland, she refused them all, she says, 'for I asked a strange bride-gift such as no woman before me had asked of a man of the men of Ireland — a husband without meanness, without jealousy, without fear.' If he were mean, their wealth could not sit together, for she is generous in gifts; if jealous, she could not live beside him, 'for I was never without one man in the shadow of another'; if fearful, he would shame her in the front of every fight. Such a man she found in Ailill mac Máta: no meanness, no jealousy, no fear. She brought him the bride-gift — the clothing of twelve men, a chariot worth thrice seven cumals, the width of his face in red gold, the weight of his left forearm in bronze — and it is into her province, not his, that he came. The Táin is blunt about the arithmetic: he is king of Connacht because he is married to Medb of Crúachan. [Táin Bó Cúailnge] The Debility and the Boy at the Ford: Medb timed the raid for the cess noínden, the pangs of the Ulstermen — the debility laid on the warriors of Ulster by [[macha|Macha]], whom they had forced to race the king's horses when she was great with child. With Ulster's fighting-men abed, Medb marched the hosting of four provinces north — Connacht's own, the Leinster Galeóin, and the exiles of Ulster under Fergus mac Róich, who knew every road and ford of the way and, the tale says plainly, shared the queen's bed with Ailill's leave, for the road could not be found without him. One boy stood against the whole hosting: [[cuchulainn|Cú Chulainn]], untouched by the debility, who held the fords in single combat and took the heads of the best of Connacht one by one. Medb spent everything on him — terms, ambushes, satirists, her daughter Findabair promised to a dozen champions at once — and the hardest price fell on Ferdia, Cú Chulainn's own foster-brother, whom she plied with drink and the promise of Findabair until he took the ford. Four days they fought; the gae bolga ended it; and the march went on over the body of the one man Medb could not buy twice. [Táin Bó Cúailnge] The Battle of the Bulls: The hosts met at Gáirech and Irgáirech when the pangs lifted and Ulster rose; Medb's army broke, but the prize was already driven south — she had the Donn of Cúailnge, and she covered the retreat herself, in the tale's most unsparing passage, when her gush of blood came on her and she asked Cú Chulainn's protection for her army's rear. He granted it: 'no coward's weapon is the weapon of a woman.' Fergus mac Róich, looking back over the ruin of the hosting, gave the raid its verdict: 'This is what usually happens to a herd of horses led by a mare — their substance is taken and carried off and destroyed as they follow a woman who has misled them.' The bulls settled the account themselves. Finnbennach saw the Donn and bellowed; they fought through the night across Ireland, and in the morning the men of Connacht found the Brown Bull standing over the White-Horned trampled to pieces. The Donn carried Finnbennach's carcass on his horns through Connacht — scattering the loin at Áth Luain, the liver at Trim — then turned north for Cúailnge and died there of his wounds and his victory. Medb had her bull, and her equality, and the Táin's dry arithmetic: the two most valuable beasts in Ireland, both dead, and nothing left to count. [Aided Meidbe] The Cheese of Inis Cloithrinn: Medb outlived the raid, outlived Ailill — slain at Conall Cernach's hand — and kept her sovereignty into age, spending her last years at Inis Cloithrinn, her island on Lough Ree, where she bathed in the pool every morning at sunrise. She had killed her sister Clothru, and Clothru's son Furbaide had been cut from his mother's womb — whence his name, Ferbend, 'of the cutting' — and he grew up with the debt of it. Furbaide found the queen's bathing place and measured it the patient way: morning after morning he stood on the shore opposite and practiced his cast against the distance, until the stone flew true by habit. Then one sunrise, as Medb came to her bath, his sling let fly — a ball of hard cheese, the tale insists, the humblest weapon in Ireland — and the queen of Connacht, who had moved four provinces against Ulster and asked no man's leave for anything in her life, died by her nephew's hand at the water's edge. Her grave, the local tradition says, is the great cairn on Knocknarea in Sligo, where she stands buried upright, facing Ulster.

instruction: Tell me a myth about "Padmasambhava".
output: Padmasambhava's mythology is a hagiography written centuries after its hero — the principal source, the Padma bKa' thang , is a 14th-century treasure-text about an 8th-century man. That distance is not a defect to apologize for; it is the figure's native element, a teacher whose whole meaning is that the teaching keeps being found . [The Birth] Found on a Lotus in the Lake: No ordinary birth attaches to him. The Padma bKa' thang — the "Chronicle of Padma," a terma (treasure-text) revealed by Orgyen Lingpa in the 14th century, our principal source, composed five centuries after its hero — tells how he appeared as an eight-year-old child seated on a blooming lotus in the middle of Lake Dhanakośa , in the land of Uḍḍiyāna , the Swat valley. King Indrabhūti, warned by prophecy and mourning a son lost to the lake, adopted the lotus-child and named him Padmasambhava — Lotus-Born. A being without parents comes from nowhere in particular, so his teaching belongs everywhere; the story inverts the Buddha's nativity deliberately — not a queen's grove but an empty lake, not a clan but no lineage at all . Later scholars note what the myth performs: the historical 8th-century teacher is all but unrecoverable, and the tradition seems not to mind — a founder born of a flower needs no biography, only a legend. [Tibet] The Guru Who Tamed the Land: In the 8th century, tradition says, King Trisong Detsen (r. 755–797) invited first the abbot Śāntarakṣita to build a monastery — and watched the local spirits demolish every wall the workers raised by day. The abbot's counsel: send for the master of the vajra . Padmasambhava traveled from Nepal through the passes, and Tibet's own account of his progress — the Padma bKa' thang again — reads like a conquest itinerary: at each valley he bound the nyen , the nāgas, and the demoness of the land by oath, converting them into dharmapālas , sworn protectors of the teaching. Only then could Bsam yas (Samye) rise (consecrated c. 779) — monastery, academy, and debating courtyard in one, modeled on the cosmic mountain. The myth's geography is exact: Buddhism in Tibet is pictured as a conquest not of men but of landscape , every river and pass given its oath-bound guardian. The teacher who entered Tibet as an exorcist left as its father. [Samye] The Council of the Two Vehicles: Under Padmasambhava's shadow, Samye hosted Buddhism's most famous doctrinal duel. Around 792–794, the Indian gradualist Kamalaśīla — Śāntarakṣita's own disciple — debated the Chinese Chan master Moheyan , the "Heshang Mahāyāna," who taught that all thought, good or bad, must be cut off at a single stroke, "like cutting a cord." The Tibetan documents (the Basm yas Debate records, famously analyzed by Paul Demiéville in Le Concile de Lhasa , 1952) declare Kamalaśīla the victor and enshrine analysis, debate, and gradual cultivation as Tibet's official path; modern scholarship doubts the contest's every detail — the minutes may be a retrospective charter — but not its consequence. The myth matters more than the minutes: Tibet chose the ladder over the leap, scholarship over silence, and stamped that choice into every monastery courtyard it would build for the next twelve centuries. [The Treasure] Terma and the Hidden Teachings: Before departing — flying from the Gungthang pass on a pregnant tigress to the southwest, to his paradise Zangdok Palri , the Copper-Colored Mountain of Glory — Padmasambhava did what no teacher had done: he hid the teaching itself. Across Tibet he concealed terma , "treasures": texts, statues, and rituals sealed in rock, lake, pillar, and palace wall, and sealed also in the minds of disciples, to be discovered — by gter ston , treasure-revealers — when the age could bear them. The Padma bKa' thang is itself such a revelation. The Nyingma, the "Ancient" school, grounds its authority in this continuing disclosure: every tertön from the 11th century onward — Orgyen Lingpa who revealed the Chronicle among them — stands in the Guru's lineage, a founder whose school is re-founded at every discovery. The interpretive point: a teaching buried is a teaching guaranteed — the future written in advance, to be read only when it is true.

instruction: Tell me a myth about "Ranginui".
output: Ranginui's mythology is Māori cosmogony itself, as recorded by Sir George Grey and John White from oral tradition in the nineteenth century: the primordial embrace, the separation, and the war among the children that followed. It is a living narrative — still told on marae, still carved into meeting houses — and it explains the visible world: rain, mist, storm, and the light between sky and earth. [The Beginning] The Embrace of Rangi and Papa: In the beginning the sky father Ranginui and the earth mother Papatūānuku clung together in an embrace that knew no end, and in the darkness between their bodies their children were born — seventy sons in the telling recorded by Grey in Polynesian Mythology (1854). There was no light: the world was the cramped hollow of the parents' clasp, and the children grew hemmed in on every side, some of them longing for room and for brightness, others content in the warm dark. The myth opens not with a bang but with an embrace, and its first claim is psychological before it is cosmological — love so complete that it suffocates: the parents' happiness is the children's captivity, and creation cannot begin until something beloved breaks. [The Separation] Tāne Pushes the Sky Away: The children argued over how to win light. Tūmatauenga, the fierce one, proposed killing the parents — a plan the others rejected with horror. Then Tāne, the resourceful one, lay on his back between them and, bracing his head against the earth and his feet against the sky, pushed (Grey; White, Ancient History of the Māori ). Ranginui cried out in agony as he was lifted, and Papatūānuku groaned beneath him, still clinging, her torn body leaving the marks of her grief in the hills and valleys of the earth. Alone among the brothers, Tāwhirimāteā, lord of winds, sided with his father and withdrew in rage to the sky. The separation is the Māori account of why there is a world at all: light, space, and death itself enter existence in the moment the divided parents grieve — the world begins as an act of necessary violence against love. [The Longing] Why the Sky Weeps: The parents never resigned themselves to the parting, and the tradition reads the weather as their continuing grief. The rain that falls from Ranginui is his tears of longing for Papatūānuku; the mist that rises from her breast is her sighs, drifting up to meet him (Grey; Orbell, Māori Myth and Legend ). In some tellings the pale bloom on the riverbanks of harakeke, the New Zealand flax, marks where the tears of the pair fell thickest. The myth makes weather into emotion: every downpour and every soft morning fog is the conversation of the divided lovers — a cosmos that is not machinery but kinship, still grieving, still in love, and entirely unashamed of either. [The War of Winds] Tāwhirimāteā's Revenge: Tāwhirimāteā, who alone had opposed the separation, took his grieving father into the sky and made war on his brothers. He gouged out the eyes of Tangaroa's children — the fish and the crawling things of the sea, which is why the sea's creatures hide in the deep — and he hurled his winds and storms against Tāne's forests, snapping the trees. Tūmatauenga stood against him and won, and the winds were driven up into the fatherless sky (Grey; Best, Māori Religion and Mythology ). The war among the children is the myth's hardest lesson: the act that creates the world also divides it. Harmony among the forces of nature is never given — it was fought for once, and it must be remade continually, which is why the winds still test the trees. [The Stars] Tāne Hangs the Lights: Left alone in the high darkness, Ranginui needed light, and Tāne set the stars in the body of his father. In the traditions recorded by White, the stars are children of the sky hung as lamps to adorn him, and among them are the navigational stars by which the ancestors steered their canoes across the Pacific to Aotearoa. The crowning act of the separation is not punishment but decoration: Tāne, who pushed his parents apart, gives his father the stars as compensation. The night sky thus carries the story in its own substance — the sky father's beauty is his children's doing, and the lights by which humans find their way across the ocean are a family's peace offering to its father, hung where the whole world can steer by it.

instruction: Tell me a myth about "Sigurðr".
output: Sigurðr is the dragonslayer of the Vǫlsunga cycle, the Norse original of the German Siegfried and the last great hero of the legendary North. Son of Sigmundr and Hjǫrdís, fostered by the smith Reginn, he reforged his father's sword, killed the dragon Fáfnir, and woke the valkyrie Brynhildr from her enchanted sleep — then lost her, and his life, to a draught of forgetfulness and the plotting of his sworn brothers. His story survives in the Poetic Edda, the Prose Edda, and Vǫlsunga saga, and through the Middle High German Nibelungenlied it became the backbone of Wagner's Ring. Where the gods of the Edda face a doom they know is coming, Sigurðr faces one he has forgotten — and that is the more human tragedy. [Vǫlsunga saga] The Reforging of Gramr: At the wedding feast of his sister Signý, a one-eyed stranger — Óðinn — thrust a sword to the hilt into the tree Barnstokkr that grew through the hall of Vǫlsungr, and only Sigmundr of all the company could draw it. Years later Sigmundr fell in battle, the sword shattering beneath him against the same god's spear, and his widow Hjǫrdís carried the shards away for her unborn son. That son, Sigurðr, was fostered by Reginn, a smith of the dwarf-kin, who urged him against the dragon Fáfnir and forged blade after blade that broke under the boy's testing — until Sigurðr demanded the shards of his father's sword be worked into the new steel. Reginn reforged them into Gramr , and the boy clove the smith's anvil to the stock and sheared a tuft of wool drifting on the current as though it were standing stone (Vǫlsunga saga 13–15; Reginsmál). The blade binds the hero to Óðinn from birth: the god who gave the sword also broke it, and the steel that passes from father to son is the visible thread of a destiny the boy never chose. In the North, inheritance is not property but appointment. [Fáfnismál] The Slaying of Fáfnir: Fáfnir was Reginn's brother, who had killed their father Hreiðmarr for the hoard paid as weregild for the slain Ótr, and crawled away to Gnitaheiðr, where greed long brooding over gold twisted him into a dragon. Guided by a one-eyed old man who would not give his name, Sigurðr dug a trench across the worm's path to the water and lay in it; when Fáfnir crawled overhead he thrust Gramr upward into the heart. The dying dragon warned him that the gold would be his death, and the hero answered with the northern creed: every man must die, and wealth must serve until that day (Fáfnismál; Vǫlsunga saga 18–20). Roasting the heart for Reginn, Sigurðr burned his finger, set it in his mouth, and the heart-blood opened the speech of birds to him: the nuthatches in the branches warned that the smith meant to kill him. He took Reginn's head, loaded the cursed gold onto Grani, and rode away the richest and most doomed man in the North. The birds that save him here will not be there at the end. The episode's point is exact: the monster's death transfers the monster's curse, and every new owner of the gold only inherits it. [Sigrdrífumál] The Flame-Wall on Hindarfjall: Before the dragon, on Hindarfjall, Sigurðr found the vafrlogi — a wall of flame no horse would cross — and within it a hall where a warrior slept in full armor, as if dead. The sleep-thorn in her corslet marked her as a valkyrie; he drew Gramr and cut the armor from her, and she woke as Brynhildr and taught him the runes and the lore of the worlds: the healing runes, the ale-runes, the speech of victory and the speech of weddings, and the caution that shapes the whole cycle — never to swear falsely (Sigrdrífumál; Vǫlsunga saga 21–22). They plighted their troth and parted, and she prophesied what he would forget. The flame-wall is the cycle's question about fate: it parts for the destined rider and for no one else, and the man it admits is not thereby saved from what comes after. [Guðrúnarkviða] The Ale of Forgetfulness: At the court of Gjúki's sons the queen Grímhildr brewed Sigurðr the ale of forgetfulness, and Brynhildr passed from his mind as if she had never been. He married Guðrún, swore oaths with her brothers Gunnarr and Hǫgni, and when Gunnarr wooed Brynhildr and could not cross the flames, Sigurðr exchanged shapes with him and rode the fire in his friend's likeness — wooing his own forgotten beloved for another man, with a drawn sword laid between them in the bridal bed (Vǫlsunga saga 28; Guðrúnarkviða I). The deception could not hold: from a ring and a quarrel at the washing-stones Brynhildr learned what had been done, and wounded in her pride she demanded the death of the man who had ridden the flames and then married another. The betrayal is the cycle's quiet engine: no one in it acts from malice until the ale is brewed — the draught of forgetfulness is the one weapon the curse of gold did not need to supply. [Brot af Sigurðarkviðu] The Death of Sigurðr: The brothers, bound to Sigurðr by oath, could not strike him; they incited the younger Guthormr, who had sworn nothing, and he stabbed Sigurðr as he slept. Some lays — Sigurðarkviða en skamma and Guðrún's own laments — have him slain out of doors, in the forest; Brot af Sigurðarkviðu , preserved only in a fragment around the Codex Regius lacuna, gives the death in bed and the last words. Dying, Sigurðr spoke gently to Guðrún, named the true traitors, and flung Gramr after the killers; the sword caught Guthormr in the doorway and took him too. Brynhildr laughed once at the bier, told the truth at last, and went onto the pyre to lie beside him (Sigurðarkviða en skamma; Vǫlsunga saga 31–32). The sources disagree on the place but not on the meaning: the hoard's curse reached the man who thought himself above it, through the only door he had left open — the trust of those he called his own.

instruction: Tell me a myth about "Sleipnir".
output: Sleipnir's dossier is three scenes and a pedigree: his begetting at the wall of Ásgarðr, his ride down the Hel-road for Baldr's sake, and the verse that crowns him best of horses. Around them the corpus keeps him the way the þulur keep him — catalogued, superlative, and never once ridden in vain. [Gylfaginning 42] The Master Builder's Wage: A smith came to Ásgarðr offering to build the gods a wall in three seasons, high and strong against the mountain-giants — and named his wage: Freyja, and the sun and the moon. The Æsir bargained him down to one winter, alone; at Loki's urging they granted him the use of his stallion, Svaðilfari. The horse hauled boulders by night that the builder set by day, and with three days left before summer the gate-pillars stood nearly finished. The gods blamed Loki, who had advised the bargain, and swore he would die an evil death unless he made the builder lose. That night, when Svaðilfari was led out to the stones, a mare ran from the wood and whinnied; the stallion broke his traces and ran after her, and the work stood still. The builder flew into a giant's rage — and the gods called on Þórr, who smashed the smith's skull with Mjölnir and sent him down to Niflhel (Snorri, Gylfaginning 42). Snorri closes the episode with the strangest sentence in his Edda: Loki had had such dealings with Svaðilfari that somewhat later he bore a foal. It was grey and had eight legs, and this is the best horse among gods and men. The gods' broken bargain, Loki's shame, the giant's death — and out of all of it, the greatest gift Óðinn ever received. [Gylfaginning 49] The Ride Down the Hel-Road: When Baldr lay dead and Frigg asked who would win her love by riding to Hel to ransom him, Hermóðr the Bold, Óðinn's son, stood up. Sleipnir was led out, and Hermóðr mounted and galloped away. He rode nine nights through dark and deep valleys, seeing nothing, until he came to the river Gjöll and rode onto the Gjallarbrú, the bridge roofed with shining gold, where the maiden Móðguðr guards the crossing. She told him the dead had passed that way the day before — five companies of them — and that the road to Hel lay downward and northward. He rode on to the gates of Hel, and there Sleipnir showed what eight legs are for: Hermóðr spurred him, and the horse leapt the gate with so much to spare that the leap itself became proverb (Gylfaginning 49). Inside, Hermóðr found Baldr in the high seat and Nanna beside him, and delivered the Æsir's plea. Hel set her famous condition — all things in the world, living and lifeless, must weep Baldr out — and the errand failed at the giantess Þökk's dry tears. But the ride succeeded: the only journey in the corpus that goes down the Hel-road and comes back, made on the back of Loki's foal. [Grímnismál 44; Sigrdrífumál 15] Best of Horses: The Poetic Edda gives Sleipnir no scene of his own, but it gives him the superlative. Grímnismál, in its catalogue of the best of all things — Yggdrasill of trees, Skíðblaðnir of ships, Óðinn of the Æsir — names Sleipnir the best of horses, one item in a list where every other entry is a god or a wonder. Sigrdrífumál lodges him in the rune-lore: among the places where runes were carved — on the shield before the shining god, on Arvakr's ear and Alsvinnr's hoof, on Bragi's tongue — the poem counts Sleipnir's teeth, the horse's mouth itself a place of writing. And the heroic cycle keeps his bloodline. Reginsmál's prose tells that Grani, Sigurðr's peerless grey, was of Sleipnir's lineage — the best horse of the heroic age descended from the best horse of the gods, the line running down from Óðinn's stable into the Völsung story. [Gotland picture stones] The Stone-Carved Rider: Centuries before Snorri wrote, the image was already carved. On the Gotland picture stones of the eighth and ninth centuries — most famously the Tjängvide stone from Alskog and Ardre VIII — an eight-legged horse bears a rider toward a figure, often a woman with a drinking-horn, waiting before a hall. The standard reading sees Óðinn carried by Sleipnir, received at the boundary of the otherworld: the myth in granite, older than any manuscript that tells it. The stones cannot be made to recite the Edda, and the identification rests on the one feature that needs no caption — eight legs, where nature and every other carved horse keep four. Whatever else the carvers meant, they meant a horse that runs between worlds; no other beast in the North was ever given the extra limbs.

instruction: Tell me a myth about "Omphalós".
output: The omphalós has no biography because it is a place made stone: the story of Delphi's navel is the story of how the Greeks decided where the middle of the world was — by eagle, by oracle, and by the stone that stood for the infant god. [The Center] The Eagles of Zeus: In the story told at Delphi, Zeus wished to know where the exact center of the earth lay. He released two eagles — some say from the eastern and western edges of the world — and bade them fly toward each other; they met above Delphi, and where they met the god fixed the omphalós, the navel-stone. The tale is preserved in the geographical tradition that culminates in Strabo (9.3.6), who repeats it as the sanctuary's own account of itself. The myth is a cartography in miniature: instead of measuring the world, the Greeks let two birds draw its diagonals and set a stone where the lines crossed. Delphi did not claim to be everywhere; it claimed to be the middle — the one point from which the whole could be surveyed, and the one point, therefore, where a god might conveniently speak to all mortals at once. Every subsequent oracle of the sanctuary traded on this founding geometry. [The Adyton] The Stone in the Innermost Room: Pausanias (10.16.3) describes what the visitor could actually see: in the innermost sanctuary of Apollo's temple, the adyton, lay the omphalos, covered — the Delphians said — with the net thrown over it, with two golden eagles standing upon it. Beside it, in the same most-holy space, stood the tripod on which the Pythia mounted to give her responses, and the ever-burning hearth of the sanctuary. The stone was thus not a cult statue but a boundary-marker of the cosmos, kept in the room where heaven and earth touched. Its material facts are modest — a carved marble boss a little over a meter high — but its placement was the whole argument: the center of the world was a place you could stand next to, touch, and consult. Pausanias's description is the one fixed point on which the identification of the surviving stone rests. [The Swaddled Stone] What Kronos Swallowed: Hesiod ( Theogony 485–497) tells how Rhea, pregnant with Zeus, asked her parents Gaia and Ouranos to save the child from Kronos, who devoured each of his newborns. They gave her a great stone wrapped in swaddling clothes; Kronos 'seized it in his hands and thrust it down into his belly, the wretch, nor did he know in his heart that in place of his son his invincible, unshaken stone was left.' The later tradition — reported at Delphi itself and recorded by Pausanias (10.24.6) — identified this very stone with the omphalos at Delphi. The world's center thus conceals a substitution: where a god should have been destroyed, a stone was swallowed instead, and Zeus lived to overthrow his father. The navel of the earth is also the stone of rescue — the dummy that fooled Time and made the present order of the cosmos possible. [The Cleft] Apollo, Python, and the Chasm: The Homeric Hymn to Apollo (300ff.) tells how the young god came to the rocky cleft at Delphi, where a spring flowed and a she-dragon, Python, lay — 'there the son of Leto with his mighty bow slew the bloated, mighty beast.' The dragon's name gave the place its older name, Pytho, and the goddess who had held the oracle there yielded it to him. On the foundation of Apollo's temple the omphalos stood beside the very chasm from which — in the later tradition reported by the sources — the prophetic power rose to the Pythia enthroned above it. The myth makes the center of the world a conquered place: the middle is not given but won by an arrow, and the stone that marks it stands where a dragon's breath once rose. Delphi's claim to centrality is thus also a claim of legitimacy — the oracle speaks from the exact spot where the god's victory made speech divine.

instruction: Tell me a myth about "Keraunós".
output: The keraunós is not merely a weapon but the emblem of Zeus's rule — forged at the beginning of his reign, decisive in his two great wars, and terrible against mortals who reach too high or are loved too much. [The Forging] The Cyclopes Arm Zeus: When Zeus came of age to challenge Kronos, Gaiä named his allies: the Cyclopes, one-eyed smiths imprisoned in the depths. Zeus freed them, and they repaid him with the three weapons of heaven — thunder, lightning, and 'the glowing thunderbolt' (Hesiod, Theogony 501–506); the same passage remembers their earlier craft, arms for the gods at the beginning (Theogony 139–141). The bolt is thus born at the exact moment Zeus's power needs a form: before it he is a younger god with grievances, after it he is the storm. Homer never forgets the connection, and calls the bolt simply the weapon when Zeus arms himself at the brink of the Trojan War (Iliad 8.75). The myth explains why no one else may hold it: the keraunós is the signature of sovereignty, forged once and never re-made. [The Titanomachy] Breaking the Old Order: The war between the Olympians and the Titans lasted ten years with no advantage on either side, until Zeus brought up the Cyclopes' gifts. Then heaven changed hands: 'from Olympus he hurled his bolts in succession, and the earth groaned, burning, and the great forests crackled on every side; the whole earth boiled, and the streams of Ocean, and the unharvested sea' (Hesiod, Theogony 687–713). The Titans were struck down, bound, and cast into misty Tartarus behind gates of bronze. The keraunós here is not one throw but a barrage — the first use of concentrated, overwhelming force in Greek myth, and the poem's theological argument that raw elder power yields to armed, organized thunder. Every later bolt-throw reenacts this one: order established by a weapon that cannot be answered, and therefore never has to be. [Typhon] The Bolt Against the Storm-Giant: The last challenger was Typhon, a being with a hundred serpent heads, eyes of fire, and voices that were by turns gods', bulls', and lions'. The whole cosmos recoiled; Zeus met him with the full armory — thunder and lightning first, then 'the thunderbolt, hard and heavy, that casts the blazing light' (Hesiod, Theogony 820–868). The bolt burned the hundred heads, struck Typhon down, and sent him beneath the land, where he still feeds the eruptions of Etna. The combat pairs like with like — storm against storm — and the keraunós wins not by being bigger but by being directed: Typhon is weather without a wielder, the bolt weather that obeys. Greek theology is compressed into the image. Power becomes legitimate only when it serves an ordered hand, and the hand is Zeus's. [Mortals] Semele and Salmoneus: Love and Hubris: Against mortals the bolt keeps two ledgers. Semele, beloved of Zeus and pregnant with Dionysus, was tricked by jealous Hera into asking to see her lover in his full godhead; the promised thunder and lightning destroyed her — though Zeus rescued the unborn child, sewn into his thigh until term (Apollodorus, Library 3.4.3; cf. Homer, Iliad 14.323–325). Salmoneus kept the opposite account: he dragged bronze bridges behind his chariot for thunder and hurled torches for lightning, demanding sacrifices as though he were Zeus; the true keraunós answered and burned him and his city (Apollodorus 1.9.7; Virgil, Aeneid 6.585–594). One mortal died for loving the storm too much, the other for impersonating it. Between them the bolt defines its narrow path: humanity must neither seize divine fire nor counterfeit it — and the keraunós, which never misses, is the eternal enforcer of that narrowness.

instruction: Tell me a myth about "Susanō".
output: Susanoo's cycle in the Kojiki and Nihon Shoki runs from cosmic vandal to culture hero: expelled from heaven, he conquers the dragon of chaos and founds a kingdom in song — the most humanly told arc of any Japanese deity. [The Birth] From the Nose of Izanagi: When Izanagi purified himself after his flight from Yomi, Amaterasu was born from his left eye and Tsukuyomi from his right; from his nose came Susanoo , whose name the Kojiki writes 須佐之男 and glosses as the swift, impetuous male deity. Izanagi charged him with rule of the sea. But Susanoo never ceased weeping for his dead mother, crying so hard that the mountains withered and the rivers dried. Exasperated, Izanagi expelled him: 'If that is your wish, go to the land of your mother, then' (Kojiki 1). The storm god is thus the grieving child of creation, defined from birth by a longing for what cannot be retrieved — the sea he was given to rule is, after all, the element his father had fled into to escape death. [The Rampage] The Test and the Trampling: Climbing to heaven to bid his sister farewell, Susanoo alarmed Amaterasu, who went out armed; he protested his innocence and proposed an ukei , a covenant of sincerity, exchanging ornaments so that she bore three goddesses from his sword and he five gods from her necklace (Kojiki 1). The test cleared him — and he repaid it by trampling down the ridges of her rice-fields, filling the ditches, and flaying the heavenly piebald horse, whose carcass he hurled through the roof of her weaving hall, killing the maiden within. Amaterasu fled into the rock cave and sealed the door. Every one of his crimes strikes at cultivation — field, ditch, loom — the arts by which heaven imposes order on nature. Susanoo's rage is the sacred vandalism of the untamed. [The Serpent] The Eight-Forked Monster of Izumo: Banned from heaven, Susanoo descended to Izumo, where he found the old couple Ashinazuchi and Tenazuchi weeping beside their eighth daughter: each year the serpent Yamata no Orochi — eight heads, eight tails, cedars growing on its back, its body spanning eight valleys — had devoured one of their daughters, and Kushinadahime alone remained. Susanoo transformed the girl into a comb, hid her in his hair, and had the parents brew eight vats of eightfold-refined sake. The serpent drank all eight, fell into a stupor, and Susanoo cut it apart (Kojiki 1). In its tail his blade struck something hard: a great sword, which he named Ame-no-Murakumo , Gathering-of-Clouds, and presented to Amaterasu in atonement — the blade later generations call Kusanagi , one of the Three Imperial Regalia. The myth tames chaos not by greater force but by appetite itself: the monster is destroyed by the one thing it could not refuse. [The Palace] Suga, Where the Clouds Rise: After the slaying, Susanoo felt his spirit suddenly clear — suga , refreshed — and on that spot in Izumo he built a palace and married Kushinadahime. Pacing its length, he composed what the Kojiki presents as his own song: 'The many-fenced palace of Suga, ah! That cloud-rising, many-fenced palace of mine!' — counted among the earliest verses in the chronicle and remembered as the foundation of Izumo's sacred landscape. The shrine that marks the site, Suga Jinja, still stands within the orbit of the Izumo tradition, and the verse he sang there is counted among the oldest human voices in Japanese literature. The storm god, having destroyed heaven's order, founds his own in song and marriage: violence converts to culture at the moment it ceases to rage — and the proof is a poem, not a sword. [The Wanderer] The Lodging at Somin's House: The Nihon Shoki adds a stranger chapter. Expelled and unkempt, Susanoo wandered as a beggar and asked lodging of two brothers: the wealthy one refused him, but the poor Somin Shōrai bathed him with sake in eight tubs and fed him well. In gratitude the god gave Somin a charm cut from a mulberry bough: hang this at your gate, and pestilence will pass your house by. The promise held, and the Somin charm became the ancestor of the epidemic-warding talisman-papers hung at gates in Kyōto and across Japan — the same charm-papers still distributed at the Gion cult's shrines today. Behind the terror of the storm stands an old cultic logic: the dangerous god is also the god who protects, and his protection is won by generosity to the stranger at the door.

instruction: Tell me a myth about "Kǒngzǐ".
output: Kǒngzǐ is a historical man — born 551 BCE in the state of Lǔ — but the tradition did with his biography what it does with all founders: it polished it into legend. The Shǐjì of Sīmǎ Qiān (ch. 47) supplies the framework, the Lúnyǔ the voice; between them stands the mythic Master, born under a portent, refused by every court, and vindicated only after death . [The Birth] The Qilin’s Jade Tablet (551 BCE): The legends of the Master’s birth are later embroidery on a plain record — Sīmǎ Qiān’s Shiji 47 says only that Kǒng Qiū was born in 551 BCE at Zōu in Lǔ, posthumous son of the aged soldier Kǒng Shūliáng Hé and the young Yán Zhēngzài. But tradition could not leave a founder without a portent: a qilin, the unicorn-beast that appears only when a sage is to come, was said to have entered the family courtyard and spat a jade tablet announcing a son whose doctrine would rule all under Heaven, though he would sit on no throne. The tablet bore the character for “hill” (qiū), and the child received it as his personal name — matching Mount Ni, beside which he was born — and the courtesy name Zhòngní, “second-born Ni.” Han thinkers gave the idea its name: the Master was the sùwáng , the “uncrowned king,” whose kingdom was the text. The legend means the tradition knew exactly what it had. [The Journey West] The Master Asks Lǎozǐ About Rites: In his thirties the young Kǒngzǐ travelled west to the royal capital of Zhōu to question the aged archivist Lǎozǐ about the rites of burial and mourning. Lǎozǐ, tradition says, received him coolly: “The men of whom you speak are bones now, and their words died with them… I have heard that a good merchant hides his store as though it were empty, and that a noble man in his bearing looks like a fool. Cast off your pride and your many desires — for neither profits you. That is all I have to say to you.” The Master returned and told his disciples: “I know how birds fly, how fish swim, how beasts run — but the dragon I cannot fathom, riding the wind and clouds up into Heaven. Today I have seen Lǎozǐ: he is such a dragon.” ( Shiji 63.) The meeting is the tradition’s way of contrasting its two great teachers — the one who withdrew, and the one who knocked on every door. [The Wanderings] Fourteen Years Between the States: From 497 to 484 BCE the Master wandered — Wèi, Chén, Cài, Chǔ — offering his Way to rulers who would not buy it. The Analects keeps the human record. At the border pass of Yì, the warden, watching a whole generation of pupils following one unheeded man, sought him out: “Heaven is going to use the Master as a wooden bell” — the clapper that warns a sleeping age (3.24). In Chǔ the madman Jiēyú passed his carriage singing: “Phoenix, phoenix, how your virtue has declined!… The past is beyond mending, but the future can still be pursued. Give it up, give it up — those who serve in court now court death” (18.5). The Master climbed down wanting to speak with him, but Jiēyú fled. Between Chén and Cài the party was cornered and out of food; the Shiji adds the scene the disciples themselves laughed at — cornered and helpless, the Master said they were “like stray dogs,” and smiled: “Yes, yes — stray dogs indeed.” The road means what he told the recluses: “If the Way prevailed in the world, I would not need to change anything” (18.6). And still he walked. [Return and Death] “I Transmit, I Do Not Create”: At sixty-eight the Master was called home to Lǔ, and his last five years were his real victory — not in office but in editing: he arranged the Odes and the Documents, said the tradition, and wrote the Spring and Autumn Annals so that “rebellious ministers and villainous sons would be struck with terror.” “I transmit but do not create,” he said; “I trust and love antiquity” ( Analects 7.1). The book keeps the cost. When his best pupil, Yán Huí, died young, the Master wept without restraint: “Heaven has bereft me! Heaven has bereft me!” (11.9). In 479 BCE he died; the Shiji has him dream of a sacrificial tripod by his door and sing, days before: “The great mountain must crumble, the stout beam must break, the wise man must wither away.” The lament means the tradition understood: a teacher’s immortality is entirely in the students — and Yán Huí’s death is the wound the Analects never closes.

instruction: Tell me a myth about "Yùhuáng".
output: The Jade Emperor's mythology is a late, literate construction — scripture, novel, and folk tale jointly building a biography and a government for Heaven. His stories ask the great bureaucratic question: who, exactly, is in charge? The answer, assembled from the fifth century to the Ming novel, is a sovereign with a résumé, a war record, and a court that even comedy cannot overthrow. [Yuhuang benxing jijing] The Making of a Sovereign: The Daoist canon answers the obvious question — where does Heaven's emperor come from? — with a full sacred biography. The Scripture of the Jade Sovereign's Former Deeds (Gaoshang Yuhuang benxing jijing, in the Ming Daozang) tells of the childless king of the Kingdom of Wondrous Bliss, whose queen, after years of prayer to the Dao, dreams that the supreme Lord hands her an infant wrapped in radiance. The prince, grown, marvels that even his happy kingdom cannot spare him from death; he gives the throne to a worthy minister and withdraws to the mountain to cultivate the Way — through kalpas of austerity, service to prior immortals, and ordeal after ordeal, until he ascends as Yùhuáng, the Jade Sovereign of the clearest heaven. The scripture thus gives the celestial throne a curriculum vitae: Heaven's ruler is not born but made, refined like an alchemist's elixir across ages no chronicle can hold. [Benxing jijing · Popular Canon] The War Against the Demon Host: The same scripture and the popular tradition that grew from it give the future emperor his proving war. While the radiant prince still rules in his father's kingdom, a demon king — lord of black clouds, master of hosts — brings plague and darkness upon the world, and the gods of the older heavens cannot end him. The prince arms himself, and in the great battle that follows his radiance alone routs the demon armies; the defeated host swears fealty, and the victor — refusing even the throne of the conquered — returns to his mountain and his cultivation. Later novels, above all the Ming Investiture of the Gods (Fengshen yanyi), pour the same pattern over heaven itself, where the mandate passes from defeated tyrants to a righteous successor. The myth's grammar is that of every dynastic founding: the old order falls not because the gods fail, but because the throne must change hands before its holder can be seen at all. [Journey to the West, chs. 3–7] The Monkey and the Throne: In chapters 3–7 of the Ming novel Journey to the West, the Jade Emperor's heaven is the most vividly drawn bureaucracy in Chinese literature. When the stone-born monkey Sun Wukong arms himself in the dragon palace and erases his name from the registers of death, the celestial court debates: execute him or enroll him? He is enrolled — as Bimawen, a groom of heavenly horses — and when he discovers the rank is beneath his power, his rebellion lays open the whole military establishment: the pagoda-bearing general Li Jing, the thunder agents, the star officers all give way, until the Jade Emperor's own high ministers advise the one move left, and the Buddha comes. The episode is comic, but its seriousness is structural: the Emperor of Heaven rules through precedent, rank, and memorial — and comedy is what happens when raw force meets paperwork that cannot imagine it. [Folk Tradition] The Decree Above the Milky Way: In the oldest tellings of the Cowherd and the Weaver Girl — a love story already glimpsed in the Shijing and given its full shape in Han-dynasty lore — the lovers' separation is the work of Heaven itself; and in the later folk versions it is the Jade Emperor, the Weaver Girl's own grandfather (or the Queen Mother of the West at his side), who draws the River of Heaven between them, decreeing that magpies may span it on the seventh night of the seventh month, and only on that night. The festival of Qixi, still kept across East Asia, is the living calendar of this decree. The myth gives the celestial sovereign his strangest office: he is the authority who separates, and the tenderness of the tale is that his separation is annually, faithfully, and by the whole bird-world, undone.

instruction: Tell me a myth about "Krátos".
output: Krátos has no independent mythology — no quests, no loves, no temples. His entire dossier is a genealogy, an oath, one terrible scene, and the trace of a word in epic: the binding of Prometheus, in which he is the speaking voice of power. [Theogony 375–403] The Children of Styx: Hesiod gives Krátos his family in the Theogony (375–383): the river Styx, daughter of Ocean, bore to Pallas four children — Zelos (Rivalry), trim-ankled Níkē (Victory), Krátos (Might), and Bía (Force). They are not decorative attendants. When the Titanomachy broke out, Styx was the first of the gods to bring her children over to Zeus's side, and for that loyalty Zeus granted them a rare honor: they live with him forever, 'for he ordained that they should dwell with him always and have honor beyond the other gods' (Theogony 383–403). Hyginus ( Fabulae , preface) repeats the list and calls them primos in omnibus — first among all. The myth explains something precise about Greek ideas of rule: victory, rivalry, might, and force are not Zeus's rivals but his household, bound to him by gratitude and oath. [Prometheus Bound 1–87] The Will of Zeus: Aeschylus stages Krátos in person. At the opening of Prometheus Bound , Might and Force — Krátos and Bía — drag the defiant Titan to a crag at the world's edge, and Krátos addresses the workman Hephaestus with the play's entire thesis: Zeus is new to power and ruthless; old loyalties count for nothing; 'there is no one free except Zeus' (Prometheus Bound 50–52). Hephaestus pities Prometheus and hesitates over the hammer; Krátos has no pity to hesitate with — he only checks that the work is done. Then he leaves the stage, his task complete, and never returns: force has nothing more to say once the chain is set. The drama built the West's first portrait of power as a functionary — efficient, unpersuadable, bored by the suffering it administers — and gave the abstraction a mask the audience could boo. [Theogony 775–806] The Oath of Styx: Krátos's mother is herself an institution. In the Theogony (775–806) Hesiod explains that when the gods must swear their most terrible oath, they swear by Styx : an Olympian pours her water, and any god who forswears lies breathless for a full year, then serves nine more years exiled from the divine company. Zeus granted her this honor precisely because her children had stood by him in the war — the oath of the gods is, literally, the reward of loyalty. So Krátos descends from the one power in the cosmos that even Zeus must respect: the pledge by which rule itself is guaranteed. The genealogy is a lesson in political theology — might and the binding oath are mother and son, because force that cannot be sworn to is only violence, and an oath that cannot be enforced is only a wish. [Iliad 8] The Kratos of Zeus: Homer never names a god Krátos, yet the word haunts his Zeus like a bodyguard. When the Father of Gods and Men challenges the whole pantheon, his boast is built on the noun itself: he claims an irresistible kratos and dares the gods to hang a golden rope from heaven and pull — 'you would not drag Zeus the high counselor from heaven to earth, however hard you strove' (Iliad 8.18–27). Later, when Hera calls his supremacy tyranny, she names exactly what she fears: a power without check or counsel (Iliad 8.478–483). The epic thus keeps two registers of the same word — the kratos that is Zeus's attribute and the Krátos who is Zeus's functionary, sovereignty in heaven and Might on stage. It is the ambiguity the Greeks lived with: the same strength that holds the cosmos up holds the Titan down.

instruction: Tell me a myth about "Tōnatiuh".
output: Tōnatiuh's mythology is the mythology of the Fifth Sun — the age we inhabit. The Nahuatl sources preserve the legend of how our sky was lit, and together they make daylight a running debt: the sun was born of a god's courage at Teotihuacan, and it moves only while it is fed. [The Fifth Sun] Nahui Ollin — The Sun of Movement: Before our sky there were four suns, each destroyed: 4-Jaguar, when jaguars devoured the giants; 4-Wind, when hurricanes swept the people from the earth; 4-Rain of Fire, when the sky rained flames; 4-Water, when the flood came and the people became fish (Anales de Cuauhtitlan; Codex Vaticanus A). After the flood the gods gathered in darkness at Teotihuacan, the 'Place Where the Gods Were Made,' and asked who would light the world. The proud Tecuciztecatl and the humble, pox-scabbed god Nanahuatzin both offered to leap into the great fire. Tecuciztecatl faltered at the flames and leapt only at the shaming of the others; Nanahuatzin, who had no pride to lose, plunged straight in — and rose as the new sun, the moon following ashamed behind him (Florentine Codex, Book VII). Our age is therefore Nahui Ollin, '4-Movement,' and its sign is the earthquake: the sun of the present world moves, and everything that moves can end. The old gods did not make our sky to last — they made it to be paid for. [The Price of Motion] The Sun That Demands Hearts: When the new sun rose it would not move. 'How shall I live?' it said. 'I cannot move — feed me, nourish me' (Anales de Cuauhtitlan). The gods understood at once: no sun moves on its own strength. Quetzalcoatl took the obsidian blade, and the gods went willingly to be opened — their hearts fed the fire, and only then did the sun begin its road across the sky. The chronicles and codices name this sun Tōnatiuh , 'he who goes forth shining,' the same deity the fate-books enthrone at 13-Olin in the tonalamatl (Codex Borbonicus; Codex Vaticanus A). The tellings differ on the fire-leaper's name — Nanahuatzin in Sahagún's version, Tōnatiuh in the calendar books — but they agree completely on the economy: daylight is a loan, and the debt is paid in what is most alive. Aztec war, tribute, and temple sacrifice are not cruelty for its own sake in this theology; they are the interest on the world's first meal. [The Sky-Road] Carried by the Warrior Dead: All day Tōnatiuh must be carried. From dawn to noon he climbs on his own heat; at noon his strength wavers, and the souls of warriors who died in battle and of those taken by the water take up the burden — the eagle-warriors lifting him on their wings toward the west (Florentine Codex, Books II and VII). Below, his light is warred over by the tzitzimime, the star-demons who wait at the edges of the sky for the world to end; when the sun darkens in eclipse they descend to devour humanity, and the people raise a din of war-cries and drumbeats to drive them back. At evening Tōnatiuh sinks into the west and the dead warriors set him down, their service done until tomorrow's climb (Florentine Codex, Book VII). The myth makes the noon sky a battlefield: every noon is a held bridge, every dusk a narrow escape, and every eclipse the world's enemies testing the door. A sun that must be carried is a sun that can be dropped — and the whole apparatus of Aztec war exists, in this theology, to keep the bearers numerous and willing. [The Calendar Throne] 13-Olin and the Day of the Sun: In the 260-day tonalpohualli, Tōnatiuh rules the trecena 13-Olin, 'Thirteen-Movement,' and his own day-sign is ollin — the 'earthquake, movement' glyph, drawn as a striped sign of trembling whose center carries heart-shapes. The Codex Borbonicus enthrones him inside the day-sign 4-Ollin, the very sign that names our world-age, with the emblems of the four past suns arrayed around him; the Codex Vaticanus A shows the sun's face flanked by the signs of the destroyed ages. The tonalamatl, the book of days, read a person's fate from the day-sign that ruled at birth — from 13-Olin came rulers and speakers, but also lives marked by the earthquake's instability (Sahagún, Florentine Codex, Book IV). The calendar thus makes time itself the god's body: every day is a station of his road, every thirteen-day count a circuit of his house, and every human destiny a position measured against his movement. To be born under a day of the sun was to owe the sun a life.
